title: Survival Guide
disclaimer: **Important.** This guide contains general advice for emergencies, collected from open civil protection and first aid sources (the State Emergency Service, the Ministry of Health, the Red Cross, international first aid protocols). It does not replace professional medical help or the official instructions of the State Emergency Service, rescuers or doctors. In a real situation, always follow the instructions of official services when they are available. First aid skills are best practised on hands-on courses in advance — reading does not replace training. Medicine doses are given as a guide according to official protocols; where possible, check them against the medicine's leaflet.

**Review status:** in versions 2.2–2.3 facts, doses and numbers were checked against open official sources (Appendix D), but the guide has not been reviewed by a doctor, a deminer or a State Emergency Service specialist. Review is recommended before wide distribution: by a first aid instructor (chapters 7, 21, 22.5), a doctor (doses), and a State Emergency Service specialist or deminer (chapters 3–6). Knowledge about threats changes — check that it is up to date every 6–12 months.

intro.text: Survival is above all about making the right decisions in the right order. This chapter gives a system of priorities that works in any disaster, from war to flood.

blocks.text: A classic rule that sets priorities. On average, a person can survive:

cells: The very first priority is safe breathing and stopping bleeding
without protection from extreme cold or heat
Shelter and body temperature matter more than water and food
Water comes before food. Find and disinfect water every day
Hunger is unpleasant, but it does not kill quickly. Do not risk your life for food

blocks.text: **The main beginner's mistake:** under stress, people rush to look for food, while the real threat is hypothermia at night or dirty water. Always set priorities by the rule of three.

sections.title: The STOP method — how to get a clear head back

blocks.text: STOP is not for the seconds when the threat itself is killing you. If there is shelling, fire, smoke or rising water nearby, act first: drop to the ground, go to shelter, get out of the danger zone (sec. 1.4). Once you are relatively safe (in a shelter, outside the danger zone) or realise you are lost, stop and use STOP:

items.text: **S — Stop.** Don't fuss and don't run at random. Panic is the main killer. Sit down and take 10 slow breaths (breathe in for a count of 4, out for 6). This physiologically lowers adrenaline.
**T — Think.** What exactly happened? What is the immediate threat to life right now? Who is nearby and is everyone unhurt?
**O — Observe.** What do you have: belongings, water, people, shelter, weather, time until dark? Take an inventory of your pockets and bags.
**P — Plan.** Make a simple plan for the next few hours by priority: safety → medical help → shelter → water → signals → food. Do one step at a time.

blocks.text: What happens to the brain in a disaster

According to observations by British psychologist John Leach (the “10–80–10” model), in acute stress 70–80% of people freeze or act chaotically, about 10–15% panic, and only 10–15% act rationally. The aim of preparation is to get into the last group. This is achieved not by bravery but by **plans thought through in advance and practised actions**: under stress, the brain does what it has already rehearsed.
Practical self-control techniques

items.text: **Tactical breathing:** breathe in 4 sec — hold 4 sec — breathe out 4 sec — hold 4 sec. 4–6 cycles lower your pulse and bring back the ability to think.
**Micro-tasks:** in despair, don't think “how do I get through the winter”, think “right now I am fetching water”. A small task completed brings back a sense of control.

**The voice rule:** say out loud, to yourself and others, what you are doing (“I am checking that everyone is unhurt. Now we take the documents”). This structures the group's actions and drowns out panic.
**Routine:** in a long crisis, a strict daily routine (getting up, work, meals, sleep at the same times) is the best protection for the mind, especially for children.
**Caring for someone:** responsibility for a child, an older person or even an animal greatly increases the will to live.

blocks.text: **Signs of a dangerous state in yourself or others:** freezing for more than a few minutes, pointless repetitive actions, refusing water and food for more than a day, talk of “it's all hopeless”. Actions: warmth, a sweet drink, a simple task, constant contact by voice and touch. Do not leave the person alone.

sections.title: A universal order of actions in any disaster

items.text: **Immediate safety.** Get out of the danger zone: away from fire, rising water, the shelling zone, a cloud of smoke. Direction: from fire, smoke and gas — at right angles to the wind; from water — uphill to high ground (chapter 19).
**Check people.** Who is nearby? Massive bleeding, consciousness, breathing (chapter 7).
**Assess second-wave threats.** Aftershocks of an earthquake, repeat strikes during shelling, structural collapse, gas leaks, downed wires.

**Communication.** A short message to your family: “Alive, I am at [place], going to [where]”. Then save battery: power saving mode, minimal screen, no video. Airplane mode only when the charge is critical or there is no network anyway; then turn on connectivity on an agreed schedule (sec. 14.4) to get replies and alert signals.
**Resources.** Water, medicines, warm clothes, documents — if they can be taken without risk.
**Meeting point.** Move to your family's meeting place agreed in advance.

blocks.text: Make and print the plan together with all family members. Everyone should know it by heart.

items.text: **Meeting point no. 1** — near home (for example, a specific tree in the yard), if you have to leave the building.
**Meeting point no. 2** — within your district (a school, church, shop), if you cannot stay near home.
**Meeting point no. 3** — outside the city (relatives' village, a specific address), if you have to leave the city.
**Contact person** — a relative in another city/country whom everyone calls and passes information to if they cannot reach each other.
**Roles:** who takes the go-bag, who takes the children, who takes the pets, who turns off the gas and water.
**Paper copies:** phone numbers of all relatives and addresses of the meeting points — in everyone's pocket and in the go-bag (phones run out of battery).
**Practice:** every six months, walk the routes to the shelter and the meeting points on foot, by day and in the evening.

sections.title: Priorities for settling in during a long crisis

blocks.text: If a crisis lasts for weeks (occupation, blackout, destroyed infrastructure), divide your efforts like this:

cells: Shelter from shelling/weather, staying unnoticed, a back-up exit
4 L/person/day, of which 2 L disinfected drinking water
One warm room or sleeping place, dry clothes
First aid kit, a supply of regular medicines for 30+ days
Radio, a schedule for listening to the news
Getting to know neighbours, sharing out watches and skills

blocks.text: **Remember:** surviving alone is a myth. All real stories of long-term survival are stories of mutual help. A group with assigned roles (medic, cook, lookout, handyman) is many times more resilient than a loner.

intro.text: A go-bag is a backpack you can leave home with in 2 minutes and live on your own for at least 72 hours. It should be kept packed by the exit at all times.

items.text: **A backpack, not a bag:** your hands must be free. Volume 35–50 L per adult, weight no more than 20% of body weight (10–15 kg).
**One go-bag per person:** each adult has their own backpack with the full minimum, because the family may get separated.
**Waterproofing:** everything that water can damage (documents, matches, electronics, medicines) goes in zip bags.
**Rotation:** twice a year (for example, when the clocks change) check the expiry dates of food and medicines and the charge of power banks.
**Access:** the most needed items (torch, documents, first aid kit) go in the top pockets.

blocks.text: Documents and money (top pocket, in a waterproof bag)

items.text: Passport, ID card, international passport

Men aged 18–60 (and women on the military register) — a military registration document: paper, or a printout of the e-document from “Reserve+” with a QR code (valid for 1 year — renew it when you rotate the go-bag). During mobilisation it must be carried together with your passport and shown on request to the TCC (territorial recruitment centre), police or border guards; a phone can run out of battery, so keep a paper copy in the go-bag
Children's birth certificates, marriage certificate
Documents for housing and car; employment record book (or copies)
Medical documents: vaccination card, prescriptions, records of chronic illnesses
Photocopies of all documents in a separate bag + scans on a USB stick
Cash in small notes (enough for 1–2 weeks of living) + some in foreign currency
Bank cards, a paper list of relatives' phone numbers
Photos of family members (in case someone has to be searched for)

blocks.text: Water and food (for 3 days)

items.text: Water: 1.5–2 L in bottles — this is less than one day's worth (the minimum for drinking is 2 L/day, sec. 8.1); more is hard to carry, the rest you get on the way
Water disinfection: tablets or a filter straw
Food that needs no cooking: nuts, dried fruit, energy bars, hard crackers, tins with a ring pull, chocolate
Estimate: ~2000 kcal/day per adult
Metal mug or pot 0.7–1 L (can be used for boiling)
Spoon, folding knife, can opener

blocks.text: First aid kit (full contents in section 7.16)

items.text: Tourniquet, bandages, hemostatic agents
Personal medicines for 14–30 days (this is the most important thing!)
Painkillers, fever reducers, antiseptic, plasters
Remedies for diarrhoea and dehydration (oral rehydration salts)

blocks.text: Clothing and warmth

items.text: A change of underwear and socks (2–3 pairs, wool)
Thermal underwear (in winter), fleece top
Raincoat or poncho (also protects from wind)
Hat, gloves, buff (even in summer — nights are cold)
Emergency space blanket (2 pcs, silver, weighs 60 g)
Sturdy shoes already on your feet or tied to the backpack

blocks.text: Light, communication, tools

items.text: Head torch + spare batteries (AA/AAA are best, they are universal)
Power bank 10,000–20,000 mAh, charged, cables
Battery radio (FM/AM) — the main source of information in a blackout
Whistle (a signal under rubble — saves your voice)
Matches in waterproof packaging + 2 lighters + fire steel
Multitool or knife
Duct tape (5–10 m, can be wound around a bottle)
Rope/paracord 10–15 m
Needles, thread, safety pins
Notebook, pencil (writes in frost and when wet)
FFP2/FFP3 respirator mask (dust from destroyed buildings, smoke; does not protect against carbon monoxide)
Safety glasses or ordinary sunglasses

blocks.text: Hygiene

items.text: Wet wipes (2–3 packs — they replace a shower)
Hand sanitiser, soap in a soap box
Toothbrush, small toothpaste, toilet paper (without the core, flattened)
Feminine hygiene products, nappies for small children
Strong rubbish bags, 20 pcs (also: raincoat, insulation, collecting water)

blocks.text: Sleeping

items.text: Compact sleeping bag (comfort down to 0°C) or 2 space blankets + a blanket
Sit pad or full sleeping mat (insulation from the ground is critical)

cells: A favourite small toy, sweets, a note with the child's name and parents' phone numbers in a clothing pocket, a family photo. A child over 5 carries their own small backpack
Spare glasses, hearing aid + batteries, medicines for 30 days, walking stick, a paper list of diagnoses and doses
Formula, bottles, nappies for 3+ days, baby wet wipes, a sling (hands free)
Carrier, lead, food for 3 days, pet passport, water, folding bowl
Insulin + cooling case, blood pressure monitor, glucose meter, inhaler — depending on the diagnosis. Medicines for 30+ days

blocks.text: Everyday Carry is the minimum you carry every day in your pockets/bag, because a disaster will not wait until you reach your go-bag:

items.text: Phone + small power bank
ID document (or a copy), cash
Keyring torch, whistle
Folding knife or multitool (where allowed)

**A tourniquet (CAT/SOF-T, certified), a hemostatic bandage and a pair of nitrile gloves** — in wartime this is the core of EDC: massive bleeding kills within minutes, an ambulance will not arrive in time (sec. 7.2). Carry it so you can reach it with one hand; without practice a tourniquet is useless — practise putting it on yourself and on someone else
Plasters, your critical medicines for 1–2 days
Lighter

blocks.text: The go-bag is for evacuation. But in most crises it is safer to stay at home. For that you need home supplies:
Water

items.text: **Norm: 4 L per person per day** (2 L for drinking + 2 L for cooking and hygiene). A family of 3 for 2 weeks = ~170 L.
Storage: factory-sealed 5–6 L bottles (shelf life 6–12 months) or food-grade jerrycans with chlorine-disinfected water (replace every 6 months).
If the water supply may be cut off, fill the bath, all pots and bottles at once.

blocks.text: Food (example for 1 person for 2 weeks)

**Rotation principle:** buy what you usually eat, +20–30% above the norm. New items go to the back of the shelf, old ones to the front and into meals. This way your supply never expires and needs no separate money.
Other household items

items.text: Camping gas stove + 4–6 canisters (cooking without electricity/gas; only with a window open — carbon monoxide)
10+ candles, a kerosene lamp or LED camping lantern
AA/AAA batteries, 20 of each; charged power banks
10 boxes of matches in a jar with a lid
Thick plastic sheeting + duct tape (to cover broken windows, sealing)
Laundry soap, washing powder, chlorine bleach (plain “Bilyzna” bleach without fragrance or gel — both disinfection and water treatment, chapter 8)
2 buckets with lids (water, toilet)
Fire extinguisher; a box of sand if you have stove heating
Tools: crowbar/nail puller (to clear rubble, open doors), shovel, axe, hand saw

blocks.text: A smoke detector, a fire extinguisher and two exits also protect against one of the most common household causes of death: a house fire, sec. 10.5.

items.text: **Windows:** tape will not stop glass from breaking, but it will hold the shards together — and it is the shards that injure. One big cross hardly works: tape over as much area as possible (a dense grid of tape, a solid protective film or strips of fabric glued on with paste) and the frames around the edges. Best of all is shatter-resistant film. Plus thick curtains, and the main rule: do not be near a window during an alert. Sleep no closer than 2 m to a window; during massive attacks, in the two-wall zone (sec. 3.3).
**Shutting off utilities:** every adult should know where and how to shut off the gas, water and electricity (circuit breakers). Label the valves with a marker.
**Safe room:** an inner room without windows (hallway, bathroom, storeroom) — by the two-wall rule (chapter 3).
**Fire safety:** a fire extinguisher in the kitchen, a smoke detector, a planned escape route from every room.
**Spare keys** — with a trusted neighbour; agree to check on each other's homes.

intro.text: The main killers during shelling are not direct hits but fragments, the blast wave and glass. Two things save you from them: the right shelter and fast reaction.

sections.title: Types of threats and reaction time

cells: Whistling, rustling before the explosion; series of explosions
Get down at once, then crawl to shelter
Alert 20–60 min ahead; a loud rising sound
To shelter by the two-wall rule or to a basement
A “ballistic” alert — and an explosion almost at once
Do not run across the city: go at once to the nearest two-wall zone. At night, already sleep in it (sec. 3.3)
Piston ones — a “moped” drone hum, they fly in straight lines in waves at night; jet ones — a turbine whistle, 300–700 km/h, much shorter warning
Minutes to tens of minutes; jet ones — minutes
Do not look out of the window, do not shine lights, go to shelter at once (jet drones are harder to shoot down — go to shelter, not “to have a look”). Debris after a shoot-down falls over kilometres
**FPV drones and drop drones** (frontline zone 30–40 km)
Buzzing, the drone hovers or follows; there is no alert
A roof over your head (building entrance, bus shelter, basement), do not run in a straight line — chapter 4
Alert, sound of an aircraft; impact without a whistle
**The two-wall rule does not work**: only a below-ground shelter (basement, parking garage, metro). It destroys a whole stairwell section of the building
A flash and a long wave, fire over an area
A below-ground shelter with openings closed: the wave and the burning-off of oxygen go into open vents and windows
A series of small explosions over an area
Lie down; afterwards do not touch “bells”/“darts” the size of a battery: up to 30% do not explode at once (chapter 5)

Get down behind **solid** cover: concrete, a kerb, an earth bank. A car body is **not** cover — a bullet goes straight through doors and glass; only the engine block stops it, so drop behind a wheel on the engine side. Do not stay near the car: it draws fire — crawl away

blocks.text: **Rule:** if you hear a whistle or a rising sound — do NOT look at the sky and do not run. Drop to the ground WHERE YOU ARE, face down, feet toward the blast, mouth slightly open (protects the eardrums and lungs from the wave), hands covering your head and neck.

blocks.caption: Fig. 3.1. Position during sudden shelling in the open

blocks.text: If there is no proper shelter, the safest place in a flat is found by the two-wall rule: there must be **at least two load-bearing walls** between you and the street. The first wall takes the hit and fragments, the second stops the secondary fragments from the first.

blocks.caption: Fig. 3.2. The two-wall rule: safe zones of a flat (green) — hallway and bathroom without windows

items.text: Best places: hallway, bathroom, storeroom, the space **under** load-bearing stairs.

Avoid: rooms with windows, balconies, lifts, stair flights and stairwells with glazing — it is dangerous to stand **on** the stairs, not **under** them: flights collapse first and stairwells have glass, while the space under a concrete flight is one of the strongest spaces in the building; top floors (a drone or missile comes in from above — into the roof and top flats); lower floors are safer by the two-wall rule (sec. 3.4).
Prepare windows in advance: board them up with plywood or corrugated sheet; if you have none, with thick cardboard and rugs. This reduces flying glass and fragments.
Keep in the “safe zone” at all times: water, a blanket, a torch, a power bank, a first aid kit, a sleeping mat or stools.
A cast-iron bath gives extra protection from fragments — in a critical situation you can lie in it, covered with a blanket/mattress.

sections.title: What to do when the air raid alert sounds

items.text: Dress for the weather (even at night — shoes and a jacket), take your go-bag.
If there is time (the alert is not “ballistic”) — turn off the gas, electrical appliances and water, close the windows and curtains.

Go to the shelter you chose in advance. If it is more than 5 minutes' walk away and explosions can already be heard, or a ballistic threat has been announced — stay in the two-wall zone: crossing the city is more dangerous.
In the shelter: do not sit opposite the door; stay closer to load-bearing columns and walls.

Leave only after the all-clear. After a series of explosions, a repeat strike on the same place is possible 10–40 min later, and sometimes 1–2 hours later (when rescuers gather) — do not run to the scene at once “to have a look”.
Artillery or mortar fire without a siren: stay in the shelter at least 40 min after the last explosion — shelling often resumes.

blocks.text: “Ballistic nights”: how to live for months under night attacks

items.text: During massive attacks, ballistic missiles give 1–3 minutes, and the blast wave and glass are the main killers in flats. The solution is to **sleep in the two-wall zone** rather than run every night: a mattress in the hallway, a cot in the bathroom, a “bed” from a sleeping mat for older people.
Keep next to where you sleep at all times: shoes, a jacket, a torch, a phone on charge, water, the go-bag. This removes 90% of the panic.
Do not go to the window “to look” at an explosion or at air defence at work: a second missile or debris arrives within seconds.

In alert apps, tell the types of threats apart: “ballistic” = to the two-wall zone at once; “drones” = there is usually time, you can reach a shelter, but jet drones arrive within minutes (sec. 4.7); “MiG-31K takeoff” = a “Kinzhal” threat across the whole country, the alert sounds in all regions, including far from the front: do not wait for a launch report — go to shelter at once while you have a few minutes; after a launch is reported, the missile arrives in 2–7 minutes — do not run along the street any more, go to the two-wall zone at once; “tactical aviation / KAB threat” — in frontline regions, only a below-ground shelter (basement, parking garage), the two-wall rule does not save you from a KAB.

Sleep: agree on one person “on duty” for the night who listens to alerts for everyone — the rest sleep (sec. 21.5). Chronic lack of sleep over weeks damages health and judgement worse than one sleepless night.

sections.title: Choosing a shelter (from best to worst)

cells: The best option if it is close
Basement of a solid building with 2 exits

Check in advance: ventilation, 2 exits, no gas pipes overhead. Basements of prefab panel blocks and Soviet five-storey blocks (khrushchovky) do not count: the floors fold, the basements are narrow and not sealed
When there is no time or no basement
In the open: a ditch, roadside ditch, crater, low ground
Fragments (they fly upward from the ground)
Lie below ground level; a crater is fine simply as a hollow; “lightning never strikes the same crater twice” is a myth

blocks.text: **Never take cover:** under lorries or cars (fuel tank, thin metal), near shop windows and glass facades, under trees (fragments bring down branches; against drones it is the opposite, sec. 4.3), near petrol stations, transformers, gas pipes.

sections.title: If your building is hit / you are under rubble

blocks.text: You are indoors near an explosion

items.text: Make sure there is no gas leak (smell, hissing). If there is — do not turn on lights and do not light a flame, open the windows, get out.
Check yourself and your family for injuries — under stress, wounds do not hurt (chapter 7).
Leave by the stairs, not the lift. Shoes are a must (glass everywhere).
Grab the go-bag and documents if it takes seconds, not minutes.

blocks.text: You are under rubble

items.text: Do not panic, do not waste strength on chaotic movements. Breathe evenly, through fabric if there is dust.
Do not light a flame (there may be gas). Do not move the structures above you.
Reinforce your space: if you can, prop up the slab above you with pieces of furniture.
Knock metal on metal/concrete in series of 3 knocks — pause — again. Rescuers regularly announce “minutes of silence” and listen.
Shout only when you hear people very close — your voice goes within an hour, and dust gets into your lungs. A whistle carries much further and does not strain your voice.
Drink water, if you have any, in small sips. People have survived under rubble for 5–10 days — the main things are air and staying calm.

blocks.text: Someone is under rubble nearby

items.text: Mark the place the sound comes from. Call people over, call rescuers (101).

The official advice of DSNS is **not to clear rubble yourself**: structures may shift and hurt both you and the person under them. Wait for rescuers, talk to the person, pass them water if it is safe.
Only if help really cannot be reached: clear from the top by hand, small pieces, do not pull out large elements — everything may shift.

If a person's limb has been crushed for more than 10 minutes (if the person is unconscious or the time is unknown, assume it has been longer) — do NOT free it yourself if medics can actually arrive: call 103 at once and follow the dispatcher's instructions. Sudden release can cause fatal crush syndrome (toxins from crushed muscles). If it has been crushed for less than 10 minutes — free it at once. If help cannot be reached or you must evacuate urgently — give the person fluids (rehydration solution, sec. 7.10), keep them warm, free them and get them to medics as fast as possible. A tourniquet is a must with massive bleeding (sec. 7.2). Guidance on crush syndrome differs: the current Ministry of Health protocol (order No. 441) says that when you have to free the person yourselves and the crushing has lasted more than 10 min, apply a tourniquet above the crushed area before freeing; military TCCC guidance advises this for crushing over 2 hours if no IV drip is available; some international guidelines (ANZCOR) do not routinely require a tourniquet. So: if you have a connection — ask the 103 dispatcher and do as they say. No connection, long crushing, you have a tourniquet — apply it right before freeing, write down the time, do not remove or loosen it yourself: medics will do that. No tourniquet — do not delay freeing because of it when help cannot be reached.

sections.title: Shelling in the street, in transport, in a field

items.text: **In a city street:** drop, then move in short dashes (3–5 sec — count in your head and drop, do not run longer) from cover to cover: concrete steps, a building's base, an underpass.
**In a car:** stop, get out, run 30–50 m from the road, lie in the roadside ditch. A car is a magnet for fragments and no protection.
**On public transport:** the driver stops the vehicle; get out and lie in low ground away from it.
**In a field/forest:** lie in any hollow. Do not hide in isolated buildings and tree lines that are obvious landmarks and targets.

**Shooting or an explosion indoors (station, shopping centre, shelter):** the “run — hide — fight” rule. Run — if the way is clear, without gathering belongings, hands visible, showing others the direction. Hide — lock/barricade the door, silence your phone, lie behind something solid, keep quiet. Fight — only as a last resort, all together, with anything at hand. When you meet police at the exit — hands up, empty, follow commands.

sections.title: Living in a shelter for a long time

items.text: Space per person: at least 1 place to lie or sit + a passage. Sleeping mats and blankets — concrete draws out heat.
Ventilation: air the space during lulls; a candle going out is a sign of lack of oxygen.
Share out duties: who listens to the radio, who watches the children, who looks after the water.
Toilet: a bucket with a lid + bags + bleach or cat litter; a screen made from a blanket.
Children's mental health: toys, tasks, roles (“you are in charge of the torch”). A calm adult voice is the main “medicine”.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 4
chapters.title: Drones: the new main threat to civilians

intro.text: Within 30–40 km of the front line, drones kill more civilians than artillery: they see an individual person, chase cars, drop grenades on a queue for water, come back to finish off rescuers. There are no alerts for them. The survival rules here are different from those for shelling — and everyone needs to know them, because drone range grows every year, and this zone grows with it.

sections.title: Types of drones and how to recognise them

cells: A small quadcopter, buzzing like a large hornet; flies fast (up to 100+ km/h), manoeuvres sharply, can “hover” and look around
Flies into the target and explodes: a car, a person, a window, a basement door. The operator sees through the drone's “eyes”
The same, but trails a thin glass-fibre line behind it (it stays on the ground, trees, wires)
Cannot be jammed by any EW (electronic warfare) — the signal goes along the line. This is the most dangerous type
Hovers high up, quiet or inaudible; by day — a dark dot in the sky
Drops grenades/mines on people, cars, basement entrances. Often twice on the same spot
Circles at height, for a long time, without attacking
Looks for groups of people and vehicles — artillery or an FPV comes after it
Sounds like a moped, flies straight at a height of 1–3 km, usually in waves at night
Strikes infrastructure and cities hundreds of kilometres away; an alert is announced in advance
A turbine whistle instead of a “moped”, speed 300–700 km/h (2–4 times faster than an ordinary “Shahed”), warhead 50–130 kg

The main threat of winter 2026–2027: according to intelligence, up to 500 launches a day; harder to shoot down, the time from alert to impact is minutes, so a “drone” alert no longer means “there is time”
**Autonomous / swarms** (a threat of the coming years)
Several drones acting together; guidance without an operator, by the image of the target
Do not react to EW and do not get “distracted”; attack anything that looks like a target (a car, a group of people)

blocks.text: **The main rule:** if you heard or saw a drone — assume it sees you. Your task is to be, within 5–10 seconds, somewhere with a roof or a thick wall over your head, and freeze. Do not look at it, do not film it on your phone, do not wave your arms.

sections.title: Four things that make you a target

items.text: **Movement and groups.** A group of people, a queue, a convoy of cars, machinery at work, rescuers gathering at a strike site — all of this “lights up” for the operator. Walk alone or in twos, 20–30 m apart; do not gather in the open.

**A car.** In the frontline zone a car is target no. 1 for FPVs. Especially: driving at dusk and at night with headlights on (the camera sees them kilometres away), stopping in the open, several cars together.

**Heat and light at night.** Thermal-imaging drones see body heat, campfires, a generator, a warmed-up car, smoke. A Dakota fire pit (sec. 10.3), cooking in daytime, a space blanket as a screen, a generator under a canopy — these are now camp camouflage rules.

**Repeat strike.** Drones wait until people run up to a wounded person or a hit car, and strike a second time. For at least 40 minutes after a strike (sometimes 1–2 hours), approach the site only in short dashes from cover to cover, or wait altogether.

sections.title: You are outside and heard/saw a drone

items.text: **A roof over your head** — a building entrance, basement, shop, a bus shelter with a concrete roof, an archway, a garage. This rule is only for FPVs and drop drones (a small charge): during strikes by Shaheds, missiles or artillery, entrances, archways and stairs are not shelter (collapse), you need a basement or two walls (chapter 3). An FPV can fly in through an open door, window or breach (especially a fibre-optic one — it does not lose its link inside a building), so do not stop in the doorway: once inside, shut the door behind you, move away from windows and glass, deeper in, round a corner — into a hallway, under load-bearing stairs or into a basement, so that there are two walls between you and the street. A lone tree or a fence does not protect you: the drone flies around them. But if there is no roof nearby, dense bushes, thickets or a tree belt are better than open ground: a drone cannot fly into a thicket, and if it explodes on the branches you may be wounded, but your chances of surviving are much higher. Get in as deep as you can, lie down and freeze; as soon as the drone is gone or has exploded, move under a roof.

No roof: **do not run in a straight line** and do not try to “dash across” an open area — a drone is faster than anyone. Hide behind something THICK (concrete, a brick wall, a tree trunk over 40 cm thick) and **switch sides of the cover** as the drone circles, so the obstacle stays between you.

An FPV attacks (dives): at the last second — move sharply aside and drop to the ground behind an obstacle, face down, hands on your head (as during shelling, sec. 3.1). An FPV blast is relatively small — 30–50 cm of obstacle saves you.

A drop drone hovers above you: do not stand still and do not look up — quickly get under a roof or at least under a tree with a dense canopy (a canopy gives some protection from a drop, unlike from an FPV), then further on, under concrete.

There is no roof nearby and a drop drone is already above you: move quickly in a zigzag, changing direction every 7–10 m — this makes it harder for the operator to hit you with a drop. This does not work against an FPV: only an obstacle saves you there.
Afterwards — do not come out at once. Count to 60, listen: a second one often comes. Do not go near the strike site itself for at least 40 min (sec. 4.2).

If you know the area has drones — drive only in daytime, without headlights, fast, without stopping in the open, with windows open (to hear the buzzing), at least 100 m from other cars. Do not lock the doors.

Heard or saw a drone: brake hard — everyone out of the car — scatter 30–50 m from the car behind cover (the target is the car; while you are near it, you are a target too). Do not try to “escape” at speed on a straight road — an FPV catches up.
If there is a roof nearby (a bridge, a concrete canopy, an archway, a garage; not a petrol station — fuel and a target), it is better to drive under it than to stay where you are.
Anti-drone nets on the body, “cope cages” (“mangals”) help only against small FPVs and drops, not against large munitions; do not rely on them instead of behaviour.
Plan an evacuation route out of a drone zone along roads with trees on both sides and buildings, not along an open highway (chapter 26).

sections.title: At home and in the yard

items.text: Windows closed, curtains thick; go out onto the balcony and into the yard briefly, not for hours.

Entrances to basements and buildings — under a protective canopy or net: in frontline towns, nets over yards and bus stops have proven effective against FPVs and drops. Working together with neighbours — chapter 17.
Queues for water/aid — only under a roof or spread out; agree on a “sky watcher” who listens and looks while the others fetch water.
Cooking and the generator — in daytime, under a canopy; at night, no light outside at all.
Children: the rule “it buzzes — we run under a roof” as a game; outside only with an adult, no further than 20 m from shelter.

**Do not approach.** Munitions may still be on board (self-detonation minutes later or when touched), and a drop drone may have grenades not yet dropped. At least 100 m (DSNS: 100–300 m), preferably behind cover. Call only from a safe distance, not next to the object: 101, 102 or 112, or tell the military. Do not take close-up photos and do not post photos with geolocation.
**Fibre-optic line** on the ground, trees, wires — do not touch it with your hands (it cuts skin like glass) and do not wind it up; if the drone is still on the line, it may come back. Go around it.
Debris of Shaheds shot down by air defence falls kilometres from where they were hit and burns; do not collect it “as a souvenir” — fuel and explosive residue.

Do not try to shoot down a drone yourself with a hunting gun — this signals to the operator that a civilian is armed and is a reason for the next strike; besides, it is legal only for the military and authorised persons.

sections.title: Long-range drones over cities far from the front

items.text: Alerts for Shaheds last for hours and come in waves; strikes hit energy facilities, warehouses and residential areas near them. Jet drones arrive within minutes of the alert and are much harder to shoot down — act as for ballistic missiles: straight to the two-wall zone or a shelter. The main danger is air defence debris and the blast wave: **stay away from windows**, in the two-wall zone (sec. 3.2). Do not film or post air defence at work (chapter 18).
A drone flies low and loud — it is not “hunting” you personally, but a drone with a warhead falling after being shot down is equal to a bomb: go to shelter, not onto the balcony.
Debris in the yard — call 101, do not touch.
Report every drone you see (101, 102, the chatbots of your region's Regional Military Administration / Armed Forces of Ukraine — write them down on paper in advance). This saves others.
Use your region's official monitoring channels, not hearsay: fake “drone maps” and rumours are a weapon too (chapter 18).
In the frontline zone, agree with neighbours on a sound signal for “drone over the yard” (a whistle, banging on a pipe) — faster than any messenger app.

intro.text: Mines and unexploded ordnance kill for years after the fighting. The only reliable tactic for a civilian: DO NOT touch, DO NOT approach, mark, report.

items.text: Former battle sites, trenches, dugouts, abandoned positions and vehicles.
Roadsides, turn-offs from the asphalt, paths that go around checkpoints.
Tree belts, fields (especially unploughed), riverbanks, fords.
Abandoned buildings, basements, gates, wickets — tripwires are possible.
Attractive objects: toys, phones, wallets, boxes — they may be booby traps.
After shelling — any “cluster” elements the size of a battery or a small ball: 10–30% of submunitions do not explode at once.

blocks.text: **The golden rule:** an object that was not here yesterday, or an object that looks military = an explosive hazard. There is no such thing as a “safe” mine. Demining is only for sappers.

blocks.caption: Fig. 5.1. Official and improvised markings of mined areas

blocks.text: Both the military and locals leave informal markings: ribbons on branches, cans on stakes, crosses made of branches, rows of stones across a path. **Any unclear “marking” = go around that place.**

sections.title: You have found a suspicious object

items.text: **Stop.** Do not come closer, do not bend over, do not touch, do not take close-up photos.
**Remember landmarks** of the place (a building, a tree, a pole).
**Leave the same way you came** — step by step in your own footprints.
**Mark** the danger once you are at a safe distance — where you moved back to (bright cloth, ribbon, a branch). Do not go up to the object itself to fence it off.
**Report:** 101 (DSNS) or 102. Describe the place and what the object looks like. Warn passers-by.
Safe distance: at least 100 m from small objects, 300+ m from shells and aerial bombs. Do not use a radio or phone near the object — call once you have moved 100+ m away.

sections.title: You realise you have walked into a minefield

items.text: FREEZE. Do not take a single step. Call for help with your voice.
If help is possible — stand/sit where you are and wait for sappers. This is the safest option, even if you have to wait for hours.
If there is no one to wait for: turn around on the spot without stepping, and go back EXACTLY in your own footprints, stepping in each print.

If footprints cannot be seen and no help will come at all (no connection, no one knows where you are, no one can hear your voice) — only then, as a last resort with a very high risk: **(a)** first look for tripwires: hold a long flexible blade of grass or a thin twig horizontally with two fingers and slowly move it from the ground up to ~1.5 m — to the left, in the centre, to the right; if you feel the slightest resistance — stop, do not touch the wire, do not step over it or cut it, look for another direction; **(b)** only after that, with a sharp rigid object (a screwdriver, knife, pen; at least 10 cm long), probe the ground at an angle of ~30° to the ground with minimal pressure every 2–3 cm across the whole width of the path (about 0.5 m), the next row 3–5 cm further on; work on your knees, lie down only on an area already checked; **(c)** if the probe hits something hard — do not press and do not dig, mark the spot and go around it. Move only along the checked strip; getting out may take hours. The UN recommends this method only for trained people: it is better to sit where you are for two days than to be blown up.

An explosion nearby: do not run straight to the wounded person — the approach may also be mined. Call sappers; the wounded person, if conscious, applies a tourniquet to themselves following your instructions (chapter 7). After a mine blast injury, the wounded person must be taken to hospital within an hour.
Learn a simple rule with your child: “**Not mine — I don't touch. I see something strange — I move away and tell adults**”.
Do not play: in abandoned buildings, trenches, near military vehicles, with any “toys” you find, shiny and unusual objects.
Agree on this: reporting a find earns only praise, never scolding (otherwise children will hide things).

sections.title: Threats of the next decade: “butterfly” mines, drone-dropped mines, returning home

items.text: **PFM-1 “butterfly” mines (“pelyustka”)** — green/brown plastic “butterflies” 12 cm long with a wing, scattered by cluster munitions over towns and fields; they lie for decades and go off under a pressure of only about 5 kg — a child's step (it tears off the foot). Do not pick them up even “as a souvenir” — they react to pressure. Especially dangerous for children and after floods, which carry them.

**Mines dropped by drones** on roads and paths: TM-62 anti-tank mines and “butterfly” mines appear overnight where it was clear yesterday. The rule of “an object that was not here yesterday” now applies to roads too: do not drive around on the verge — go back along your own track, report, do not “kick it off the road”.
**Fires and floods move mines:** after a forest fire or a flood, treat previously “safe” areas as mined until sappers have checked them.
**Demining will take more than 10 years.** Fields, roadsides and forests in the former combat zone are dangerous by default: walk only along checked routes, follow the DSNS mine contamination maps.

blocks.text: Returning to a de-occupied or abandoned home

items.text: Do not go in first: call sappers (101). In abandoned houses, traps are set on doors, gates, cupboards, fridges, toilets, books, toys, bodies of the dead, household appliances.

If you cannot wait for sappers: inspect the outside from a distance — wires, fishing line, new “objects” by the threshold, a door suspiciously left ajar. Open doors with a long rope from behind cover.
Inside: move slowly, look at your feet and at knee level, do not pick anything up, do not turn on electricity (traps on switches), do not move objects that are “not lying right”.
If you find anything suspicious — leave the same way, call 101.

blocks.text: **Weapons or ammunition found:** do not touch them, even “to hand them in”. Mark the place, report to 102/101. There will be more weapons in circulation after the war — teach children to treat them like a mine.

intro.text: Radiation and most chemical warfare agents cannot be seen or heard. Three principles save you: time (less exposure), distance (further from the source), barrier (walls, sealing, respiratory protection).

items.text: **Go indoors** — at once. Best: a basement or the middle of a multi-storey building (brick/concrete weakens radiation by 10–100+ times).
**Seal yourself in:** close windows, doors, ventilation, chimneys. Gaps — with wet towels, tape, plastic sheeting.

**If you were outside:** take off your outer clothing BEFORE entering the living area, put it in a bag and take it far away. Take a shower with soap (do not scrub the skin hard), wash your hair without conditioner (it holds particles in).
**Listen to official announcements** (battery radio). Do not go out until the authorities say so.
**Water and food:** only from closed containers, tinned food, bottled water. Do not consume milk from local animals, leafy greens, mushrooms.
If you must go outside: covered clothing, do not undress, do not sit on the ground, do not swim in open water, do not pick mushrooms and berries, do not smoke.
**Evacuation** — only on the authorities' command, at right angles to the wind direction relative to the source.

sections.title: Iodine prophylaxis — only the right way

blocks.text: **Potassium iodide protects ONLY the thyroid gland from radioactive iodine and ONLY if there has been a release from a reactor. It does not protect against external radiation or other isotopes.** Take it only after an official announcement, 6 hours before or in the first hours after the cloud passes. Do NOT drink alcoholic iodine solution — that is poisoning.

cells: Not prescribed (the thyroid gland hardly accumulates radioiodine any more; the risk outweighs the benefit). **Exception:** pregnant and breastfeeding women take 125 mg at any age

blocks.text: Taken once after a meal, washed down with water/milk/kysil (a thickened fruit drink). A repeat dose only on official instruction during a prolonged release. Potassium iodide protects only against radioactive iodine (nuclear power plant accident, nuclear explosion); it is not taken after a “dirty bomb”. Doses follow the Regulations on iodine prophylaxis (order of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine of 09.03.2021 No. 408); if the official announcement gives other doses, follow it.

sections.title: Improvised protection for breathing and body

items.text: An FFP2/FFP3 respirator is the minimum against radioactive dust. None — 4–8 layers of damp gauze/fabric over the nose and mouth.
Body: thick clothing with long sleeves, a raincoat/plastic sheeting on top, a hood, gloves, rubber footwear. Tape over cuffs and joins.
Eyes: any close-fitting glasses (swimming goggles are ideal).
After coming back: everything outer goes in a bag outside the door, then a shower.

blocks.text: Signs of chemical contamination

items.text: Unexplained fog, smoke or a cloud that creeps along the ground; oily drops/stains on surfaces.
Sharp smells (ammonia, chlorine — a “swimming pool” smell, “bitter almonds”, “freshly cut grass”, garlic) where they should not be.
Dead birds, insects, animals in a small area; people with the same symptoms: watering eyes, coughing, choking, seizures, constricted pupils.

blocks.text: **Tear agents (CS, chloropicrin)** are increasingly used away from the front too. Burning eyes and skin, choking without loss of consciousness — that is them: go upwind into fresh air, do not rub your eyes, rinse with water/saline for 10–15 min, take off and bag your clothes, wash skin with cool water and soap (hot water makes the burning worse), throw away contact lenses. People with asthma — use the inhaler. Go to a medic at once (103) if shortness of breath, chest tightness or a strong cough do not pass within 30 min in fresh air, get worse or come back within a day: chloropicrin damages the lungs, and pulmonary oedema can develop with a delay of several hours, even if you felt better at first. For the first day — rest, no physical exertion, do not stay alone.
Actions

items.text: Hold your breath, cover your nose and mouth with fabric (preferably damp — for chlorine, soak it in a baking soda solution, for ammonia in a weak solution of vinegar/citric acid — or at least in water).

**Go at right angles to the wind** and UPHILL if the gas is heavier than air (chlorine creeps low) — that is, not into a basement! Ammonia, on the contrary, is lighter — then the lower floors. If you do not know the substance: simply get away at right angles to the wind as fast and as far as possible.
Indoors: close windows, turn off ventilation, seal gaps with wet fabric; go up to the upper floors (for chlorine) — and listen for announcements.
Do not eat or drink anything that may have been exposed to the chemical until it is confirmed safe.
Once out of the zone: take off your outer clothing (not over your head — cut it off if possible), rinse your skin and eyes with plenty of clean water for 10–15 min.
For those affected — rest, fresh air, a half-sitting position if they are choking. Do not induce vomiting if the substance is unknown. Medical help — as soon as possible.
Choose a room with as few windows as possible (for chlorine — on an upper floor).
Close windows and doors, turn off extractor fans and air conditioning, close stove dampers.
Tape/seal with plastic the window frames, ventilation grilles, sockets on outer walls, the keyhole.
A wet towel rolled up under the door. A supply of water and a radio — inside. Drink only water from closed containers stored in advance: boiling does not remove radioactive substances.
Remember: a fully sealed room holds enough air for a few hours per person. Watch how you feel; do not light a candle.

sections.title: Nuclear explosion: the protocol that saves most people

blocks.text: The probability is low, the cost of a mistake is the highest. The main thing to know: most of those killed more than 3–5 km from ground zero die not from the explosion itself but from **radioactive fallout in the first hours** — and that is exactly what you can shelter from.

items.text: **Flash** (brighter than the sun, even by day): do NOT look at it (blindness). Drop face down behind any cover at once, feet toward the flash, cover your head and exposed skin (the light radiation burns within seconds). The blast wave will arrive a few seconds later — up to 30–60 sec at a distance of 10–20 km. Stay down until it has passed and debris has stopped falling.

**10–15 minutes** after the explosion is your time to reach the best shelter within 5–10 minutes' walk: **a basement or the middle of a large concrete/brick building**, as far as possible from outer walls and the roof. The more concrete and earth between you and the sky, the better. A car, a wooden house, upper floors do not protect. Do not run across the whole city “to the children”: it is better to survive the first hours and meet afterwards — agree on this in advance.

**In the shelter — at least 24 hours, better 48–72.** Fallout radioactivity drops rapidly: 10 times after 7 hours, 100 times after 2 days (the “7–10” rule). Take off your outer clothing into a bag outside the door, wipe yourself with a damp cloth, wash your hair, nose, ears. Water and food — only from closed containers. A battery radio is the main source of instructions.

**Potassium iodide** (table 6.2) — only if the authorities announce iodine prophylaxis; it protects only the thyroid gland from radioiodine, not from external radiation from fallout. An FFP2 respirator/fabric in several layers — against breathing in dust.

**Leaving** — on the authorities' instruction, or after 48–72 hours if there is no information: briefly, at right angles to the wind, in covered clothing, to organised points. Nausea and vomiting in the first hours after exposure are a sign of radiation sickness — get to medics urgently.

blocks.text: **A household dosimeter** (from ~$100) in the go-bag is the only way to know whether water, food and the street are safe: without it you are blind. Normal background radiation in Ukraine is up to 0.3 µSv/h; above 1–2 µSv/h — limit your time there; above 10 — go to shelter at once or leave the zone.

intro.text: In an emergency, an ambulance may not come. These protocols are a civilian adaptation of modern first aid standards. Reading is not enough: find a chance to take a hands-on course.

blocks.text: **Before you help — SAFETY:** look around. Is shelling still going on? A live wire? Gas? Fire? A dead hero saves no one. First remove the threat or move the injured person (and yourself) into shelter.

sections.title: Order of assessment: the MARCH algorithm

blocks.text: The international order of trauma care follows the letters MARCH, from the fastest causes of death to the slower ones:

cells: Massive bleeding (a pool of blood, soaked clothing, a pulsing spurt)
Tourniquet / wound packing / pressure on the wound — IMMEDIATELY (sec. 7.2)
Tilt the head back, push the jaw forward; if vomiting — onto the side (sec. 7.4)
Circulation, shock (pallor, cold sweat, fast weak pulse)
Stop all bleeding, lay the person down, keep warm (sec. 7.6)
Insulate from the ground, cover; monitor consciousness

blocks.text: Losing 1.5–2 L of blood is fatal; from a damaged femoral artery that takes 2–4 minutes. Actions in order of priority:
Step 1: Direct pressure

Press on the wound with all your weight through cloth/a bandage (if there is nothing — with bare hands). Do not let go. In 80% of cases, strong continuous pressure for 10+ minutes stops the bleeding. But if blood is spurting from an arm or leg — do not wait, apply a tourniquet at once (step 2).
Step 2: Tourniquet — if it is a limb and blood is "spurting" or pressure does not help

blocks.caption: Fig. 7.1. Applying a tourniquet to a limb

items.text: Apply the tourniquet 5–8 cm above the wound (between the wound and the heart), not on a joint. If the wound location is unclear under clothing and blood is flowing heavily — as high on the limb as possible ("high and tight").
Pull the strap tight, then turn the windlass until the bleeding stops COMPLETELY and there is no pulse below the tourniquet.
Secure the windlass. **Write down the time** of application with a marker on the tourniquet/forehead/hand of the injured person (for example "T 14:25").

A tourniquet is NOT loosened "to let the blood flow" — that is a myth that kills. Only a medic removes or converts it. The time is written down for the medics — once it is applied, you do not need to do anything with the tourniquet, no matter how much time passes.

No factory-made tourniquet: **direct pressure on the wound** with both hands and all your weight, or wound packing (step 3) — and hold until the medics arrive. An improvised tourniquet (cloth 5+ cm wide and a stick as a windlass) is a last resort when pressure and packing have not worked: without training it usually does not stop the bleeding and wastes time. Wire, a shoelace, a belt — never. There is only one reliable answer: carry a factory-made tourniquet (sec. 2.4).

blocks.text: Step 3: Wound packing — for wounds of the neck, groin, buttocks, shoulders (where a tourniquet is impossible) and for deep limb wounds if there is no tourniquet

items.text: Find the point in the wound where the blood is spurting from and press it with your finger right in the depth of the wound.
Tightly, layer by layer, pack the wound with a bandage (preferably hemostatic) without releasing pressure. Fill the whole cavity.
On top — pressure with both hands for 3 minutes (with hemostatic gauze) or 10 minutes (plain bandage).
A tight bandage over it. Do not remove the packing — only in hospital.

blocks.text: Pressure bandage (moderate bleeding)
A pad made from a bandage — right on the wound, bandage it tightly, crossing over the pad. If it soaks through — do not remove it, add another layer on top.

sections.title: Checking consciousness and calling for help

items.text: Speak loudly, gently shake the shoulders: "Can you hear me?"

No response — check breathing: tilt the head back (palm on the forehead, fingers lift the chin), for 10 seconds watch the chest, listen with your ear and feel the breath with your cheek near the mouth.
Call 103 (or give the task to a specific person: "You, in the blue jacket — call 103, then come back and tell me!").
Breathing — recovery position (sec. 7.4). Not breathing or only occasional "gasps" — CPR (sec. 7.7).

blocks.caption: Fig. 7.2. Recovery position for an unconscious person who is breathing

items.text: Move the person's arm nearest to you out at a right angle, upwards (palm up).
Place the far arm with the back of the hand against their cheek on your side, and hold it there.
Bend the far leg at the knee, pull the knee towards you — the person will roll onto their side.
Tilt the head back for breathing; the mouth faces the ground. The upper knee acts as a prop.
Check breathing every minute. Every 30 min — turn the person onto the other side (if the wait is long).

blocks.text: **Do not use** if a spinal injury is suspected (fall from height, road crash, blow to the back) — then leave the person on their back, hold the head still by hand and push the jaw forward so the tongue does not block breathing; if this does not help or vomiting starts — log-roll them (three people, keeping the head-neck-torso line straight).

items.text: **Penetrating chest wound** (air whistling, frothy blood): cover it with your palm at once, then with an airtight (occlusive) seal or plastic film/a bag stuck down with tape. If the condition suddenly gets worse after sealing (increasing breathlessness) — peel back one edge, let the air out, stick it down again. Position: half-sitting or lying on the injured side.

**Abdominal wound with protruding organs:** do NOT push them back. Cover with a clean damp cloth, film on top, a loose bandage. Knees bent. Give nothing to drink or eat (moistening the lips is allowed).
**Object stuck in the wound** (knife, fragment): do NOT pull it out. Surround it with rolled bandages, secure it, transport as is.

blocks.text: Signs: pallor, cold clammy sweat, thirst, fast weak pulse (over 100), confusion, yawning. Actions:

items.text: Stop all bleeding (this is the main "medicine" for shock).
Lay the person flat; if there are no head/chest/abdominal injuries — raise the legs slightly (on a backpack).
Insulate from below and cover from above (emergency blanket, clothes) — in shock people get cold even in summer.

If an ambulance is on its way — give nothing to drink (surgery under anaesthesia may be needed). Only when help will not come for many hours — a conscious person without an abdominal wound may have a warm sweet drink in small sips.
Talk to them, reassure them, check their condition every 5 min.

blocks.text: Do it if the person is unconscious and NOT breathing (or only occasional agonal "gasps").

blocks.caption: Fig. 7.3. Chest compressions

items.text: Hard surface. Heel of the hand on the centre of the chest, the other hand on top, fingers interlocked.
30 compressions: depth 5–6 cm, rate 100–120 per minute (the rhythm of the song "Stayin' Alive"), let the chest rise fully.

2 breaths: tilt the head back, pinch the nose, seal your mouth tightly over theirs, breathe in for 1 sec until the chest rises. If you do not want to or cannot give breaths — do continuous compressions only, that also saves lives.
Do not stop until: breathing/movement returns, medics arrive, or you are completely exhausted. Swap with a helper every 2 minutes.

Children from 1 year old to adolescence: with one or two hands (depending on the child's size), depth ~5 cm (1/3 of chest depth); infants — with two thumbs, hands encircling the chest (if that does not work — with the heel of one hand), ~4 cm (1/3 of chest depth). For both children and infants, start with 5 breaths.
Stop the burning: put out the flames (roll the person, cover with thick fabric), remove smouldering clothes. If stuck to the skin — do NOT tear it off, cut around it.
Cool under cool (15–20°C) running water for at least 20 minutes. Not with ice.
Remove rings/watches from the injured limb before swelling starts.
Cover with a clean lint-free cloth or cling film (not tightly). Do NOT put oil, sour cream or toothpaste on it; do NOT pop blisters.
Pain relief (paracetamol/ibuprofen), drink plenty.

Always see a doctor: a burn larger than the injured person's palm, burns of the face/hands/genital area/joints, in children, electrical and chemical burns, any deep burns (white-grey or charred skin without pain).
Chemical burn: rinse with water for 20+ minutes; brush powder off dry first.
Signs: deformity, abnormal movement, crunching, sharp pain under axial load, swelling.

Splint principle: immobilise **the two neighbouring joints** (for a lower-leg fracture — the knee and the foot). A splint can be a board, a branch, a rolled-up sleeping mat, cardboard; bandage it on not too tightly, with soft padding.
Medics are already on their way — do not apply a splint: it is enough to hold the limb still in a comfortable position. Splint when you will have to drive or carry the injured person yourselves.
The limb is secured "as is", without forcing it straight. Leave the fingers/toes visible — check their colour (turned blue/white — loosen the bandage).
Arm: a sling (a triangular scarf around the neck) + bandage the arm to the body.
Open fracture: first stop the bleeding and cover the wound, then splint. Do not push the bone back in.
Suspected spinal/pelvic injury: do not move the person unless absolutely necessary; the pelvis can be stabilised by tying the knees and feet together and putting a roll under the knees.
Dislocation: do not put it back. Secure it in a comfortable position, cold, pain relief.

blocks.text: Hypothermia

items.text: Signs by stage: strong shivering → shivering stops, sluggishness, slurred speech, "paradoxical undressing" → unconsciousness.
Into shelter, remove wet clothes, into dry ones + an emergency blanket (silver side to the body), insulation from the ground.

A warm sweet drink for a conscious person. NO alcohol, NO rubbing with snow, NO hot bath (sudden rewarming stops the heart) — rewarm gradually, with another person's body heat, with warm (not hot) bottles on the torso (armpits, groin, neck), not on the limbs.
With severe hypothermia, handle the person extremely gently (rough movements can cause cardiac arrest); CPR — if there is no breathing.

blocks.text: Frostbite

Rewarm in warm water at 37–39°C for 20–30 min or with body heat. Do not rub, do not warm near a fire (the skin has no feeling — it will burn). Dry padding between fingers/toes, do not touch blisters. If there is a risk of refreezing — better not to rewarm until you reach a safe place.
Heatstroke

Signs: hot dry or heavily sweating skin, high temperature, confusion, nausea. Into the shade, undress, cool: wet cloths on the neck/armpits/groin, fan, cool drinks in small sips. Unconscious — recovery position, cooling, urgent help.
Dehydration and diarrhoea

In a crisis, intestinal infections kill more often than bullets. Rehydration solution: to 1 L of disinfected water — 6 level teaspoons of sugar + 1/2 teaspoon of salt. Drink often in small sips; for children — from a spoon every 2–3 min. Danger signs: no urine for 8+ hours, sunken eyes, sluggishness — a medic is needed.

items.text: **Choking on a foreign object:** ask them to cough → 5 blows with the heel of the hand between the shoulder blades → 5 abdominal thrusts (hold from behind, fist above the navel, pull sharply in and up) — alternate. Pregnant/obese people — chest thrusts. Infant: 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, face down along your forearm → 5 chest compressions on the breastbone with two thumbs, hands encircling the chest (or with the heel of one hand).

**Seizure:** do not hold the person down, do not force the teeth apart, put nothing in the mouth. Remove dangerous objects, something soft under the head. After the seizure — recovery position. Over 5 min or a repeat seizure — a medic urgently.
**Fainting:** lay the person down, raise the legs, fresh air. Does not come round within 1–2 min — act as with an unconscious person (sec. 7.3).

**Carbon monoxide poisoning** (stoves, generators indoors!): headache, nausea, "drunk" behaviour, cherry-pink skin. Carry the person into fresh air, rest, CPR if needed. Generator — only outdoors, no closer than 6 m to windows, doors and vents (DSNS recommendation), exhaust pointing away from the house; never on a balcony, in a garage, basement or stairwell. At home — a carbon monoxide detector.

**Concussion/blast injury:** ringing in the ears, being stunned, blood from the ears/nose, disorientation. Rest, quiet, monitor consciousness; examine carefully for hidden wounds. Worsening consciousness — to medics urgently (possible internal bleeding/brain swelling).

**Heart attack:** squeezing/burning pain behind the breastbone for over 15 min, spreading to the left arm, jaw, back; shortness of breath, cold sweat, fear. Stress and physical overexertion in a crisis trigger it more often. Actions: sit half-reclining, rest, loosen clothing, 103; **chew aspirin 150–300 mg (½ of a 500 mg tablet or 2–3 "cardio" tablets of 75–100 mg)** if there is no allergy and no bleeding; nitroglycerin — only if it has been prescribed to the person. Lost consciousness and not breathing — CPR (sec. 7.7).

**Stroke — the FAST test (Ukrainian «ОРМЧ»):** **F**ace drooping (ask them to smile), **A**rm does not rise or drops, **S**peech slurred or they do not understand, **T**ime — call 103 immediately and remember when it started. Give nothing to eat or drink, lay them down with the head raised, do not leave a conscious person alone. The treatment window is 3–4.5 hours: "let them lie down, it will pass" costs brain tissue.

**Sudden drop in blood sugar (a diabetic or a hungry person):** trembling, sweating, irritability, confusion, "drunk" behaviour. Conscious — something sweet (sugar, juice, honey) immediately, then bread/biscuits; no better in 15 min — repeat. Unconscious — nothing in the mouth, recovery position, do not put honey/sugar in the cheek, 103. If you do not know whether sugar is high or low — give something sweet: sugar does not kill someone whose level is high, while low sugar kills within minutes.

**Electric shock:** do NOT touch the person until the power is off (circuit breaker, plug) or the wire has been pushed away with a dry stick/plastic; high-voltage line — no closer than 8–10 m, only power engineers. Then — breathing/CPR, look for entry and exit burns (treat both as burns); even someone who seems "fine" should see a medic: heart rhythm problems can appear hours later.

**Drowning:** do not swim out to a drowning person without something that floats — they will drown the rescuer. Order: **reach** (a stick, an oar, clothing) → **throw** (bottles in a bag, a jerrycan, a rope) → **swim** out with an improvised float, approach from behind. Once pulled out: not breathing — 5 breaths, then CPR 30:2; do not try to "pour the water out". Breathing — onto the side, warm them, see a medic without fail even if "everything is fine" (lung swelling can come hours later). From winter water — hypothermia, sec. 7.10.

**Fell through ice:** do not panic, arms on the edge, frog kick with your legs — crawl out onto the ice on your belly towards where you came from, roll away from the hole. Someone has fallen through: do not go up to them — lying down, hold out a stick/rope/scarf from 3–4 m away, pull. Get the wet person into dry clothes at once, rewarm (sec. 7.10).

**Dust/a speck in the eye:** do not rub! Blink, rinse with clean water from the nose towards the temple, pulling the eyelid open. If that does not work — cover BOTH eyes (they move together) with a loose bandage, see a medic.
**Chemicals in the eye:** rinse with water continuously for 15–20 minutes, holding the eyelids open with your fingers. This is more important than any medicine.

**Object sticking out of the eye / eye injury:** do NOT remove it, do not press. Surround it with rolled bandages, cover with a cup/glass, bandage in place, cover the healthy eye too, to medics urgently.

**Welder's flash/snow blindness:** stinging pain, tears hours after bright light (snow in sunshine — without glasses!). Darkness, cold compresses, moisturising drops — it passes in 1–2 days. Prevention: any sunglasses; as a last resort — slit "Inuit goggles" made of bark/cardboard.

**Nosebleed:** sit down, head slightly FORWARD (not back!), pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 min without letting go, cold on the bridge of the nose. Does not stop within 30 min — a bandage plug in the nostril, see a medic.

**Insect in the ear:** in the dark, shine a torch into the ear (it often comes out towards the light) or fill the ear with warm oil/water — it will float out. Do not pick solid objects out of the ear — only a medic.
Find out WHAT, HOW MUCH and WHEN was eaten/drunk — this determines everything.

**Food/mushrooms/medicines (swallowed, conscious):** call 103 and follow the dispatcher's instructions. Do NOT induce vomiting and do not wash out the stomach the home way (drinking lots of water): this has been removed from the current Ministry of Health procedure (Order No. 441 of 09.03.2022), and the Red Cross (IFRC) explicitly prohibits it — little poison comes out, while the risk of inhaling vomit is high, especially if the person starts to lose consciousness. Rinse the mouth and spit, lay the person on their left side, do not leave them alone. Lots of water — only on a medic's instruction. A sorbent (activated charcoal) — only for a conscious person who can swallow on their own and is not vomiting, best within the first hour after poisoning, and on the advice of the 103 dispatcher/a toxicologist. Do NOT give it for acid/alkali/fuel, alcohol and methanol, iron preparations — it will not help or will do harm. The effective dose for poisoning is not "1 tablet per 10 kg" (that is the dose for bloating, dozens of times too small): adult 20–30 g at once (toxicology protocols allow up to 50 g), child from 3 years old — about 1 g/kg (children under 3 — only on medics' instructions). That is 80–120 tablets of 0.25 g, so keep powder or granules in your first aid kit; stir into 1–2 glasses of water and drink. No contact with medics, the person is conscious, the poison is not on the list of exceptions — give this dose once and make your way to doctors. Keep the packaging and leftovers of food/mushrooms/medicines for the doctors.
**Acid/alkali/fuel:** do NOT induce vomiting, do NOT "neutralise" (baking soda against acid = gas and rupture). Rinse the mouth, drink water in small sips, to medics.

**Mushroom poisoning:** symptoms 6+ hours after eating = the most dangerous (death cap). Act as for food poisoning above (103, do not induce vomiting, sorbent 20–30 g), get to medics at any cost; keep the leftover mushrooms for the doctors. "Feeling better on the second day" after a death cap is a deceptive pause; the liver damage continues.

**Carbon monoxide** — sec. 7.11. **Bootleg alcohol** (methanol: blindness, "drunk" with or without the smell of alcohol): do not try to "treat" it yourself with anything, to medics urgently — delay costs eyesight.
Unconscious after poisoning: recovery position (sec. 7.4), nothing in the mouth, monitor breathing.

sections.title: Feet on the trail: blisters and chafing

items.text: Prevention is everything: broken-in shoes, dry socks without creases, lubricate friction spots (petroleum jelly) BEFORE the hike, plaster on your "usual" blister spots in advance.
Feel burning — stop IMMEDIATELY (in 30 min there will be a blister): plaster/tape on the red spot, straighten the sock, shake out sand.

Blister intact — do not pop it, stick a "doughnut" of plaster around it. A large blister that makes walking hard: pierce it near the edge with a needle sterilised in a flame/wiped with alcohol, squeeze out the fluid, do NOT tear off the skin, antiseptic, plaster.
Torn blister = wound: rinse, antiseptic, dressing, change it daily (sec. 21.1).
At rest stops: take shoes off, dry socks, feet up for 10 min (swelling).
Rule: do not move them without need, especially if a spinal injury is suspected (sec. 7.9). Move them if: the place is dangerous, they need to get to medics and the medics will not come.
**Dragging** (one person, quickly out of danger): by the clothing at the shoulders/on a blanket placed underneath, head first, keeping your back low.
**Hand-lock seat** (two people, conscious casualty): each grips their own forearm and the partner's forearm — this makes a seat; the injured person holds on around their necks.
**Stretcher:** two poles 2.5 m long + two jackets (poles through the sleeves of buttoned jackets), or a rope zigzag (sec. 15.3), or a strong blanket (carry by the rolled edges, 4–6 people).
Carry an unconscious person on their side or with the head turned to the side (vomiting). Feet first on level ground, head first up stairs/slopes.
Every 100–150 m — check the condition: breathing, bleeding, consciousness.

blocks.text: Trauma section (carry within reach, not at the bottom)

items.text: CAT/SOF-T type tourniquet — at least 2; the Ministry of Health advises 2 for each family member (certified, not cheap market-stall copies)
Compression bandage ("Israeli") — 2
Hemostatic bandage (kaolin/chitosan-based) — 1–2
Chest occlusive seals — 2 (or thick film + tape)
Sterile gauze bandages 7 m × 14 cm — 5, non-sterile — 3
Trauma shears (for cutting clothing)
Nitrile gloves — 4+ pairs
Emergency blanket — 2
Marker, adhesive tape on a roll, safety pins

blocks.text: General section

items.text: Paracetamol 500 mg, ibuprofen 200–400 mg (pain, fever)
Oral rehydration salts — 5+ sachets; loperamide (diarrhoea in adults)

Sorbent: for a home first aid kit the Ministry of Health advises silicon dioxide-based products. Activated charcoal (powder or granules, 50 g; you cannot reach the dose with tablets) — for poisoning on the instruction of the 103 dispatcher or a doctor; no contact — dose and exceptions in sec. 7.13

Wound antiseptic: chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine; 70% alcohol and alcohol wipes — for the skin around the wound and for instruments, not into the wound itself. Brilliant green, alcoholic iodine and hydrogen peroxide are not used on wounds
Rescue breathing face shield with valve — 1
Assorted plasters, sterile adhesive strips for closing wound edges
Antihistamine (allergy)
Burn product with dexpanthenol
Moisturising eye drops (dust, smoke)
Thermometer, tweezers
**Personal regular medicines for 30+ days + a note with diagnoses and doses**

blocks.text: **Tip:** antibiotics without a doctor are dangerous, but in a long crisis keep a supply prescribed in advance by your family doctor "just in case", with the indications and doses written down. Discuss this with your doctor now, while everything is working.

intro.text: Without water — 3 days. With dirty water — dysentery, which in a crisis is more dangerous than thirst. Rule: treat any water you obtain as contaminated until you have disinfected it.

blocks.text: This is the minimum for survival. For a home supply, dovidka.info advises more: 3 L of drinking water + 10–12 L for hygiene and cooking per person per day, for at least 72 hours.
A sign you are drinking enough is pale urine. Dark urine, headache, sluggishness = you are already dehydrated. Drink before you get thirsty, not after.
In a city without running water

items.text: **Boiler/water heater:** 30–100 L of drinking water. First cut its power (unplug it or switch off the circuit breaker; for a gas one — shut off the gas), close the cold water valve at the boiler inlet and open the hot tap on the mixer — to let air in, otherwise the water will not flow. Drain through the drain valve at the bottom, or if there is none — by lifting the lever of the safety valve on the cold water inlet (it flows slowly, put a bucket underneath). Careful: the water may be hot. Do not switch on an empty boiler — first fill it until water comes out of the hot tap, otherwise the heating element will burn out.
**Toilet cistern** (the upper tank, not the bowl!) — if no chemical tablets are used in it: non-potable water, drinkable after disinfection.
**Building pipes:** open the highest tap to let air in and drain the water from the lowest tap in the building.
Ice/frost from the freezer, liquid from tinned vegetables.
Distribution points, wells, neighbours' boreholes; rain from the roof (let the first 10 min of rain run off — it washes away dirt).

blocks.text: In nature — where to look

items.text: Low ground, the foot of slopes, ravines — water flows downhill. Strips of lush greenery, willows, reeds = water is close.
A stream is better than a river, a river is better than a lake, a lake is better than a puddle (flowing water!). Take water upstream of villages, roads, pastures.
A spring at the foot of a hill is the best find.
Rain: stretch film/a raincoat at an angle into a container. Dew: before dawn, drag cloth through the grass and wring it out.
Birch sap in spring. Snow and ice — only melted (eating snow = loss of heat and little water).
Seep hole: in damp low ground/near a river, dig a hole 30–50 cm deep, let water collect and settle.

blocks.text: **Never drink without disinfecting** even crystal-clear stream water (giardia and bacteria are invisible). **Do not collect at all**: water from stagnant puddles with a film, near animal carcasses, with a chemical smell, in a combat zone downstream of military vehicles — fuel, chemicals and heavy metals are NOT removed by boiling, chlorine or SODIS — only distillation (partly) or giving up this source.

**Filtering removes cloudiness but not germs. Disinfecting kills germs but works poorly in cloudy water. So always do all three steps: let it settle (pour the clear water off the sediment), filter, disinfect.**
Homemade filter

blocks.caption: Fig. 8.1. Homemade filter from a bottle. Charcoal — from a burnt-out campfire (not embers!)

blocks.text: Pour away the first 2–3 litres (flushing the filter). No bottle — filter through 4–8 layers of cloth. After the filter, the water still needs disinfecting!

cells: A rolling boil for 1 min (in the mountains 3 min) — the minimum per WHO/CDC; the Ministry of Health advises 10 min if there is enough fuel
Kills everything living. Con: fuel, time; does not remove chemicals
As per instructions, usually 30 min wait
Light, exact doses. Con: limited supply
**Household chlorine bleach** ("Bilyzna" (Білизна), sodium hypochlorite, WITHOUT fragrances or surfactants; check the concentration on the label)

Check the label first — the concentration of "Bilyzna" in Ukraine varies a lot. 5–9% hypochlorite (or 50–90 g/dm³ active chlorine): 2 drops per 1 L of clear water (4 for cloudy or very cold water). About 1% (10–15 g/dm³) or concentration unknown: 10 drops per 1 L (20 for cloudy or very cold water). Stir, wait 30–60 min. A slight smell of chlorine should remain; if not — repeat the dose and wait another 15 min. If the smell or taste is too strong — let the water stand uncovered for a few hours or pour it several times from one container to another. A product older than a year gets weaker.
Available everywhere. Con: dosing accuracy, pure hypochlorite only
Clear PET bottles up to 2 L with filtered water — in the sun for 6+ hours (cloudy — 2 days), preferably on a shiny surface
Free. Con: slow, clear water only, PET only (not glass)
Boil under a lid, collect the condensate in a cup (turn the lid upside down, hang a cup under its handle; or a tube/gutter)
The only method against salt and partly against chemicals. Con: uses a lot of fuel

blocks.text: **Iodine:** 5% alcoholic iodine solution — 2 drops per 1 L of clear water (4 for cloudy), wait 30 min, in cold water — 60 min. Not for pregnant women, children or people with thyroid disease, and not for longer than a few weeks in a row.

items.text: Only food-grade plastic/glass/stainless steel with a lid; a dark, cool place.
Chlorine-disinfected water in a clean closed container keeps for up to 6 months. Mark the date.
Do not touch drinking water with your hands or dirty dishes — scoop it out with a clean ladle.
Drinking and non-potable water — kept separate and labelled.

intro.text: Remember the rule of three: without food — weeks. Do not risk your life for calories. But a long crisis requires knowing how to store food, cook without gas and replenish supplies from nature.

sections.title: How much you need to eat

items.text: Survival (little movement): 1200–1500 kcal/day. Normal: 1800–2200. Hard work/frost: 3000+.
Priority in a shortage: fats (9 kcal/g — oil, salo (cured pork fat), nuts) and carbohydrates. Protein is critical for wound healing.
Children, pregnant women, sick people eat first and eat properly.
