Going without food for 1–2 days is safe for a healthy adult — but you must keep drinking, and drink more.
**Camping gas burner** — the main tool. A 220 g canister = ~1 hour of burning = 8–12 meals cooked.
**Campfire/potbelly stove:** chapter 10. A pot with a lid saves 30% of fuel.
**"Thermos" cooking:** bring grains to the boil for 2–3 min, wrap the pot in blankets/a sleeping bag for 1–2 hours — it will finish cooking by itself. Fuel savings 50–80%.
**Brick rocket stove:** 16–20 bricks stacked like a well with a side opening for wood — many times more efficient than an open fire, runs on twigs.
Soaking grains for 4–8 hours halves the cooking time.
**Never** light a fire/barbecue/generator indoors — carbon monoxide kills silently (sec. 7.11).

cells: Fish must be gutted immediately after catching (all the innards and gills) and rinsed inside and out: ungutted dried river fish is one of the most common causes of fatal botulism in Ukraine, and the toxin changes neither appearance, nor smell, nor taste. Salting (rub coarse salt on the outside and inside the belly cavity, salt 20% of the fish's weight — 200 g per 1 kg) in a cool place, then air-drying in a draught in the shade, in gauze to keep flies off
Hot smoking over alder/fruit wood is a way of cooking, not of preserving (little salt, a lot of moisture)
Eat the same day; in warmth — no longer than a few hours. In the cold up to +5 °C (an "outdoor fridge" in winter, ice) — up to 2–3 days. For storage — salting and air-drying (row above)
Drying in slices in the sun/near a stove
Transfer to glass/ceramic, eat within a day (in winter — 2–3)

Fermenting under a weight. Cabbage: 2–2.5% salt by weight (20–25 g ≈ 1 level tablespoon per 1 kg), work it until it releases juice, no water. Cucumbers: brine 4–6% (40–60 g per 1 L of water, ideally 50 g ≈ 2.5 level tablespoons); under 3% (30 g/L) — they go soft, slimy, mouldy. Non-iodised salt; keep everything under the brine; after 3–5 days of fermentation — into the cold (cellar)
"Outdoor fridge": a box outside the window/on the balcony, protected from birds

blocks.text: **Botulism danger:** bulging lids, cloudy brine, foam, smell — throw the jar away without opening it. The toxin changes neither taste, nor smell, nor appearance, so boil any home-canned meat/fish/mushrooms before eating (the contents, in an open pot) for 10–15 min — the toxin is destroyed.
**Iron rule:** eat only what you recognise 100%. Not sure — do not eat it. In a crisis it is better to rule out wild mushrooms completely: a mistake = poisoning with no hospitals.

cells: Stings; toothed leaves grow in pairs, square stem
Young leaves — 2 min in boiling water: soup, "spinach". Rich in protein and vitamins
Yellow flower, rosette of toothed leaves, white sap
Leaves (soak to remove bitterness), roasted root
Rosette of oval leaves with curved veins
Young leaves in soup; a leaf — on small wounds
White young shoots and the rhizome (baked) — starch
Only after soaking for 2–3 days with changes of water, then roasted/as flour
Raspberry, blackberry, wild strawberry, bilberry, guelder rose, rose hip, rowan (after frost)
Fresh; rose hip — tea, vitamin C

blocks.text: Deadly "look-alikes" — learn them so you can avoid them

items.text: **Poison hemlock and water hemlock** (look like parsley/wild carrot, mousy smell, spots on the stem) — do not pick any "wild dill" or any "wild carrot".
**Herb Paris** (one black berry on 4 leaves), **lily of the valley** (red berries), **mezereon**, **belladonna** — no unfamiliar berries, especially single red or black ones.
Apricot/cherry stones in large quantities, green potatoes, raw elderberries — also poisonous.

blocks.text: The edibility test for an unknown plant is a last resort, not a method

**The honest truth about this test:** it does not detect poisons that accumulate and does not protect against allergies; experts consider it unreliable. The right strategy is to learn 5–7 guaranteed plants from the table above NOW and never need the test. Use it only during many days of hunger, when there is no alternative.

Order: rub on the wrist — wait 15 min → touch to the lips — 15 min → hold on the tongue — 15 min → chew and spit out — an hour → eat half a teaspoon — wait 8 hours without food → a small portion — 8 hours. Any burning, nausea, numbness — stop immediately, drink water. Avoid plants with milky sap (except dandelion), an almond smell, shiny leaves, umbrella-shaped flower clusters.

items.text: Kit for your bag: 20–30 m of 0.25–0.3 mm fishing line, hooks No. 5–10 (10 pcs), sinkers — weighs 50 g, feeds you for years.
Bait: worms (under logs, in damp leaves), grubs, grasshoppers, soft bread, bits of any meat.
**Bottom line (throw line):** line with a sinker and 2–3 hooks, cast it, tie it to a stake with a bell/tin can. Set 3–5 overnight — passive fishing while you do other things.
**Bottle fish trap:** cut the top off a large bottle, insert it neck-first inside, bait inside — small fish swim in and cannot get out. For fry and live bait.
Fish are active at dawn and dusk, in the shade of the banks, near snags, at the boundary between current and still water.
Fresh fish — only thoroughly boiled/fried (parasites); for storage — salting and air-drying as in sec. 9.3.

blocks.text: Traps work while you sleep — set a dozen simple ones rather than one complicated one. Check them twice a day. Set them on animal trails (worn paths, droppings, gnaw marks), mask the smell of your hands with smoke.

items.text: **Snare:** a wire loop the size of a fist on a hare/rabbit trail, a palm's height above the ground, fixed to a stake or a bent sapling.
**"Figure 4" deadfall trap:** a stone/log propped on three sticks shaped like the number 4, bait on the horizontal one.
Birds: pigeons in cities are a real source of protein; they are caught with a box on a prop with a string, using grain as bait.
All meat must be thoroughly cooked. Do not eat: animals found dead, animals behaving strangely (rabies!), the liver of predators.

blocks.text: Hunting with traps (snares, leg-hold traps) outside a real crisis is prohibited by law (Art. 20 of the Law of Ukraine "On Hunting Economy and Hunting"); fish traps and more than 7 hooks per angler are likewise prohibited (Amateur Fishing Rules, 2022). These skills are for a situation where life is at stake.

items.text: Your own supplies in unusual places: flour, gelatine, stock cubes, baby formula, pet food, etc. Neighbours' abandoned supplies — only by agreement or in case of extreme need, with a note and the intention to pay back.
City fruit trees: apple, apricot, walnut, mulberry; sour does not mean inedible.
Vegetable gardens, greenhouses, grain stores outside the city; barter with villagers (valuable for barter: fuel, batteries, medicines, salt, sugar, matches, alcohol as an antiseptic and currency).

intro.text: Fire means warmth, disinfected water, cooking, a signal and psychological support. Being able to light it with the first match in the rain is a basic survival skill.

sections.title: The fire triangle and three sizes of fuel

blocks.text: Fire needs: **heat + fuel + air**. Most failures come from haste: a big log is put on a weak flame and smothers it. Always prepare THREE piles in advance:

items.text: **Tinder** (catches from a spark): birch bark, dry reed, cattail fluff, cotton wool (ideally with petroleum jelly), a nest of rubbed dry grass, "feathers" shaved with a knife on a stick; from a flame (not a spark) — inner tube rubber, paper.
**Kindling** (match-to-pencil thickness): dry lower spruce twigs, split splinters. An armful as thick as your arm can hold.
**Main fuel** (finger-to-wrist thickness, then logs). Dry = snaps when broken. Split wet logs: they are dry inside.

blocks.text: **In the rain:** dry wood — under the trunks of fallen trees, dead lower spruce branches under the canopy, the core of split logs; birch bark burns even wet. Light the fire under a leaning tree/a tarp, on a platform of logs (not on wet ground).

cells: Keep in 3 different places, sealed. A lighter in frost — warm it in your fist
A shower of sparks with the striker into the tinder, held right up against it
Works wet, thousands of strikes — the best for your bag
Magnifying glass, glasses for long-sightedness, a torch lens, a clear bottle of water: focus the sun to a point on dark tinder
Bright sun only. Smoke in 5–30 sec
Narrow a strip of foil (from chewing gum) in the middle to 2–3 mm, ends to the +/– of an AA battery: the narrow bridge flares up
Keep tinder ready, the foil burns for 1–2 sec

First attach the jump leads to the + and – terminals. With the free clamps (hold only by the insulated handles), 1–2 m from the battery, briefly touch a tuft of fine steel wool or a thin wire laid on the tinder. Do not short the clamps against each other or the terminals directly.
Last resort. A spark near the battery = hydrogen explosion and acid in the eyes; a red-hot wire — a burn. Do not lean over the battery, protect your eyes.

blocks.caption: Fig. 10.1. Main types of fires

blocks.text: Dakota fire hole — hidden and highly efficient

blocks.caption: Fig. 10.2. Dakota fire hole: two pits joined by a tunnel. Almost no smoke or light, minimal wood, strong draught

blocks.text: Ideal when you must not give yourself away (chapter 17) or in a strong wind. Dig a pit for the fire and, 30 cm away, a sloping air channel to its bottom on the windward side.

sections.title: Lighting a fire: step by step

items.text: The site: remove the turf down to the soil, 1.5 m clear of grass in all directions, ring it with stones (NOT wet river stones — they crack and "shoot"). In winter — a platform of green logs on the snow.
A tinder "nest" the size of two fists — in the centre.
Spark/flame — at the bottom of the tinder (flame goes up!). Blow on it with long, gentle breaths.
Gradually add kindling in a tepee over the tinder — starting with the thinnest. Do not dump it in an armful.
Steady flame — only now add finger-thick fuel, then larger.

blocks.text: Keeping a fire going

items.text: For the night: cover the thick embers with a layer of ash — in the morning blow them back to life in a minute.
Carrying fire: put an ember in a tin can with dry moss/punk from rotten wood; it smoulders for hours.
Putting it out completely: douse, stir, douse again, check with the back of your hand — it must be cold. A forest fire in a crisis is a disaster within a disaster.

sections.title: Fire at home: how not to burn in your own home

blocks.text: A house fire is the most frequent deadly emergency in both peacetime and wartime: in Ukraine more than a thousand people die in fires every year, and in winter every fifth fire is caused by stoves, heaters and candles. During a blackout the risk rises many times over. It is not the flames that kill but the smoke: 2–3 breaths of hot smoke and a person passes out.
Prevention (essential during a blackout)

items.text: Candles — only in a glass jar on a non-flammable stand, far from curtains and at arm's length from where you sleep; **never sleep with a lit candle**. Better — an LED torch/lamp (chapter 20.2).
Heaters and potbelly stoves: 1 m of clear space around them, do not dry clothes on them, the chimney checked, the floor under the stove non-flammable; switch them off at night and when you go out.
Electricity: no "adapters plugged into adapters" for heaters, get rid of old extension cords; when power comes back, check what was left switched on.
Gas canister and burner — not near fire, not in the sun; smoking in bed is the main killer in DSNS statistics.

A **smoke detector** (from 300 UAH, the battery lasts a year) in the hallway and bedroom is the cheapest life-saver; a **fire extinguisher** of 2–4 kg in the kitchen + a fire blanket/thick blanket. Two exits from the flat/house — know both (a balcony to the neighbouring section, a ground-floor window, a ladder).

blocks.text: Fight it or get out

items.text: Fight it yourself only while the fire is smaller than a bucket and smoke is not making it hard to breathe: aim the extinguisher at the base of the flames; oil/fat in a pan — cover with a lid (preferably metal), a fire blanket or thick damp wrung-out cloth, **NOT with water** (a steam explosion throws the burning fat around); electrical appliance — unplug it first, then put it out.
Not out in 30 seconds, or smoke is gathering under the ceiling — **get out**. Belongings, documents, pets — only what is already in your hands.

blocks.text: Escaping from smoke

items.text: Shout "Fire!", wake everyone, call 101 — from outside or on the way.
**Close** the door to the room with the fire — this gives you 10–15 minutes; before opening any door, touch it with the back of your hand: hot — do not open it.
Move crouching or crawling (the air is cleaner and cooler low down), wet cloth over nose and mouth, along the wall to the exit.
**Never use the lift.** Down the stairs; if there is thick smoke on the stairs — back into the flat, close the door.
Clothes on fire: **stop — drop — roll**, cover with a blanket; do not run (it fans the flames). Burn — cool running water for at least 20 min, not ice (sec. 7.8).

blocks.text: If the exit is cut off

items.text: Close the door, block the gaps with wet towels/clothes, open the window, stand by it, signal (bright cloth, torch, shouting), call 101 with the exact address and floor.
Do not jump from above the second floor — wait for the rescuers: in a closed room with a window you have 10–20 minutes.
Balcony: close the balcony door behind you — less smoke gets through.

blocks.text: **Fire after a strike** (debris, fuel, gas): first — consider whether there will be a second strike (sec. 3.3), shut off the gas, switch off the electricity. Do not go into a smoke-filled stairwell for belongings or pets: in thick smoke you can lose consciousness within a few breaths. Tell the rescuers about people and animals left inside — they have breathing apparatus.

intro.text: By the rule of threes, in frost or a storm without protection a person dies within hours. A shelter is not a "little house" but anything that stops wind, water and the loss of heat into the ground.

items.text: **Water** nearby (100–200 m), but not right next to it (fog, insects, rising water level, animal trails).
**Wind:** a sheltered spot — behind a hill, a wall of forest; the shelter entrance on the leeward side.
**Height:** not in a hollow/riverbed (cold air and water drain there), not on a summit (wind). Ideal — the middle of a slope.
**Safe overhead:** no dry branches or dead trees above your head ("widowmakers"), not under a cliff with rockfall.
**Visibility/concealment:** depending on whether you want to be found (chapters 14 and 17).

sections.title: Quick shelters from what is at hand

blocks.text: Lean-to from plastic sheeting/tarp (30 minutes)

blocks.caption: Fig. 11.1. Single-slope lean-to: the quickest shelter, works with a reflector fire

items.text: A rope between two trees at chest height. Throw the tarp/sheeting over it, lower edge to the ground at 45° with its back to the wind, weigh it down with logs/pegs.
Bedding: 20+ cm of conifer boughs/dry leaves/grass — WITHOUT it the ground will draw out all your heat (losses into the ground are greater than into the air!).
A fire along the open side at 1–1.5 m; behind the fire — a reflector wall of logs/stones that throws heat inside.

blocks.text: Debris hut (no tarp, 2–3 hours)

blocks.caption: Fig. 11.2. Debris hut: 1 — ridgepole on a support and ribs of branches; 2 — covered with a thick layer of branches and leaves. Drawing: U.S. Army, field manual FM 21-76, public domain

blocks.text: A strong ridgepole with one end on a forked stick/stump (waist height), the other on the ground. Along the sides — ribs of branches at 45°. On top — a layer of conifer boughs/leafy branches laid from the bottom up, like roof tiles, as thick as from elbow to wrist (30–60 cm — then it keeps out rain). Inside — thick bedding. The entrance is small; plug it with your backpack.
Snow shelters

items.text: **Snow trench:** dig down to the ground, cover with branches + tarp + snow. Quick and warm (snow is an excellent insulator: ~0° inside when it is –20° outside).
**Spruce "tent":** under a large spruce next to the trunk there is always a snow cavity — deepen it and line it with conifer boughs.
In any snow shelter: a ventilation hole (made with a stick in the roof), the entrance lower than the sleeping platform (cold flows down), mark the shelter on the surface.

blocks.text: In a destroyed city

items.text: Choose intact low-rise buildings, basements with two exits; check ceilings and walls for cracks and for the smell of gas.
One small room is easier to insulate than a whole flat: live in one room, hang blankets over the doors and windows.
Do not spend the night in buildings that act as targets: near military sites, relay towers, warehouses.

intro.text: Cold kills unnoticed: first it takes the dexterity of your fingers, then the clarity of your thoughts. Manage your heat deliberately — through layers of clothing, dryness and calories.

blocks.caption: Fig. 12.1. Three layers of clothing: base (thermal underwear, synthetics/wool — NOT cotton), insulation (fleece, sweater, down), shell (membrane, raincoat). It is not the fabric that keeps you warm but the air between the layers

items.text: **Cotton kills:** a wet cotton T-shirt conducts heat away 25 times faster than air and does not dry. The layer next to the skin — synthetics or wool.
**Do not sweat:** take off a layer before work/walking. Sweated = frozen. Better to walk feeling cool than wet.

For a dressed person, an uncovered head and neck are the biggest "hole" for heat (not because the head is special, but because the rest of the body is already covered): a hat + scarf/buff give more than a second jumper.
Two pairs of socks (thin + wool), shoes that do not pinch (tight = cold feet). An insole cut from a foam mat/felt.

Improvisation: newspapers/dry leaves/hay between layers of clothing, plastic bags over socks (vapour barrier in wet shoes), an emergency foil blanket under your outer clothing over the back and chest.
**Reduce the volume:** everyone lives in one small room with as few outside walls as possible. Doors closed, gaps stopped with blankets.
**Windows** are the main heat hole: plastic sheeting/blankets/mattresses at night; during the day uncover the sunny side.
**A tent in the room** or a "den" of blankets over the bed — inside it is 5–10° warmer just from breathing.
Sleep together; pets are hot-water bottles too. Hot water in bottles into the sleeping bag 30 min before sleep.
Warmth from within: hot drinks and fatty food before sleep; a well-fed person gets less cold.
A candle + a ceramic pot over it warms your hands and your spirits a little, but NOT the room; watch the ventilation and fire safety.

Burzhuika (small makeshift stove)/stove: flue out through the window via a metal sheet, 50+ cm from walls, a box of sand nearby, NEVER leave it unattended. Burn fuel only in a stove with a working flue; a barbecue grill, brazier, charcoal "in a bucket" indoors — never. NEVER run a generator in a home, basement, garage, stairwell or on a balcony, even with windows open or the exhaust piped out: only outdoors, 6+ m from windows and doors, exhaust pointing away from the building — carbon monoxide (sec. 7.11, rules in sec. 20.4).

Do not heat a room with a gas cooker or oven: carbon monoxide has no colour or smell, and a person loses consciousness without noticing. The cooker is only for cooking, in short cycles, with ventilation.

sections.title: Rules for sleeping in the cold

items.text: Double insulation underneath: there should be more insulation below you than above you (body weight compresses the insulation).
Before sleep — warm up by moving (squats until warm, not until sweating) and eat.
Sleep dry: change socks and underwear; do not put on damp daytime clothes, place them beside you instead (they will finish drying).
Do not hide your face inside the sleeping bag — condensation from breathing will wet the insulation. Cover your nose with a buff.
A full bladder takes away heat — go before sleep, however much you want to stay warm.

intro.text: GPS is the first thing to go: batteries die, the signal is jammed — or faked (spoofing), and the navigator confidently shows a point hundreds of kilometres away. A paper map of your oblast + a compass + these methods are navigation that never switches off.

items.text: Hold the compass level, away from metal, magnets, your phone (0.5+ m), a car (15–20 m) and power lines (50+ m).
The red needle points north. Turn the map so that its top faces north — now the terrain matches the map.
Azimuth: a direction in degrees from north, clockwise. When walking on an azimuth, pick intermediate landmarks (a tree, a building) every 100–200 m and walk to them.

Going around an obstacle: 90° to the side, counting steps → 90° back onto the original azimuth, past the obstacle (add these steps to the main count) → 90° to the opposite side and count off as many steps as you went sideways → back onto the original azimuth.
Step pairs: count every left step; ~65 pairs = 100 m on flat ground. This is how you measure distance covered without GPS.

**GPS spoofing:** if the navigator shows you at sea, in another city, or the point "jumps", the signal has been faked (widespread in the combat zone and near military sites). Trust the compass, the paper map and road signs; offline maps on your phone (Organic Maps, maps.me) work without internet, but GPS coordinates can still lie.

blocks.text: By the sun and a watch (analogue or drawn)

Hold the watch level and point the **hour hand at the sun**. Halve the angle between the hour hand and the "12" (in winter time) or the "1" (in summer time) — this line (the bisector) points **south**, the opposite direction is north. The method is approximate and works only in the northern hemisphere; check it with other methods.

blocks.caption: Fig. 13.1. The "sun + watch" method (northern hemisphere): hour hand at the sun, the bisector of the angle to "12" (in summer, to "1") = south

blocks.text: By shadow (the two-mark method)

Set a stick upright and mark the tip of its shadow with a stone. After 15–20 min, make a second mark. The line from the first to the second points **east**; stand with your left foot on the first and your right foot on the second — north is in front of you. At solar noon (in summer time around 13:00, in winter time around 12:00) the shortest shadow points due north.
By the North Star (at night)

blocks.caption: Fig. 13.2. Finding the North Star using the Big Dipper

blocks.text: Natural signs (only as an aid; check several)

items.text: Moss and lichen are thicker on the north (damp) side of stones and trees; bark is darker and rougher on the north side.
Anthills are on the south side of trees/stumps; the south slope of an anthill is gentler.
Snow melts faster on south-facing slopes; berries redden first on the south side.
The altars of Orthodox churches face east; satellite dishes in Ukraine point roughly south.
STOP (chapter 1). Do not walk in circles — without landmarks a person veers to one side.
The line method (if nobody is looking for you): get to a "line landmark" — a river, a power line, a road, a forest cutting — and follow it. Water flows towards people: stream → river → village.
The sounds of a village carry 2–3 km (dogs, machinery), the smell of smoke — for kilometres. Listen at dawn and in the evening from high points.
Stop moving 2 hours before dark and make camp — a night on the move is more dangerous than a night in a shelter.
If people are looking for you, stay where you are, in the open, and signal (chapter 14). A moving target is 10 times harder to find.

intro.text: The signalling rule: anything repeated THREE times is an international distress signal. Three fires, three whistle blasts, three flashes.

items.text: **Whistle:** 3 long blasts — a minute's pause — again. Heard at 1.5–3 km (a voice carries 200–500 m, and it gives out).
**Torch at night:** series of 3 flashes towards houses/a road/an aircraft. SOS: 3 short — 3 long — 3 short (··· ––– ···).

**Fires:** 3 fires in a triangle or in a line, 20–30 m apart. By day — smoke (into the fire: green leaves or wet branches give white smoke, rubber or plastic give black; choose a colour that contrasts with the background: black on snow, white against forest), at night — bright flames. Keep a pile of "smoke" fuel ready next to the fire you keep burning.

blocks.caption: Fig. 14.1. Aiming a sun flash by sighting through your fingers

blocks.text: Any shiny surface works: a small mirror, foil on cardboard, a phone screen, a tin lid. The flash is visible from an aircraft at 10–20+ km. Sweep the flash along the horizon in series, even if you see no one — they may see you first.
Lay them out in an open place using contrasting material (fabric, logs, trampled snow, stones); symbols at least 3 m in size (better 5–10 m):

cells: We are moving in this direction

blocks.text: You have spotted an aircraft/helicopter: first attract attention with movement — wave a brightly coloured cloth, lie down and stand up, flash the mirror (movement is more noticeable than colour). Once you have been spotted, stand in an open place facing it, raise BOTH arms up (the silhouette of the letter **Y**) and hold them still: this is the international signal "yes, we need help / pick us up". One arm up, the other down (the letter **N**) = "no, we do not need help"; a pilot reads one arm waved over the head as "all is well, do not wait" or a simple greeting — so do NOT wave one arm if you need help. Do NOT cross both arms over your head — to a pilot this means "do not land here".

items.text: **Saving your phone:** power-saving mode, minimum brightness, switch off everything unnecessary; airplane mode only when there is no network or the battery is critical (in airplane mode, air raid alerts will not come through). Then switch the connection on to a schedule (for example, for 10 min every 3 hours — agree on this with your family in advance!).
**An SMS gets through where a call does not** — an overloaded network lets short packets through. Write an SMS: who, where, condition, plan.

**National roaming:** if your network is down, a phone in Ukraine can connect to another operator — switch airplane mode on and off, or choose a network manually in the settings. Emergency calls to 112 are possible through any operator, usually even without a SIM card — but do not rely on this: keep an active SIM. In advance, install and sign in to the official Ministry of Internal Affairs app "112 Ukraine" — it calls the 112 service over any internet connection (Wi-Fi in a shelter or at a Point of Invincibility) when there is no mobile network.

**Satellite SOS:** newer phones send emergency messages to rescuers via satellite without a network — but only in countries where the feature is enabled. **iPhone 14+:** among EU countries only Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Germany, Portugal, France (and also the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Iceland, Andorra); in Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Romania, the Baltic states and Scandinavia it does NOT work on iPhone. **Google Pixel 9/10:** almost the whole EU, including Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Romania, the Baltic states and Scandinavia. In Ukraine, emergency SOS from Apple and Google does not work (as of September 2026); check the list of countries on the manufacturer's website before a trip. Open sky is needed.

**SMS via satellite in Ukraine:** Starlink Direct to Cell from Kyivstar (since November 2025). A 4G smartphone (Android, or iPhone 13+ with iOS 26.2+) with a Kyivstar 4G SIM, where there is no ground network, connects by itself to the "Kyivstar | SpaceX" network (on iPhone the status bar shows SAT) and sends and receives ordinary SMS; delivery takes 3–10 min. Automatic network selection and open sky are needed. It does NOT work in the occupied territories, in the combat zone or in the border strip. This is an addition to other channels, not a replacement: agree with your family about SMS in advance.

**Official channels:** write down on paper the frequencies of Ukrainian Radio for your oblast and the names of the official Telegram channels of the Oblast Military Administration (OVA)/DSNS. The two-source rule for any "evacuation orders" — chapter 18.
**A radio receiver** is the main source of official information during a blackout. Listen at set times (official announcements are usually at the top of the hour).

PMR446 walkie-talkies (licence-free): family communication over 0.5–1 km in dense built-up areas (up to 3–5 km in open terrain). Agree on a channel and times to come on air. Remember: everyone can hear the airwaves — no names or addresses.
Offline backup: a paper list of phone numbers, agreed meeting points (sec. 1.5), notes left in an agreed place, not in plain sight ("alive, gone to auntie's, 14.05").

intro.text: Six knots cover 95% of survival needs: tie on, tie together, tension, lift. In the diagrams: a solid line — rope in front, a dashed line — rope passing behind; a green arrow — movement of the working end. Practise until it is automatic: your hands should be able to tie them in the dark and in the frost.

items.text: **4 mm paracord, 10–15 m** — the gold standard: breaking strength ~250 kg (new, without knots; paracord is not meant for lowering or belaying a person), and 7 thin threads can be pulled out of its core (fishing, sewing, snares).
Protect the rope from: sharp edges (put fabric underneath), rubbing on stones, fire. Wet and knotted rope loses up to 30–50% of its strength.
Melt the ends of synthetic rope with a lighter so they do not fray.
Terms: **standing part** — the long part of the rope (the one that takes the load); **working end** — the end you tie with.

blocks.text: 1. Figure-eight — a stopper knot and a reliable loop

blocks.caption: Fig. 15.1, step 1. Loop: the end over the standing part
2. The end BEHIND the standing part and up
3. Down through the loop — there is your "eight"

blocks.text: **What for:** stops the end slipping out of a hole or carabiner; tied on a doubled rope it makes a strong loop for a carabiner, hook or hanging point. It can be untied even after a heavy load. Fig. 15.1.
2. Bowline — the "king of knots": a loop that does not tighten

blocks.caption: Fig. 15.2, step 1. A small loop in the standing part; the end from below
2. The end from below UP through the small loop
3. Behind the standing part and back into the loop — downwards

blocks.text: **Mnemonic:** "The rabbit comes out of the hole (small loop), goes round the tree (standing part) and goes back into the hole". **What for:** a loop that does NOT tighten under load and is easy to untie afterwards: tying around a person to pull them out (in that case it is MANDATORY: first pull the bowline tight, then with the free end tie a backup knot — an overhand, or better a double overhand — around the adjacent leg of the loop, right up against the bowline; the tail after it no shorter than 10 cm. Without a backup knot a bowline can come undone with jerks and changing loads), attaching guylines, a loop at the end of a rope. Check: pull the standing part — the loop must not get smaller. Fig. 15.2.
3. Square (reef) knot — tying two equal ropes together

blocks.caption: Fig. 15.3, step 1. Left over right — the first half-knot
2. Right over left — the second half-knot on top
3. Done: two interlocked loops

blocks.text: **Rule:** "left over right, then right over left". A correct knot is flat, and the ends of each rope come out on the same side. If the ends "stick out" crosswise, it is a "granny knot", and it slips. **What for:** bandages, packing, tying together ropes of the SAME thickness. Not for loads that a life depends on and not for ropes of different thickness. Fig. 15.3.
4. Clove hitch (knot to a post)

blocks.caption: Fig. 15.4, step 1. A turn: in front to the right, behind to the left
2. Second turn — diagonally, crossing the first
3. The end under its own last turn, pull tight

blocks.text: **What for:** the start of any lashing — lean-to, tarp, debris hut frame, hanging a pot, tying to a pole. Ties and unties in seconds, but holds only under steady, constant tension: under a changing load it slips — always add a half hitch on top (see "Round turn and two half hitches" below). Fig. 15.4.
5. Round turn and two half hitches — fastening under strong pull, easy to untie

blocks.caption: Fig. 15.5. Round turn and two half hitches: a turn around the support and two half hitches. Drawing: Sawims, Wikimedia Commons, public domain

items.text: Wrap the rope around the support (tree, peg, ring) one full time — this is the "turn"; it takes the load.
With the working end make a **half hitch**: take it around the standing part and push it under its own turn (like a small loop on the standing part).
Make a second identical half hitch in the same direction. Pull tight, sliding it up to the support.

blocks.text: **What for:** tensioning a tarp to a tree, a boat to a peg, a tow rope. Holds under strong pull and can be untied even afterwards.
6. Adjustable tension knot (taut-line hitch)

blocks.caption: Fig. 15.6. Adjustable tension knot: the loop slides when the rope is slack. Drawing: Dontpanic, Wikimedia Commons, public domain

items.text: Take the rope around the peg and bring the working end back along the standing part.
Inside the loop formed, make two turns with the working end around the standing part (towards the peg).
Then one more turn OUTSIDE the loop (on the side of your hands), and push the end under it. Pull tight.

blocks.text: **What for:** the knot slides along the rope by hand and holds tension — adjusting tarp guylines without retying.
**How to learn:** tie each knot 20 times following the diagram, then 10 times with your eyes closed, then in gloves. That is 2–3 hours for all six — and a skill for life.

items.text: **Tensioning a rope without strength:** an improvised pulley system — a figure-eight loop in the middle of the rope, the working end round the support and back through the loop: you pull with double force and immediately secure it with two half hitches around the tensioned rope (tensioning a tarp, pulling a frame together).

**Lashing frames:** square lashing — start with a clove hitch on one pole, 3–4 turns around the crossed poles in both diagonals, tighten with frapping turns between the poles, finish with a clove hitch.
**Carrying a casualty:** a rope "stretcher" — rope zigzagged between two poles + clothing/a blanket on top (sec. 7.15).
**Storage:** rope — coiled and tied off; paracord — as a "chain" (a crocheted braid that comes undone in one pull).

intro.text: In most wars before the 20th century, more people died from infections than from weapons. Clean hands, a safe toilet and control of rubbish are survival weapons, not "comfort".

sections.title: Hands — the main route of infection

items.text: Always wash: before eating and cooking, after the toilet, after contact with a casualty, raw meat, rubbish, animals.
Economical washing: 0.5 l of water from a bottle with a small hole in the cap + soap = a full wash. Order: wet → lather 20 sec (between the fingers, nails) → rinse with a thin stream.
No water: hand sanitiser (70%+ alcohol) or wet wipes; ash with fat is an improvised soap (it is lye: caustic, so do not leave it on the skin for long); wood ash on its own is also a cleaning agent.
Keep nails short — all the worst things live under them.

blocks.text: In a flat (blackout, you cannot go out)

items.text: **A bucket with a lid + strong bags:** a double bag in the toilet bowl (bail out the water from the bowl) or in the bucket.
After each use, sprinkle on: cat litter, sawdust, ash, soil, or spray with a bleach solution — this blocks the smell and flies.
When the bag is 1/2–2/3 full, tie it off and take it to a designated place away from homes and water (not into the shared bin if it is not being collected!). Bury it if possible.
Separate collection: urine separately (wide-necked bottles) — it is almost sterile and easy to pour away at a distance; solids separately — this way the bags are lighter and safer.

blocks.text: Outdoors / camp

items.text: **Latrine trench:** 50–70 cm deep (deeper — it decomposes poorly, closer to the surface — animals will dig it up), **at least 60 m from water and 30+ m from camp**, on the leeward side. After each use — a layer of soil/ash. When it is 15 cm from the top, fill it in completely and make a new one.
Quick option, the "cat hole": a hole 15–20 cm deep for a single use, then fill it in.
Out of toilet paper: burdock/plantain leaves (not stinging and not shiny!), moss, snow, smooth stones, scraps of fabric that are boiled afterwards.
Handwashing is a mandatory station next to the toilet (a bottle + soap hanging on a branch).
**A "shower" with 2–3 litres:** wipe down part by part with hot water, a cloth + soap; critical areas daily: armpits, groin, feet, face. A full wash once a week is enough.

**Feet — daily check:** dry socks, powder/starch if they sweat. Wet cold feet = risk of "trench foot" (no frost needed — temperatures below +15 °C are enough): near zero it can develop within 12–14 hours, usually within 1–3 days; then blisters, ulcers, infection up to tissue loss. Change wet socks at once, do not sleep in shoes, dry your feet overnight.
Teeth: brushing is a must (toothache in a crisis is a disaster). No toothpaste — baking soda, ash, a chewed oak/linden twig as a "brush".
Laundry without detergent: boil for 15–20 min with laundry soap/soda; dry in the sun (ultraviolet disinfects). Against lice: wash at 60°C+, iron the seams, cut hair short.
Dishes: wash at once (dried-on food is a breeding ground), rinse with boiling water; on a hike — sand and ash as abrasive and lye. Always a separate board for raw meat.
Organic waste — into a compost pit/bury it; what burns — burn it; tins — scorch them in the fire (destroys food remains) and flatten them, bury separately.
Piles of rubbish near a home = rats and flies = disease. The rubbish collection point is 30+ m from homes and 60+ m from water.

Dead animals: do not touch with bare hands. Bury at least 1 m deep, away from water, wash hands thoroughly. Never eat livestock that died of an unknown cause. Do not touch dead wild birds at all (especially several in one place) — bird flu; report to the veterinary service.
Anyone with diarrhoea/fever — separate dishes, a separate sleeping place if possible, cared for by one person (not everyone in turn).
Drinking water — only disinfected, for everyone, no "I just had a sip from the river" exceptions.
Rehydration is the main medicine for diarrhoea (recipe for the solution — sec. 7.10).
Wounds, even small ones — rinse, antiseptic, cover: in the field a scratch becomes infected within a day.
An outbreak in the group (several sick people with the same symptoms within 1–2 days) — isolation protocol: sec. 21.6.

blocks.text: In a prolonged crisis this happens, and you need to be prepared for it — both practically and psychologically. The body of a deceased person is not in itself a source of epidemics (except for death from cholera, typhus or similar infections), but it requires dignified and safe handling.

items.text: **Safety of the site:** in an area under shelling or in mined terrain, a body may be "bait" for a repeat strike or may be booby-trapped (sec. 5.6). Do not rush.

**Documentation:** photograph (face, distinguishing marks, clothing, location), write down the date, time, circumstances, documents found, witnesses. This is critical for relatives, for insurance and legal matters, and for tracing.
**Documents and belongings** — separately in a labelled bag; do not leave them on the body, but do not keep them for yourself either.
**Temporary storage:** in the cold (basement, shade), cover the body with fabric/plastic sheeting, keep it away from animals. Gloves for any contact, wash your hands.

**Burial only if the body cannot be evacuated for weeks:** 1.5+ m deep (the bottom of the grave at least 1.2–1.5 m above the groundwater level; do not bury in low-lying places or where water seeps into the pit), at least 200 m from wells, boreholes, springs, rivers and lakes; if that is impossible — as far from water as possible, downslope from a well, and away from homes; mark the place (a sign with the name/description and date), write down the coordinates/landmarks and report at the first opportunity to the police (102) or DSNS — bodies are later exhumed for proper burial.

**Relatives and children:** tell children the truth briefly and honestly ("he died, it is not because of you, we are together"); do not leave someone who has lost a loved one alone in the first days (sec. 21.5).

intro.text: In a prolonged crisis, the threat comes not only from circumstances but also from people in despair. Your strategy: stay inconspicuous, careful and — above all — not alone.

items.text: Do not display your resources: food, equipment, a generator (the noise!), light in the windows (heavy curtains), cooking smells — all of this is "advertising".
Inconspicuous clothing, not military style (in the combat zone a civilian look means safety) and without showing off valuables.
Tell only those you are ready to share with about your supplies. Explain to children without frightening them: "our business is not for strangers".
Split money and documents: some on you, some hidden at home, some in the go-bag. A "give-away" wallet with a small sum — in case of robbery.
The "grey man" online is the same: no photos of supplies, shelters, strike aftermath with geotags (chapter 18).
The main rule: **avoiding a conflict is always cheaper than winning it.** Giving up belongings is not a defeat if everyone is unharmed.
Distance: strangers no closer than 2–3 m, especially if there are more of them. If you are asked to "come over and help" in a deserted place, help without getting close, or call other people.
Danger signs: people splitting up to surround you; glances at your hands and bag; "accidental" touching; persistently closing the distance after being asked to stop.
De-escalation: a calm, low voice, hands visible, no insults, an offer for "each to go our own way". Firmness without aggression.

At checkpoints and during checks: hands visible, no sudden movements, take out documents slowly, saying what you are doing. Do not argue, do not take photos. Your phone may be checked — what should and should not be on it, see chapter 18.

**Martial law and curfew:** the hours differ in each oblast (in rear oblasts usually 00:00–05:00 or 01:00–05:00, in frontline oblasts longer; the schedule is changed by orders of the Oblast Military Administration (OVA), check the current one) — know them and do not go out unless absolutely necessary: at night on the street you are either a violator or a target. Men aged 18–60 — always carry your military registration document (paper or in "Reserve+" [Резерв+]): it is checked at checkpoints and on transport. Moving around during curfew — only with a pass; in an emergency, call 103/101 rather than driving yourself.
Strengthening your home: extra bolts, a prop under the door handle, "noise" obstacles (tins on a string) on the approaches, agreed signals with neighbours (knocking on the wall).
Never open the door to "representatives of services" without checking — in a crisis, looters work this way. Talk through the door, check through neighbours.
Watches in the group: at night one person stays awake (2–3 hours each), especially in the first weeks of chaos.
Backup plan: an escape route from home (2 options), a cache of part of your supplies outside the home (at relatives', a garage, buried).

**Armed attack on a home** (after the war there will be more weapons in circulation): do not open the door, gather everyone in a room with a strong door and no windows facing the attackers, lie down below window level (bullets go through doors and walls), call 102, make noise for the whole building to hear — neighbours and witnesses deter better than "heroics". Do not go out to "sort it out" and do not negotiate through the door longer than necessary.

sections.title: Documents and money in a crisis

items.text: A full set of copies of documents — in 3 places: go-bag, cache, at relatives'/in the cloud. Photos of documents — on the phone of every adult.

Cash in small notes matters more than cards: ATMs and card terminals are the first to fail (and a cyberattack can "switch off" a bank for several days — chapter 18). Spread it across different places; part of it in euros/dollars.

The real "currencies" of a prolonged crisis: fuel, batteries, medicines (painkillers, antibiotics), matches/lighters, salt, sugar, coffee, cigarettes, alcohol, candles, hygiene products. A small stock for trading is worth more than gold.
Write down debts and agreements, even with neighbours — memory lies under stress, and conflicts are costly.

**Damaged home:** before cleaning up — photos and video of everything (every room, windows, roof, appliances, date on the image), call DSNS/police to draw up an official report, keep receipts for repairs. Without this there is no compensation (programmes such as "eRecovery" [єВідновлення]) and no insurance payouts. Documents for your home — in the set of copies.
Get to know your neighbours NOW. A list for your building entrance/street: who is a medic, who has a car, a generator, a borehole, who lives alone and needs help.
Roles in the building/neighbourhood: water, first aid post, information (radio), looking after children, watches.
Shared resources are more efficient: one field kitchen for 5 families burns 2–3 times less firewood than five separate fires; shared watches let everyone sleep.
Help the vulnerable (the elderly, single mothers) — this is not only ethics: a strong community = your safety, and a reputation as a reliable person in a crisis is capital.
Information hygiene: panic spreads faster than fire. Check rumours against official radio, do not pass on anything unverified, note the time and source of important news.

sections.title: Evacuation: when to leave and when to stay

cells: Your home is intact, the area is relatively safe
There is an official evacuation order (verified by two sources!)
You have supplies of water/food/medicines for weeks
Fighting is getting closer, your home is damaged, drones are "hunting" in the area
The road is more dangerous than home (roads under shelling, FPV drones on highways)
There is no water/heating in winter and no prospect of it being restored
There are sick people who cannot be moved
Someone needs medical care that is not available here

items.text: Leave in daylight, by verified routes, with a full tank (always keep the tank at least half full!), with food/water/warm clothes inside the car, not in the boot. In detail — chapter 26.
A convoy of several cars of people you know is safer than a single car.
On foot: 15–25 km/day with a load is a realistic pace for an adult; children — half that. Plan overnight stops in advance.
Leaving home: shut off the gas/water, switch off the electricity, take documents and valuables, leave a note for agreed relatives in the agreed place.
The first step is always the contact intermediary (sec. 1.5): everyone tells them where they are. Most "missing" people are found exactly this way within a day.

Not found: report to the police (102) — a disappearance is registered at once, without waiting "three days"; the Tracing Service of the Ukrainian Red Cross and the National Information Bureau, and the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War (for captivity/occupation; create an account with the Headquarters and keep the details of your request updated); hospitals and morgues in the area; reception points for displaced people.

Prepare in advance for each family member: a recent photo, distinguishing marks, blood type, a copy of an ID document — a "tracing" folder in the go-bag. For children — a card with their details in a pocket (sec. 22.1).
Write down every contact with the services: date, name, request number. This speeds everything up many times over.

sections.title: Human trafficking, personal safety on the road, detention

blocks.text: Crisis and displacement are a time when people are hunted: under the guise of "volunteers", "employers", "free housing". Victims include women with children abroad and men looking for work in Ukraine. Rules of the National Hotline on Countering Human Trafficking (**527** from a mobile, **0 800 107 527** from a landline or mobile, daily 7:00–22:00, free; abroad — IOM offices and the consulate):

items.text: **Your passport stays only in your hands.** Show it only to officials (border guards, police); never leave it "as a deposit", "for registration", "for paperwork". If it was taken by force — go immediately to the Ukrainian consulate and the police of that country.

Do not get into cars with strangers and do not travel with unofficial carriers; photograph the number plate and send it to your family together with the route and time. Register at official reception points, not through an advert.

An offer that is too good (work without papers, housing "for free", "we will take your child for a few days while you settle in") is a trap. Do not make decisions when you are exhausted or being rushed: give yourself a night to think, consult the hotline.
Do not take other people's parcels "to pass on" and do not hand your phone to anyone. Agree with your family on regular check-ins: "every day at 20:00 — a message saying where I am".
For children — a card with contacts and the rule "never go anywhere with anyone without mum"; at stations and reception points, always keep the child in sight.
**Domestic violence, or violence from "landlords",** rises in a crisis: hotline 1547 (24/7), La Strada 116 123; abroad — 112 and local shelters. This is not a "family matter", it is a threat to life.

blocks.text: If you are detained (checkpoint, filtration, captivity)

items.text: Calm and compliance: do not argue, do not run, do not resist, do not joke; hands visible. Heroics will not save you here.
The first 45 minutes of detention are the most dangerous: everyone is tense and acts impulsively. Follow commands, move slowly, do not look them in the eye — a direct gaze is taken as a challenge.

Answer briefly and truthfully about the obvious (name, where from, where to); about relatives in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, volunteering, your views — stay silent; do not sign anything without reading it, do not give "confessions".

Remember: date, place, names and appearance, car number plates, where you are being taken — this will save you and help others. Ask for your family and the Red Cross to be informed; relatives should immediately report to the police (102), the National Information Bureau and the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman).
Keep your dignity and a routine (sleep, movement, water, any routine) — this is the main support in prolonged isolation.

intro.text: In the coming decade, crises will also arrive through the screen: a bank knocked out by a cyberattack, a navigator that lies, your son's voice on the phone asking for money that is not your son, an "evacuation order" from a fake channel. Protection is simple and almost free — if you prepare it in advance.

items.text: **Scenario:** a cyberattack or a strike on a data centre — and for 1–5 days banking apps, card terminals, ATMs, Diia, electronic queues and tickets do not work. This has already happened and will happen again.
**Cash:** in small notes, enough for 2–4 weeks of living, spread across several places (sec. 17.4). Part of it in euros/dollars in case you need to exchange.

**Paper documents and copies:** Diia does not replace your passport when there is no network. Copies of all documents — printed, in a plastic sleeve, in the go-bag; as scans — on a USB stick and in the cloud.
**A paper list** of phone numbers, addresses, doctors, policy and account numbers, passwords to critical services (in a sealed envelope in your cache).
**Offline copies:** maps of your oblast in an offline app (Organic Maps, maps.me) and a paper map; this book — on paper; audiobooks/games for children — downloaded, not "streamed".
**Information without a network:** a battery-powered radio remains the only channel when the internet is down. Frequencies — on paper (sec. 14.4).

GPS jamming (no signal) and **spoofing** (faking: the phone confidently shows you at sea or 300 km away) are widespread near military sites, in the combat zone and sometimes in large cities. The result: the navigator leads "nowhere", taxis and deliveries "disappear", clocks and car navigation systems go wrong.
Signs: the point "jumps", a speed of 500 km/h on foot, a route across water. Solution: compass + paper map + road signs (chapter 13); do not trust a navigator that contradicts your eyes.
For evacuation (chapter 26), write out the route in words in advance: "to the fork after the bridge, left onto the N-08, 12 km to the village…".

sections.title: Deepfakes, voice clones and fraud in a crisis

items.text: **Voice clone:** a few seconds of recording from social media are enough for "your child" to call from an unknown number: "Mum, I'm in trouble, send money, don't tell anyone". Other variants: "police/hospital/volunteers" with plausible details taken from your own social media.

**Protection No. 1 — a family code word.** Agree now on a word/question that only the family knows (a made-up phrase like "blue tangerine" — not a fact that can be found on social media or guessed). Any "I'm in trouble" call is checked with it; if they do not say it, call back on a known number. Children and older people need to know this rule too.
**The pause rule:** any request to transfer money "urgently and without telling anyone" is always a sign of fraud. Urgency is a pressure tool.

**Fake volunteers and "payments":** links saying "get compensation/humanitarian aid, enter your card details" steal your account. Payments are arranged only through official apps and websites that you open yourself, not through a link from a message.
**A video of the "president/mayor"** ordering you to surrender or evacuate is a classic deepfake of the first days of an offensive. How to check is below.

sections.title: The two-source rule: how to check orders and news

items.text: Any important message (evacuation, a "corridor", a radiation threat, a change in rules) must be confirmed by **two independent official channels**: for example, Ukrainian Radio + the official channel of the Oblast Military Administration (OVA)/DSNS/police. One channel can be hacked.

Make a list of the official sources for your region NOW and write it down on paper (Appendix C): radio frequencies, channel names, websites, hotline numbers. In a crisis it is too late to look for them.

Signs of a fake: a call to share it "urgently with everyone"; no date or source; emotions instead of facts; "inside information from a soldier I know"; a link to an unknown website; a video with strange facial expressions or sound.
Do not pass on anything unverified, even "just in case" — panic in queues and on the roads kills. Note the time and source of important news.
Everything is gone (radio, communication, power): act according to your family plan (sec. 1.5) and this book, not according to rumours.

cells: Photos/videos of strike aftermath with the place and time, "where it hit"

The enemy assesses the hits and adjusts the next strike. If air defence, soldiers, military vehicles or a military site are in the frame — criminal liability (Art. 114-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, 5–8 years, up to 12 if the consequences are grave); the SBU (Security Service of Ukraine) treats such posts as fire adjustment. Wait for the official announcement
Air defence activity, movement of military vehicles, checkpoints, deployment locations
Addresses of shelters, water/aid distribution points, queues
Crowds of people are a target for drone drops and strikes (chapter 4)
Your supplies, generator, weapons, "we have left, the house is empty"
Children with their names, school, timetable

blocks.text: Geotags in photos (metadata) — switch them off in the camera settings for good.

sections.title: Your phone at a checkpoint and in the occupied zone

items.text: At enemy checkpoints and during "filtration", phones are checked: chats, photos, subscriptions, contacts, deleted files (they are recovered). Having the "wrong" subscriptions or photos costs freedom or life.

**A "clean" phone for leaving:** back up everything to the cloud/to relatives in advance; on the device leave everyday chats, family photos, a few neutral apps. Deletion — followed by filling the memory (recording a long video) or a factory reset — but no later than 1–2 weeks before leaving (better a month), followed by "living in" the phone again: bring back old neutral photos and videos, everyday chats, your usual apps and subscriptions. Both a fresh reset and an empty phone arouse suspicion. It is more reliable to clean gradually, a little each evening, and add neutral content straight away.

Leave sensitive channels and groups, remove contacts of soldiers and volunteers (saved with labels like "ZSU" [ЗСУ, Armed Forces], "TrO" [ТрО, Territorial Defence]), turn off syncing that would restore what you deleted.
Do not lie about having a second phone — they look for it. Better one "clean" phone than two.
Passwords and biometrics: they are demanded at the border; be prepared for the phone to be unlocked. Secrets should not be on it but in your head and in a safe place.
Ukrainian checkpoints: your phone may also be looked through (searching for saboteurs) — "cleanliness" is not needed here, but you should not have photos of military vehicles and positions either.
PMR446 walkie-talkies (sec. 14.4) — family and neighbours, an agreed channel and times; no names or addresses on air.
Mesh messengers (Bridgefy, Briar) work over Bluetooth between phones at 10–30 m indoors (up to 100 m in open space) — for a courtyard and a queue, not for a city.
National roaming and satellite SOS — sec. 14.4. A second SIM from another operator (or an eSIM) is cheap insurance.
The most reliable thing is agreements: meeting points, notes in agreed places, times to come on air (sec. 1.5, sec. 14.4).

blocks.text: A rare but real scenario for the coming decade: a powerful geomagnetic storm or a high-altitude nuclear explosion knocks out power grids and some electronics for weeks. Preparation costs next to nothing: a spare radio, an old push-button phone, a torch, a USB stick with documents — in a metal box (a tin with a lid, a biscuit tin), wrapped in cardboard inside so they do not touch the metal; the lid must fit tightly metal-to-metal all the way round — otherwise such a "Faraday cage" will not protect against the pulse. Paper copies of everything important are already a rule of this book. Everything else — as in a prolonged blackout (chapter 20).

intro.text: Flood, storm, earthquake, wildfire, extreme heat or frost, dam breach — each has its own "signature" and its own fatal mistakes. The climate of the coming decade makes them more frequent and more severe: heat above 40°, droughts in the South, downpours in the Carpathians, fires in mined forests.

blocks.text: The threat is approaching

items.text: Valuables, documents, medicines — to the upper floors/attic
Charge everything, store drinking water (flood = contaminated sources for weeks!)
Switch off electricity at the circuit breaker, shut off the gas, gas cylinders — up high
Prepare "floats": empty jerry cans, bottles in a pillowcase — an improvised flotation aid
Untie livestock and drive them to high ground

blocks.text: The water has come

items.text: **Main rule: do not walk into moving water.** Just 15 cm of fast water can knock an adult off their feet; 30 cm of moving water sweeps away a car, 60 cm — an SUV or pickup.
Rescuing someone being swept away: do not go into the water yourself at all — the current will knock you down too. Throw a rope, hold out a pole, approach by boat.
Do not drive through flooded stretches of road: under water you cannot see a washed-out roadbed or open manholes. "Turn around, don't drown" — a rescuers' rule.
Car stalled in rising water: abandon it, get onto the roof/high ground. Life is worth more.

**Car falls into water / is swept away:** in the first 30–60 seconds, while it is afloat: **belt — window — children — out** (unbuckle, lower a side window before the electrics go under, push the children out first, climb out through the window onto the roof). The doors will not open in water until the cabin fills. Window won't go down — break a side window (not the windscreen!) with the corner of a metal object, a headrest, a key — in the corner of the window. A window-breaker/belt-cutter hammer in the car door costs next to nothing.

Ended up in the water: feet first downstream (your feet absorb impacts with obstacles), paddle at an angle towards the bank, grab onto trees. Do not swim near electricity poles — the wires may be live.
On a roof/tree: signal with bright cloth, a torch; tie yourself on if you may have to wait a long time.

blocks.text: After the water

items.text: Into the house — only after checking: cracks, smell of gas, electricity switched off (water + wiring = death).
ALL water from wells and the mains is contaminated: only boiling/disinfection for weeks, until the official "clean". After floods in combat zones there are also mines carried by the water (sec. 5.6).
Food touched by floodwater (even in closed jars with rust) — throw away. Tinned food in intact cans — wash with chlorine bleach.
Drying out: mould appears within 24–48 hours — open everything, carry out wet things, wash walls with a bleach solution.

blocks.text: During the shaking (indoors)

blocks.caption: Fig. 19.1. "Drop — cover — hold on": the international standard for what to do during shaking

items.text: Do NOT run down the stairs during shaking (stairs collapse first) and do not jump from windows. Most injuries come from falling objects and glass, not from collapse.
No table — go to an inner load-bearing wall/a corner, crouch, cover your head with your hands, away from windows, wardrobes, chandeliers.
In bed — stay there, cover your head with a pillow (if there are no heavy shelves above the bed).
Outdoors — to an open space, away from buildings, poles, wires. In a car — stop in the open, stay inside; not under bridges, overpasses or power lines, away from balconies, cornices and trees.

blocks.text: After

items.text: Expect aftershocks — they finish off damaged buildings. Damaged house — leave it, do not go back for belongings.
Check the gas (smell — do not switch on lights, open windows, get out), check on people, help neighbours (sec. 3.5 — rubble).
Shoes! There is glass everywhere. Do not use lifts for several days.

**Hail** (with warming, more and more often "hen's-egg" size): under a sturdy roof, car — under a shelter/bridge, not under trees and not in the open; outdoors — backpack/jacket over your head. Damaged roof — plastic sheeting at once (sec. 24.2).

In advance: clear away/secure everything in the yard and on the balcony (every object becomes a projectile); car — away from trees. Windows: protective film or shutters/boards of plywood or OSB; tape — even in a dense grid — does not save glass from hurricane winds and hail and can produce larger shards (for a blast wave — see sec. 2.6).
During: an inner room on the ground floor/basement, away from windows. Do NOT go out into the "eye of the storm" — a lull of 10–30 minutes, then the wind from the opposite side.

In open country during a tornado: do not run from it in a straight line, move at right angles to its path; lie down in a ditch/roadside ditch, cover your head. Do not hide under bridges (wind tunnel) or in cars/trailers.

Thunderstorm: heard thunder — move to shelter at once (a solid building or a car with a metal roof, windows closed — a Faraday cage); a tent, awning or bus stop does not protect. Not under lone trees, away from water and metal fences, from summits and open fields — down into low ground; in a group — spread out. Do not lie flat. If shelter is out of reach or your hair stands on end (strike imminent) — last resort: crouch, feet together, head down; the position itself gives almost no protection, so as soon as you can — keep moving to shelter. Go out no earlier than 30 minutes after the last thunder.
Downed wire: no closer than 8–10 m; when leaving the area near the wire — "shuffle step", feet together, not lifting them off the ground (step voltage).
Assessment: smoke and wind coming TOWARDS you = the threat is real. A crown fire moves at up to 20–30 km/h, faster than you can run.
Escape: **at right angles to the wind**, downhill (fire moves uphill many times faster), towards natural breaks: rivers, lakes, roads, ploughed fields, already burnt areas.

Couldn't escape: lie face down on a burnt area or ploughed soil, cover yourself with non-flammable (wool, cotton) clothing or a blanket — do not wet the covering itself: wet fabric conducts heat to the skin faster. Breathe right at ground level (it is cooler there with less smoke) through a separate wet cloth over your face.
Body of water: wade in, cover your head with wet cloth; beware of suffocation from smoke over the water.
The main killer is smoke, not flames: stay low when moving, breathe through wet cloth.

**Fire in a mined forest** (East, South, North of Ukraine for decades): mines detonate from the heat and get scattered; do not go into such a forest to fight the fire yourself, after the fire — treat it as mined all over again (sec. 5.6).
Protecting your house in advance: a 10–15 m strip cleared of dry dead wood, a water supply in barrels, a ladder to the roof (sparks on the roof are the main cause of ignition).

Heat of 38–42° for several weeks is becoming the norm in the South and Centre. Peak danger 11:00–17:00: heavy work — only in the morning/evening. Drink 3–4 L, BEFORE you get thirsty; urine should be pale.
Salt: salt leaves the body with sweat — water without electrolytes is dangerous when you drink litres. Salt your food, drink oral rehydration solution (sec. 7.10), mineral water.

Home: during the day windows closed and covered (light-coloured/foil facing out), airing — cross-ventilation at night. Wet sheets on the windows work like an air conditioner. Without electricity, the top floors of panel blocks overheat to dangerous levels — sleep low down: on the ground floor or in the basement.
Clothing: light-coloured, loose, long sleeves (a covered body is cooler in the heat than an exposed one), a hat, a wet cloth on the neck.
Overheating and heatstroke — sec. 7.10. Watch especially: children, older people, people with heart conditions — check every 2 hours.
NEVER leave children or animals in a car, even "for 5 minutes" — the interior heats to deadly temperatures in 10–15 minutes.

**Drought and water shortage:** wells run low, mains water is supplied on a schedule. Drinking water at home for 2+ weeks (sec. 2.5), collect rainwater from the roof into barrels (discard the first 10 minutes of rain), mulch the vegetable garden (sec. 25.2), grey water (after washing) — for flushing and watering. Disinfection after supply is restored — mandatory (chapter 8).
Blizzard: do not go out. Most people who die in blizzards are those who decided to "just walk over, it's close". Visibility drops to metres, all sense of direction is lost.

Stuck in a car in snow: STAY in the car (it will be found; you in a field — will not). Engine — 10 minutes per hour for heating, regularly clear snow from the exhaust pipe (carbon monoxide!), the window on the side away from the wind — open a crack for air. Bright cloth on the antenna, keep moving your arms and legs.
On foot in frost: cheeks/nose/fingers white and numb = frostbite has begun — warm them at once (sec. 7.10), check each other's faces every 10–15 minutes.
Ice: "penguin walk" — short steps on slightly bent knees, weight over the supporting leg, hands out of pockets. When falling — tuck and roll onto your side, do not put out straight arms.
Frost of –15° and below with no heating in a high-rise is no longer an "inconvenience" but an evacuation scenario: draining water from the pipes and criteria for leaving — sec. 20.5.

blocks.text: The blowing up of the Kakhovka dam in 2023 showed: the wave arrives within hours, the water stays for weeks, carrying fuel, chemicals, mines, animals and corpses, and afterwards — epidemics. Millions of people live downstream of the Dnipro cascade, the Dniester and other large dams.

items.text: **Find out now:** whether your home is in a potential flood zone (flood zone maps are available from the regional military administration (OVA)/DSNS), how long the wave takes to reach you (from 20 minutes to a day) and where to go uphill — a specific route to high ground, not "somewhere".

**Breach signal** = leave at once for high ground on foot or by car, without packing anything beyond one suitcase: at first the wave moves at the speed of road traffic, then traffic jams block everything.
Do not try to save property; untie animals in sheds on your way.

Then — as for a flood (sec. 19.1), with corrections: the water is toxic (do not touch it unless necessary, rinse your skin), all water sources in the region are contaminated for months, mine danger in silt and sediment (sec. 5.6), mass death of fish and animals → epidemic risk (chapter 16).

sections.title: Industrial accidents: chemical plants, oil depots, storage facilities

items.text: Strikes on oil depots, fertiliser warehouses, chemical and gas facilities are a yearly reality. Find out which facilities are within 5–10 km of you and what is stored there (ammonia — cold storage plants and meat-processing plants; chlorine — water utilities; ammonium nitrate — fertiliser warehouses, ports).

Oil depot fire: the black cloud is toxic soot and benzene; downwind of it — close windows, switch off ventilation, do not go out, children and people with asthma — to the opposite side of the building; the cloud can hang for a day.
Chlorine/ammonia — the procedure in sec. 6.4 (chlorine — go up, ammonia — go down, always at right angles to the wind).

Ammonium nitrate/ammunition depot: an explosion can happen hours after the fire starts — do not watch from the balcony or go near windows, take your family away at once: ammonium nitrate depot — at least 3–5 km; ammunition arsenal — at least 10 km, because shells and missiles fly for kilometres (in 2017 a 10 km zone was evacuated in Balakliia and Kalynivka, in 2018 in Ichnia — 16 km). If the warning names a larger zone — go further and do not return until officially allowed: unexploded ordnance remains around (sec. 5.6).

chapters.label: CHAPTER 20
chapters.title: Blackout: light, energy, daily life off the grid

intro.text: A prolonged loss of electricity drags everything down with it: water (pumps), heat (boilers), communications, banks, fridges. Strikes on the power system in winter are a scenario for years: weeks without light and heat at –15° in the city. Those who have planned their energy by priority live almost normally.

sections.title: The first hours of a blackout

items.text: Fill all containers and the bathtub with water (pumps will stop within hours).
Unplug sensitive electronics (the surge when the grid comes back burns out appliances), leave one lamp on as an indicator that power is back.
Do NOT open the fridge/freezer unless you must: a closed freezer stays cold for 24–48 hours. In winter — an "outdoor fridge" (sec. 9.3).
Cook and eat what spoils first: meat/dairy → vegetables → tinned food and grains last.
Power-saving mode on gadgets (sec. 14.4), battery radio — tuned to the official station.

**Lifts:** during alerts and scheduled outages — stairs only. Stuck: call button/dispatcher or 101, do not force the doors open or climb out yourself (the shaft is deadly), sit down, save your phone battery, there is ventilation — you cannot suffocate.

cells: Hands free — the main working tool
Cheap, warms your hands / fire hazard No. 1 in a blackout: only in a glass jar, on a plate, far from curtains, do NOT sleep with one lit (sec. 10.5)
A jar + any oil + a wick made from a cord/bandage on a wire holder — a lamp out of nothing

blocks.text: **Life hack:** a head torch pointed into a water bottle turns into a soft "chandelier" for the whole room.

sections.title: Electricity off the grid: what to choose

cells: Cheap, quiet; always keep them charged
Router, lighting, laptop, fridge for a few hours, boiler pump, chargers

**The 2026 standard for the city:** quiet, no carbon monoxide or fuel, safe in a flat, lasts 10+ years, delivers power even in frost, but must not be charged below 0° — bring it somewhere warm to charge. Downside: price; in winter the sun gives 20–30% of the summer output
Chargers, lamps, the boiler if needed
Many people have one; outdoors only, exhaust away from windows and doors — not in a garage, even with the doors open (carbon monoxide); fuel
Powerful / noise (gives away your position, sec. 17.1), carbon monoxide, fuel, maintenance — rules in sec. 20.4
Standardise everything on one type; lithium works in frost, alkaline "dies" in frost (warm it in a pocket — it comes back)

items.text: **Car:** charging from the cigarette lighter with the engine idling (10 minutes of engine running ≈ 10–15% of a phone) — outdoors only.
**A 20–30 W solar panel**, even without a power station, charges a power bank on a sunny day. Cheap and lasts forever — the best investment for a long crisis.
Power priorities in a blackout: 1) communications and light, 2) medical devices (oxygen concentrator, fridge for insulin), 3) boiler/pump, 4) fridge, 5) everything else.

**ONLY outdoors**, at least 6 m from windows, doors and vents, exhaust pointing away from the house. A generator in a garage/on a balcony/in a stairwell = carbon monoxide = a family dead in their sleep. This is the most common cause of death during blackouts.
Refuel only with the engine switched off and cooled down.
Do not plug it "directly" into a house socket without a transfer switch — you will kill an electrician working on the line and burn out the generator.
Saving fuel: run the generator for 2–3 hours a day in blocks — freezing, charging, pump — not around the clock.
Fuel: petrol keeps for 3–6 months, with fuel stabiliser — up to a year or more (in metal jerry cans, in a non-residential space, away from fire), diesel — 12+ months. Rotate it as with food.

sections.title: Winter without heat: pipes, home, when to leave

items.text: **Decide "where we spend the winter" in September–October,** not at –15° without power: intelligence and energy experts warn that in winter 2026–2027 strikes on heat generation will intensify (jet drones, ballistic missiles), and large cities may stay without heat for weeks. Families with small children, older and sick people should have an agreed place in a village/small town/abroad and a plan for leaving (sec. 17.6, chapter 26).

**Pipes freeze** at –5…–10° in an unheated building within 1–3 days. If the heat does not come back: drain the water from the pipes (open all taps, drain the boiler, water heater, toilet cistern, pour antifreeze/salt into the drain traps), otherwise the ice will burst the system and the flat will flood once the heat is restored.
One warm room, body heat, a tent inside the room — sec. 12.2. A potbelly stove and fuel-burning heaters — only with a flue/ventilation (carbon monoxide, sec. 7.11).
A battery carbon monoxide detector — in the room where you sleep, if the house has a stove or a gas water heater, or a generator is running nearby.
**Points of Invincibility / warming points** — find the nearest ones in advance (schools, DSNS, housing offices): there is heat, charging, water, communications, tea. Write the address in Appendix C.

**Criteria for leaving a cold city** (for families with children, older or sick people): below +5° in the flat for more than 2 days with no prospect of change, no water and no way to bring it in, someone's health is getting worse. This is not panic but a decision (sec. 17.6): better to go to relatives or a warm village for 2–3 weeks than to treat pneumonia without a hospital.

No pump: water from the lowest taps in the building, the water heater (30–100 L), then — distribution points and chapter 8. Flushing the toilet — a bucket of non-drinking water; sewerage without water — sec. 16.2.
Washing by hand: soak with soap overnight → scrub only collars/cuffs → two rinses. Saves 3 times the effort.
Money: ATMs are dead — keep cash (sec. 17.4); shops may sell "on credit" to people they know — one more reason to be on good terms with your neighbours.

intro.text: Chapter 7 is about the first minutes after an injury. This one is about the days and weeks when there is no doctor: wound care, fever, teeth, chronic illnesses, epidemics and mental health over the long haul.

items.text: **Irrigation** is the main "medicine": clean (boiled, cooled) water under pressure — from a syringe without a needle or a bottle with a small hole in the cap, 0.5–1 L, wash out ALL the dirt. It hurts, but it prevents infection better than any ointment.
The skin AROUND the wound — with antiseptic; do not pour alcohol/iodine into the wound itself (it burns the tissue and harms healing).
Pull the edges of a clean cut together with strips of plaster across the wound (do not stitch without training!). Do NOT close torn, bitten or dirty wounds tightly — only a loose sterile dressing.
Dressing changes: 1–2 times a day; a bandage stuck to the wound — soak it off with boiled water, do not tear it off.

**Signs of infection:** pain that increases after day 2, spreading swelling and redness, pus, streaks running up the limb from the wound, fever. Actions: frequent irrigation, saline dressings (2 tsp of salt per glass of boiled water), rest and keeping the limb raised. Red streaks + fever = a threat to life, find a medic at any cost. Antibiotic-resistant wound infections are a reality in wartime hospitals: that is exactly why irrigation and cleanliness matter more than a pill.

Animal bites: wash with soap for 15 minutes, then, if available, treat the wound itself with povidone-iodine (Betadine — an exception to the rule against pouring iodine into a wound: it kills the rabies virus), do not close it tightly, do everything you can to get rabies vaccination — rabies is 100% fatal, and a bite even from a healthy-looking animal is dangerous.
Fever is a defence: up to 38.5°C in an adult without serious illnesses — do not bring it down, but drink (+0.5–1 L for every degree above 37) and rest.

To bring it down: paracetamol 500–1000 mg up to 4 times a day (no more than 4 g/day, caution with the liver) or ibuprofen 200–400 mg up to 3 times a day (after food). Children — only children's doses by weight, NOT aspirin.
Physical cooling for high fever: sponging with room-temperature water, something cool on the forehead/armpits, light clothing. Do not bundle the person up "to sweat it out" at 39+.

Cough/cold: drink plenty of warm fluids, humidified air, honey; getting worse on day 5–7, shortness of breath, chest pain = possible pneumonia — a medic/antibiotic as prescribed is needed (sec. 7.16).
Diarrhoea: rehydration (sec. 7.10) is the main thing; there is no need to fast (rice, crackers, banana); blood in the stool, fever, severe pain = see a medic.
"Exhaustion crisis": after 2–4 weeks of stress people's immunity drops — vitamins, sleep, any greens and fermented foods (vitamin C against scurvy when living on tinned food for a long time).
