Prevention in a crisis matters more than ever: brush twice a day (toothpaste substitutes — sec. 16.3), do not bite hard things.

Toothache: rinse with a warm baking soda and salt solution (1/2 tsp of each per glass) every 2 hours, take a painkiller by mouth (do NOT put the tablet on the gum — it burns), a clove/clove oil on cotton wool against the tooth.
Lost filling/chipped tooth: seal the hole with softened wax/temporary dental cement from the first aid kit, chew on the other side.

Gumboil (swelling of the gum/cheek): frequent rinsing, cold on the outside of the cheek for 15 minutes with breaks, do NOT apply heat! Swelling spreading to the neck/under the eye = dangerous, find a medic.

Knocked-out permanent tooth: hold it by the crown (not the root), do not rub or scrape it. Best of all — put it back into the socket yourself right away (within the first 15 minutes): if dirty, rinse it with milk, saline or for up to 10 seconds with clean running water, put it in place and bite on gauze/a clean handkerchief. If that fails or the person is unconscious — do not let the tooth dry out: put it in milk (if there is none — wrap it in cling film, in the injured person's saliva in a glass, in saline; a conscious adult can hold it in their cheek, a child — no, they will swallow it) and get to a dentist as soon as possible, preferably within 60 minutes. Later the outlook is worse, but still do not throw the tooth away — the dentist may try. Baby teeth are not put back.

**Main rule: a 30–90-day supply of your own medicines is item No. 1 of all preparation.** Discuss with your doctor in advance: what can replace your drug, how to lower doses if supplies run short, what must absolutely not be stopped abruptly (beta blockers, hormones, anticonvulsants, insulin, antidepressants).

Diabetes on insulin: insulin without a fridge lasts ~28 days at room temperature (not in the sun, do not freeze!); cooling — wet cloth around the container + a draught, a buried container, an "outdoor fridge". Eat regularly in small portions, always keep something sweet in your pocket.

Hypertension/heart: without a blood pressure monitor, signs of getting worse are a headache at the back of the head, shortness of breath with usual activity, swollen legs. Less salt; people with heart conditions keep nitroglycerin in their pocket, not in the go-bag.
Asthma: inhaler — always on you + a spare; an attack without an inhaler — sitting, leaning on your hands, slow breath out through pursed lips, warm drinks, calm (panic narrows the airways further).
Oxygen-dependent (concentrator): backup power (LiFePO4 station, sec. 20.3) is critical; arrange priority evacuation with the hospital/DSNS.

sections.title: Mental health over the long haul

items.text: A normal reaction to abnormal events: insomnia, irritability, "flashbacks", tears — in the first weeks this is expected. Act: a routine (sec. 1.3), physical work, talking.

**Sleep under alerts** is the main resource the crisis steals for years. Rules: sleep in the two-wall zone from the start (sec. 3.3), so you do not have to decide half-asleep at every alert whether to run to the shelter; one person "on duty" per night for the family/stairwell; daytime nap of 20–30 minutes; no screens an hour before sleep; caffeine — before lunch only. Three nights in a row with less than 5 hours is already a state in which people make fatal mistakes at the wheel and with gas.
**Psychological first aid** for someone else: safety → warmth/water/food → listen without pressure ("if you don't want to, don't tell me, I'm here") → connect them with family → a useful role/task.
For children: the truth in small doses and calmly, without frightening details; more physical contact; play is their way of digesting fear (playing "war/evacuation" is normal).

**PTSD** (in veterans in the family, in those who lived through occupation or loss): months later — nightmares, outbursts of anger, avoiding people and places, emotional numbness, alcohol as "medicine". It can be treated, and it does not go away by itself: look for a psychologist/psychiatrist when there is a connection; in the family — no "pull yourself together", but routine, work and presence.

**Caregiver burnout:** someone who cares for a sick or older person for months breaks down without anyone noticing. The shift rule: at least 1 day off a week and 1 hour a day "not about caregiving" — otherwise one sick person becomes two.

Warning signs that professional help is needed at once: talk of not wanting to live, complete refusal of food/contact for more than a few days, cruelty, alcohol as daily "medicine". Do not leave the person alone, remove dangerous items, look for a doctor/helpline when there is a connection.

sections.title: Epidemic and quarantine in a group

blocks.text: Cholera after floods, measles due to missed vaccinations, flu and COVID in crowded shelters, bird flu from sick poultry — in a prolonged crisis an outbreak in a group is almost inevitable. The protocol is simple and has worked since the days of the plague.

items.text: **Isolation at the first signs:** the sick person — in a separate room/a corner behind a screen, separate dishes, towel, bucket; one caregiver in a mask (FFP2 — in the go-bag, sec. 2.2), who does not cook for others.

**Hands and surfaces:** wash hands after every contact; door handles, taps — with a bleach solution (1 part "Bilyzna" chlorine bleach to 50 parts water, for the sick person's excretions — to 10) twice a day.
**Water and toilet:** with intestinal infections — disinfect the sick person's excretions with bleach before carrying them out; water — only boiled, for everyone without exception (chapter 8).
**Drinking and feeding:** oral rehydration solution (sec. 7.10) is the main medicine for cholera and rotavirus; most deaths come from dehydration, not from the germ itself.
**Air:** with coughing infections — ventilation, masks on everyone in the shelter, distance, sleep "top to tail" (head next to your neighbour's feet).
**Report** to a doctor/DSNS/aid point at the first opportunity: several people with the same illness is already an outbreak, and help (vaccines, antibiotics) responds to that.

**Vaccination in advance** is the cheapest protection: measles, diphtheria/tetanus (tetanus — with every dirty wound!), hepatitis A and B, flu, and if possible cholera vaccination for the South. The vaccination card — with the documents in the go-bag.

blocks.text: **Bird flu (H5N1):** do not touch dead wild birds, do not buy poultry "from private sellers" during a die-off, keep domestic poultry separate from wild birds (sec. 25.4); fever after contact with sick poultry — to a medic urgently. In the coming years this virus is one of the main candidates for a pandemic.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 22
chapters.title: Children, older people, animals in a crisis

intro.text: Survival plans are written for healthy adults — and they break down on a child's crying, a grandmother's slow walk and a cat in a carrier. Plan from the start for the weakest member of the family.

items.text: A child knows by heart (from age 4–5): their full name, their parents' names, the address, one phone number. Practise it like a rhyme.
Always in the jacket pocket: a card with the child's details and contacts (+ blood type, allergies), a whistle around the neck, a small torch.

Rules practised as a game: "siren — we go to the hallway", "buzzing — get under a roof" (chapter 4), "lost — stay where you are, don't go anywhere with anyone, shout my name loudly", "we don't touch strange objects" (sec. 5.5).
The "Go-bag in 2 minutes" game: who packs correctly fastest — under stress a child will repeat the game, not panic.
A reunion point if you get separated in a crowd/evacuation: a noticeable fixed place ("the main entrance", "the fountain"), and the rule — the one who is lost stays put, the older one searches.
A family code word against scammers who "call on behalf of Mum" (chapter 18) — know it from age 6–7.
Your calm = their calm: children read not words but faces and voices. The tone "we have a plan, we're doing step 1" calms better than a hug with a frightened face.
Give them a role: "you're in charge of the torch", "you count all of us at the stops". A busy child does not panic.
Meals/sleep on schedule even in the shelter — an anchor of stability. A familiar toy and a "bedtime ritual" matter more than an extra tin of food in the go-bag.
Infants: breastfeeding in a crisis is gold (sterile, always warm, calms both) — support the mother with water and food first. Formula — only with disinfected water, boil the bottles.
Carrying: a sling/ergonomic carrier frees your hands, for a child up to 2–3 years — put it in the go-bag without fail.

Dehydration in a child is more dangerous than in an adult: nappy dry for 6+ hours, crying without tears, sunken eyes/fontanelle = give oral rehydration solution from a spoon every 1–2 minutes (after vomiting — wait 10 minutes and give it more slowly), find a medic.

sections.title: Older people and people with limited mobility

items.text: A list on paper in large print: diagnoses, medicines with doses, doctor, family contacts — on the fridge and in the person's pocket.
Medicines — a weekly pill organiser + a 30–90-day supply; spare glasses and hearing aid + batteries for it.
Evacuation: cane/walker/wheelchair — checked and by the door; agree with two neighbours who will physically help get down the stairs (lifts are the first to be switched off).

Moving an exhausted person: a "chair" made of two pairs of linked hands, carrying on a strong blanket (dragging it along the floor by the corners is easier than carrying), an improvised stretcher (sec. 15.3, sec. 7.15).

In the cold, older people get cold faster and without noticing it themselves: check hands/feet by touch, an extra layer of clothing by default. In the heat — the opposite, they overheat without noticing: water every hour (sec. 19.5).
Dementia: under stress the person "drifts off" and wanders away — a card with the address in every pocket, a bell on the door, do not leave them unattended in an unfamiliar place.
Phone scammers target older people in particular: the rule "hang up and call your family back" (chapter 18).
The animal's go-bag: food for 3–7 days, water, bowl, lead + harness (a frightened cat/dog slips out of a collar), carrier, pet passport, familiar bedding, litter + tray for a cat.

A tag with your phone number on the collar + a photo of the animal on your phone and on paper. A microchip — if you can, get it done in advance. To travel to or through the EU a chip and vaccination are not enough, preparation takes about 4 months: chip (always BEFORE the vaccination or on the same day) → rabies vaccination (from 12 weeks of age), entries in the pet passport → no earlier than 30 days later, a blood test for rabies antibody titre at an authorised laboratory → another 90 days of waiting after the blood sample → 5 days before departure, a veterinary certificate and an international veterinary certificate (State Service of Ukraine on Food Safety and Consumer Protection). Get the vaccination and the test done now and revaccinate every year without missing a single day — then a repeat test and the 90-day wait will not be needed, only the documents before departure will remain.
In the shelter: the animal always on a lead/in a carrier (panic from explosions), water — animals need more than you think.

No time to take the animal in a sudden evacuation: do NOT shut it in completely — leave access to the outside or a large supply of water (bathtub, bowls) and food, room doors open, a note on the door "cat inside, [phone]".
Large animals (goats, livestock): drive them to high ground in a flood, leave them untied in a fire — a chance to survive on their own.
Remember: a dog is also an alarm, a hot-water bottle and the group's therapist. The cost of food pays off.

blocks.text: During a blackout, occupation or evacuation, labour may begin where there are no medics. Childbirth is a natural process: in 90% of cases the helper's task is not to interfere, to keep things warm and clean, and to call for help.

items.text: 103 and the nearest midwife/nurse — at the first regular contractions; there is time to get to hospital while contractions are less frequent than every 5 minutes and the waters have not broken. Contractions every minute, the urge to push, the head is visible — the birth will happen here.

Prepare: a clean place (oilcloth/plastic sheeting + clean sheets), washed hands/gloves, clean towels, warm swaddling cloths, a bowl, scissors and threads/laces boiled for 10 minutes, a bag. A warm room is the main thing for the baby.
Position — whatever is comfortable for the woman (half-sitting with support, on her side, on all fours). Drink, breathe, do not panic; push — only with a contraction, when there is the urge.

The head is coming out — support it gently with your palm, without pulling; ask her to "breathe, don't push" to prevent tearing. Cord around the neck — carefully slip it over the head. After the head, the shoulders come out by themselves within 1–2 contractions; catch the baby firmly (slippery), at the level of the mother's body.

The baby: dry them, place them on the mother's belly/chest skin to skin, cover both with something warm; not breathing after 30 seconds — rub the back and soles of the feet, wipe visible mucus from the mouth and nose with a clean cloth (do not put a finger in the mouth), keep the head level — do not tilt it back or bend it forward; not breathing after a minute — 5 breaths "mouth to mouth and nose" very gently, then 3 compressions with two thumbs, hands wrapped around the chest, to 1 breath, 103.

Do not rush the cord: when it stops pulsing (3–5 minutes), tie it with boiled threads in two places (10 and 15 cm from the baby's belly), cut between them with clean scissors. Nothing sterile — do not cut at all, wrap the placenta in a bag next to the baby, wait for medics.

The placenta comes out by itself within 5–30 minutes (do not pull on the cord); keep it for the doctors. The breast — to the baby at once: suckling contracts the uterus and stops bleeding. Massaging the belly below the navel in circular movements does too.

**Danger — get to medics at any cost:** bleeding of more than 2 soaked cloths in an hour, the placenta has not come out within an hour, the baby's feet/buttocks come first, seizures, fever, the baby is blue or limp.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 23
chapters.title: Weather forecasting without forecasters, and the seasons

intro.text: When there is no internet, the sky, the wind, smoke and the behaviour of nature predict the weather 6–24 hours ahead quite accurately. Folk methods are not 100% accurate, and a changing climate makes the "usual" seasons less predictable: read several signs together and prepare for extremes.

cells: High, thin "feathers" (cirrus) thickening and stretching in from the west
Warm front: rain in 12–24 hours, prolonged
The sky is covered by a milky veil, a halo (ring) around the sun/moon
Cumulus "towers" growing upwards in the afternoon, dark at the bottom
An "anvil" cloud with a flat top
A severe thunderstorm is already close — find shelter
Separate "cotton-wool" puffs that disperse in the evening
Ragged low clouds moving fast, gusty wind
A rapid change in the weather, squalls

items.text: **"Red sky at night, sailor's delight":** a crimson sunset with a clear sky in the west = dry tomorrow; a red SUNRISE in the morning — rain is possible by evening.
The sun sets into a "wall" of clouds — expect rain overnight/in the morning; it sets clear — a fine day tomorrow.
Stars twinkle strongly — wind and a change in the weather; steady dim starlight — stable.
Campfire smoke rising in a column — stable pressure, fine weather; smoke spreading low and "pressed down" — pressure is falling, precipitation is coming.
The moon in a hazy halo — humidity is rising, rain is coming; a sharp "horned" moon — dry.
Heavy dew/frost in the morning — the day will be dry; grass dry at dawn — expect rain during the day.
Distant sounds (a train, bells) heard unusually clearly — humidity is rising, precipitation within 12–24 hours.
Smells (of marshes, flowers, silage) suddenly get stronger — pressure is falling, rain is coming.
Swallows/swifts fly low — moisture has pressed insects down to the ground, rain within hours. High — dry.
Bees hide in the hive in the middle of the day, ants close their entrances, dandelions close their flowers — rain is coming.
A steady wind from one direction for days — stable weather; the wind "swings around" during the day — a front is near.
Aching joints, old fractures throbbing — not superstition: many people really do feel a pressure drop 12+ hours ahead.
Count the seconds from the flash to the thunder and divide by 3 — you get kilometres (sound: ~340 m/s). 9 seconds = 3 km.

If you hear thunder, lightning can already reach you (it strikes 10–15 km from the cloud): go to shelter without waiting for the storm to come closer. Less than 30 seconds between flash and thunder (≈10 km) — the storm is "yours": shelter immediately (rules — sec. 19.3).
The interval gets shorter with each flash — the storm is coming towards you; it grows longer — moving away. Safe to go out — 30 minutes after the last thunder.

sections.title: What this gives you in practice

items.text: You see signs of rain within 12 hours — today: stock dry firewood under cover, reinforce the shelter roof, have rainwater collection ready (clean containers, gutters).
Signs of a thunderstorm — do not plan crossings of open country or water for the afternoon.
A sudden thaw in winter after frosts — be careful with ice on water and snow on roofs.
A stable anticyclone in winter (clear, calm, frost getting harder every night) — plan your fuel: the cold will last for days.
Main threats: hypothermia and frostbite (sec. 7.10), carbon monoxide from heating, icy surfaces (fractures), snowdrifts on roads, weeks without heating during strikes on the power system (sec. 20.5).
Advantages: snow = water (melt it, do not eat it); cold = a natural fridge; tracks in snow = navigation and hunting; snow = a building material (sec. 11.2).

In a car in a snowdrift: do not leave the car (a landmark for rescuers and a shelter!), engine 10 min/hour with a clear exhaust and a window opened slightly (carbon monoxide), bright cloth on the antenna, keep moving.
Icy surfaces: "penguin walk" — short steps on the whole foot, body leaning slightly forward, hands free (not in pockets). For older people — a stick with a spike.

Ice on water: safe — from 10 cm of clear ice for a person, from 30 cm for a car; cloudy, cracked, near currents, river mouths, reeds, outflows — do not walk on it. Fell through or someone fell through — sec. 7.11.
Daylight is short: plan all work for 9:00–15:00.

Climate: winters are getting warmer and wetter, but with sudden short frosts down to –20° — exactly these "jumps" are the most dangerous for pipes, roads and people who did not manage to change into warmer clothes.
Floods and high water (sec. 19.1); do NOT cross ice on water once thaws begin — spring ice is treacherous even when thick.

Ticks are active from the first warm days (now — from February–March to November): light-coloured clothing, trousers tucked into socks, check your body twice a day, repellent. A tick — pull it out smoothly with tweezers/thread by the head, without twisting and without oil; the wound — antiseptic; watch for a rash and fever for 30 days (sec. 27.1).
The first greens are the main vitamin resource (nettle, dandelion — sec. 9.4). Birch sap.
Cellars and basements after winter — air them out before going in (gases from rotting).
Meltwater carries mines and ammunition in former combat zones (sec. 5.6).
Heat and dehydration (sec. 19.5), thunderstorms (sec. 19.3), wildfires (sec. 19.4).
Water "blooms" — filtration is critical (chapter 8); food poisoning — everything spoils quickly (storage — sec. 9.3, what to do in case of poisoning — sec. 7.13).

Mosquitoes and midges: smoke from a smouldering fire, covered clothing at dawn and dusk, a net over the face. Mosquitoes now also carry diseases (West Nile virus — sec. 27.5). Wasps/bees: a sting — remove the stinger as quickly as possible with anything (a fingernail, a card, tweezers — speed matters more than the method), cold; people with allergies — always carry an antihistamine.
Snakes (adder): high boots in tall grass, watch where you step, do not touch. A bite: stay calm, immobilise the limb, drink plenty, get to medics; do NOT cut, do NOT suck out, NO tourniquet.
Advantages: the most food from nature (berries, fish, vegetable gardens), warmth — you can dry supplies for the winter.

The main work: stocking up for winter — drying, salting, fermenting (sec. 9.3, 25.3), firewood (saw dead standing trees before the rains), insulating your home (sec. 12.2), draining water from pipes in case of outages (sec. 20.5) — all BEFORE the cold.
Fog and short days: reflectors on clothing, a torch always on you.
Wet cold of +2…+8° is more dangerous than frost: wet clothes + wind = hypothermia (sec. 7.10). A raincoat and dry socks are the main items of the season.
Mushrooms — a reminder: in a crisis, without an experienced mushroom picker — do not pick them at all (sec. 9.4).

intro.text: In a crisis nothing is bought — everything is repaired, reworked and used for something other than its purpose. Here — a minimal tool kit, working with it safely and a "second life" for ordinary things.

cells: Clear rubble, lever up a slab, open a jammed door, defend your home
Firewood, stakes, trimming poles, hammering and breaking
Wood saw + hacksaw blades for metal
Quieter and safer than an axe; metal — rebar, pipes, locks
Spade (+ a folding entrenching shovel in the go-bag)
Toilet, trench shelter, Dakota fire pit, vegetable garden
Board up windows, reinforce doors, nail together a platform
A blunt knife is more dangerous than a sharp one: it slips
Glass and rebar everywhere; an injured hand in a crisis is a disaster

blocks.text: **Safety over speed:** in a crisis an injury from your own axe is more likely than any other. Chop on a chopping block, not on the ground; line of swing — so that a missed blow goes PAST your leg; knife — away from yourself; working at height — only with a safety line; lift heavy things with a straight back, using your legs.

items.text: **Broken window in winter:** two layers of polythene with an air gap of 2–5 cm (stapler/battens/tape) keep heat in almost as well as glass. A large opening — a blanket + plastic sheeting on top. Ready-made "emergency windows" of OSB/polycarbonate cut to size are good preparation for frontline towns.
**Holed roof:** plastic sheeting/a banner/linoleum overlapping the intact roofing by 30+ cm, held down with battens or bricks along the edges (nails into slate make new holes).
**Leaking pipe:** shut off the water; temporarily — wrap it with rubber (a bicycle inner tube) + hose clamps/wire on top; epoxy putty ("cold weld") holds for months.
**Footwear:** sole coming off — stitch it around the edge with waxed thread (awl + nylon thread) or tie it with wire through holes made right through; reinforced tape — for one day of walking.
**Clothing/gear:** the repair kit from the go-bag (needles, nylon thread, safety pins); a hole in a tent/raincoat — a tape patch inside and outside.
**Loose door/lock under threat:** hinges on the inside, the door opens towards you — a beam wedged from the floor under the handle; an extra bolt — in 10 minutes from hinge plates and a padlock.

cells: Filter (sec. 8.3), fish trap (sec. 9.5), funnel, float, scoop, mini greenhouse, spoon (from the neck), rope (cut in a spiral into a 3–5 mm strip)
Mug, mini wood-chip stove, candle holder and windshield, a signal "bell" on a string, a grater (punch holes with a nail)
Patches, holding splints in place for a fracture, blisters (stick it on the heel BEFORE a blister forms), repairing everything; wind 5 m around each bottle in the go-bag
Waterproof cover for matches and documents, a water container (up to 1 L, with a sock as a frame)
Pre-filter for water, drying net, rope, storing onions
Battery — light and fire starting (sec. 10.2), mirrors — for signalling, seats — a bed, wire — fastening, tyre — a signal fire (black smoke)
Washing, laundry, antiseptic for minor wounds, lubricant for screws and saws, temporary "putty" for small leaks
Heat reflector behind a candle/campfire, cookware for baking, signal mirror, drying shoes (stuff inside with newspaper)
Insulation for clothing and footwear, kindling, "vacuum" storage of vegetables, hygiene
A "Faraday cage" for a spare radio and a push-button phone (chapter 18)

sections.title: Sharpening a knife without a sharpener

items.text: Find a flat fine-grained stone (a river pebble, a concrete kerb, the ceramic bottom of a cup — the unglazed ring underneath).
Wet the surface. Angle ~20° (template: a sheet of paper folded in half twice = 22.5°; one or two coins under the spine give only 5–10°).
Strokes as if "shaving a thin layer off the stone" — 10 times on one side, 10 on the other, gradually reducing pressure.
Honing: on a leather belt (stroke AWAY from the edge) — removes the burr, the knife shaves.

Siphon fuel only from your own car or with the owner's consent. Someone else's car, even an "abandoned" one, has an owner: siphoning without permission is theft. Under martial law it carries 5–8 years (Part 4, Art. 185 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), and for small amounts (up to 2 non-taxable minimum incomes (НМДГ)) — a fine or administrative arrest under Art. 51 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offences. Modern tanks — only from below through the drain plug, or a hose into the filler neck with a bulb/hand pump. NOT by mouth — inhaling petrol into the lungs is deadly dangerous.

Petrol goes "stale" over time — fresh petrol is suitable for a generator/chainsaw; old petrol — NOT for lighting a stove or campfire: DSNS explicitly prohibits lighting fires with flammable liquids (the vapours ignite, not the liquid — using "just a few drops" does not help; a typical cause of fires and burns). If it is clear, with no sediment or water — add it in small portions to fresh petrol (roughly 1 part old to 4–5 parts fresh) for an undemanding engine; cloudy or with sediment — do not put it in an engine, store it in a closed jerry can outdoors, away from homes and fire, until it can be handed in for disposal; do not pour it out or burn it. For kindling — paper, birch bark, wood shavings, solid fuel tablets.
Used engine oil — impregnating wood against rot, lubricating tools, a very smoky signal.
Fat candles: rendered animal fat + a cotton-cord wick in a jar — light and emergency food (calories) at the same time.

intro.text: Stocks will run out. If a crisis drags on for months, food has to be grown. Even a windowsill gives vitamins, and 2–3 hundredths of a hectare (200–300 m²) is a real contribution to a family's survival.

sections.title: Sprouting: vitamins in 3 days without a garden

items.text: Suitable: wheat, rye, oats, lentils, peas, mung beans (small green beans), sunflower, green buckwheat (not roasted!). Do NOT sprout ordinary beans (white, red, speckled) for eating raw: raw, soaked and sprouted beans contain a poisonous lectin — just 4–5 beans cause severe vomiting and diarrhoea. Eat ordinary beans only cooked: soak, pour off the water, boil in fresh water at a vigorous boil for at least 10 min (30 min is safer); slow simmering on low heat does not destroy the toxin. Also do NOT sprout potatoes and tomatoes (nightshades — the sprouts are poisonous) or seed treated for sowing (coloured).
Rinse, soak for 8–12 h in disinfected water.

Drain, spread in a 1–2 cm layer in a jar under gauze or on a plate under a damp cloth. Rinse 2 times a day only with disinfected (boiled and cooled) water, with clean hands, in clean dishes: salmonella and E. coli multiply quickly in warmth and moisture — they may already be on the grain itself. Throw away sprouts that are slimy, smell or are mouldy. Do not give raw sprouts to children under 5, pregnant, elderly or weakened people — only sprouts boiled for 1–2 min in boiling water.
Eat when the sprouts are 2–5 mm (1–3 days). Sprouting multiplies the vitamin content several times — the main protection against scurvy and exhaustion on a diet of grains and tinned food.

sections.title: What to plant in a crisis: maximum calories and reliability

cells: High in calories, undemanding, keep until spring
Plant sprouted tubers or even peelings with "eyes" 8–10 cm deep in May; earth up twice; dig after the tops have dried
Protein! Keep dry for years, fertilise the soil themselves
Sow in warm soil, climbing varieties with a support; dry the pods until they "rattle"
Huge harvest per plant, pumpkin keeps all winter
2–3 seeds per hole with compost, water at the root
Keep in sand until spring, the tops are edible too
Sow early, thin out, store in boxes of sand somewhere cool
Vitamin C all winter through fermenting
Natural antiseptic, flavour for a monotonous diet, keep very well
Garlic — before winter (October), onion sets — in spring
First vitamins in 30–40 days, grow on a windowsill too

items.text: Seeds: keep a "strategic packet" of seeds of these crops at home (dry, cool, in a jar) — it costs pennies and keeps 3–5 years (exceptions — onion, parsley, parsnip: 1–2 years, renew every year).
Your own seeds: take them from the best fruits, but not from F1 hybrids (they degenerate); dry completely, label with the year.
Fertiliser without a shop: compost (all plant waste + ash), ash (potassium), nettle infusion 1:10 (nitrogen).
Saving water in dry years: mulch (straw/grass in a 5–10 cm layer) halves watering; water in the evening at the root; drip watering from PET bottles with small holes buried next to the plants.
A garden in a former combat zone — only after checking by deminers (sec. 5.6); soil near burnt-out vehicles and craters is contaminated with heavy metals, do not plant there.
**Root cellar/basement (0…+5°C):** potatoes and beetroot — loose or in boxes; carrots — in damp sand; cabbage — hung by the stalk; apples — separately from potatoes (ethylene gas spoils them).

**Clamp (no cellar):** a pit 50–70 cm deep in a dry spot → a layer of straw → potatoes in a heap → straw 20–30 cm → earth 30–40 cm (add in 2 stages, add more when frosts come) → a small ditch around it to drain water; leave a vent along the ridge (a bundle of straw or a pipe), otherwise the potatoes will rot. Take them out in portions from the end.

**Fermenting** is the main winter technique; use non-iodised salt. Cabbage: 20–25 g of salt per 1 kg of shredded cabbage (2–2.5%), rub and pack it down so that its own juice covers it completely; if there is too little juice, top up with brine of 20 g salt/l. Cucumbers, tomatoes: cover with 4–6% brine (40–60 g salt/l, ideally 50 g). Beetroot: 2–3% brine (20–30 g/l). Everything under a weight, vegetables fully under the liquid; ready in 1–2 weeks, keeps in the cold for months, vitamin C is preserved. Slimy, softened or rotten-smelling — do not eat.
**Drying** — apples, pears, mushrooms (careful! — sec. 9.4), greens, berries: on strings or nets in a draught in the shade, or above a stove. Store dried food in jars with lids.
Grain and cereals against pests: jars or bottles with lids, with a bay leaf or a garlic clove inside; PET bottles are ideal containers.
3–5 laying hens = 2–4 eggs a day = steady protein for the family. They do not need an incubator, forage on their own, eat kitchen scraps, grass, grain.
Minimum: a dry, draught-free shed or coop, perches, water at all times, protection from polecats and foxes (wire mesh, shut them in at night).

Rabbits: grow fast, are quiet (staying unnoticed!), hutches can be built from pallets; but they are vulnerable to disease and fight — keep adults one per hutch (only young ones up to 3 months together).
In a city, pigeons and quail are more realistic (a cage on the balcony, quiet, laying eggs 40 days after hatching).

blocks.text: **Biosecurity against bird flu (essential in the coming years):** feed and water under a roof, out of reach of wild birds; netting over the run; separate shoes and gloves for the henhouse; do not touch dead wild birds nearby, report them to the veterinary service; if several hens suddenly die — do not eat them, do not sell them; report at once to the veterinary service (State Service of Ukraine on Food Safety and Consumer Protection, Derzhprodspozhyvsluzhba) and do not bury them yourself or take them anywhere — the vets must take samples and dispose of them themselves; until they arrive — wearing gloves, a mask or respirator and goggles, put the carcasses in a double bag and move them away from the other birds, children, dogs and cats, and shut the remaining hens in. Only if the veterinary service cannot be reached for more than a day (no connection, fighting) — burn them or bury them 1+ m deep away from wells and water, covered with lime; afterwards wash hands, shoes and tools with soap and a chlorine solution. People catch it from sick birds — fever after contact = go to a medic (sec. 21.6).

items.text: Specialisation is more efficient: you do potatoes, a neighbour keeps chickens, a third person fishes. Exchanging surpluses feeds everyone better than "everyone does a bit of everything".
Agree on exchange "rates" in advance and in writing (sec. 17.4): a bucket of potatoes = ten eggs = ... This removes conflicts.
Seeds and seedlings are also a currency and a gift that builds relationships.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 26
chapters.title: Evacuation: on foot and by car

intro.text: The decision "leave or stay" is covered in section 17.6. This chapter is about HOW to leave once the decision is made: routes, the car, convoys, checkpoints, drones on the roads, multi-day journeys on foot.

items.text: **Three routes out of the city:** main (highway), backup (secondary roads), on foot/"quiet" (paths, railway embankments, field tracks). Draw them on the paper map in your go-bag and write them out in words (the satnav may lie — chapter 18).

For each route find in advance: filling stations, hospitals, water sources, places to spend the night (churches, schools, acquaintances), detours around bridges (bridges are bottlenecks; they get closed and targeted).
Destination — a specific address (relatives, friends, an official centre) agreed in advance, plus a backup option in a different direction.

Listen to official announcements: times of "green corridors", permitted routes — and check them against two sources (chapter 18): fake "corridors" are a weapon. Straying from an announced corridor is life-threatening.

Evacuation hotlines: government line **1548** (free, 24/7); **203** — single line of the charity "Coordination Humanitarian Centre"; Vostok SOS charity 0 800 332 614; Proliska 0 800 888 888; Save Ukraine (families with children) 0 800 333 129. Numbers change — check on dovidka.info.
The main timing rules: leave as early as possible (in the first hours the roads are still clear) or, if you missed the moment, wait out the first wave of panic and traffic jams.
Tank always at least half full (a peacetime habit)
Jerrycan with 10–20 l of fuel (carry outside or in a ventilated boot)
Spare wheel, jack, wheel wrench, compressor/tyre plug repair kit, tow rope
Jump leads or a booster
Folding shovel, knife, hatchet, work gloves
Water 10+ l, no-cook food for 2–3 days for everyone
Blankets/sleeping bags for everyone (a winter night in the car without the engine is a real scenario)
Car first aid kit + your extended one (section 7.16), fire extinguisher
Charger for the cigarette lighter socket, 150–300 W inverter, paper map
Tape, wire, WD-40, fuses, bulbs
Cash in small notes (card terminals on the road will not work)

blocks.text: **Fuel:** in a crisis filling stations run dry within hours. Consumption in a traffic jam is 2–3 times higher. Calculate range as tank ÷ 2. Fill the jerrycan at the first opportunity, even if you "still have half a tank".

items.text: **Loading:** heavy items low down and against the back of the rear seats; nothing heavy on the rear parcel shelf (when braking it flies into people's heads). Each person's bag next to their door.
**People:** everyone buckled up; children in car seats. In a shelling zone windows slightly open (less barotrauma, the glass will not jam, and you can hear drones), jackets on, doors not locked.

**Distance in a convoy** — increased (sudden stops, craters); in a drone zone — 100+ m between cars. Do not overtake the convoy unless absolutely necessary, do not drive in the oncoming lane "because everyone did".

Do not drive into moving water at all (30 cm sweeps away a car — chapter 19); into standing water — no deeper than the middle of the wheel. Do not turn onto roads with an unknown surface off the asphalt (mines — chapter 5: do not leave the asphalt; after a night, mines dropped from the air may appear on the road, sec. 5.6).
**Night:** if possible do not travel at night in a combat zone; headlights are visible for kilometres and are a beacon for drones.

**Drones on the road** (30–40 km from the front): travel by day, without stopping in the open, with windows open; if you hear buzzing — stop, everyone away from the car into cover. Details — chapter 4.
**Shelling on the road:** section 3.6 — stop, everyone out, into the ditch 30–50 m from the car.

**Breakdown:** car onto the roadside, hazard lights, warning triangle; flag down a lift — in a crisis people pick others up more often than in peacetime. Do not abandon the car in the middle of the lane — you will block the way for everyone.
In advance: dipped headlights, music off, windows open, sunglasses off, hands on the wheel. Passengers — hands visible, no sudden movements.
Follow commands slowly and precisely, announce your movements ("the documents are in the glovebox, I will get them").
Do not photograph checkpoints or military vehicles — it is dangerous for you.
Keep documents in one clear plastic sleeve that is easy to hand through the window.
Your phone may be checked. At enemy checkpoints and when leaving occupied territory — a "clean" phone prepared in advance (chapter 18).
Politeness and calm; do not argue. If you are turned back — turn around and take the backup route.

sections.title: Spending the night in a car

items.text: Place: not on the side of a highway (drowsy lorry drivers), but in lay-bys, at filling stations, next to other cars with people; in a drone zone — under a canopy, trees, next to buildings, not in the open.

In winter: run the engine periodically (about 10 min per hour) BUT only with a clear exhaust pipe (snow!) and a window slightly open on the side away from the wind — carbon monoxide (sec. 7.11). Better: sleeping bags + everyone in one car.
Insulation: sleeping mats on the seats and against the windows (glass is the main source of cold), a blanket over the windscreen from inside.
Park facing the exit, doors locked, valuables out of sight.

blocks.text: The real pace of a loaded adult is 3–4 km/h, 15–25 km a day. With children and elderly people — 8–15 km a day. Plan honestly.
Walking technique

items.text: Rhythm: 50 minutes walking — 10 minutes rest (backpack off, feet up). A long lunch — half an hour, with food and a foot check.
Pace — set by the slowest member, who walks second in the group (the first is the navigator).
Short, even steps; do not run downhill (knees and feet are your "transport", protect them above all).
Water: drink 2–3 sips every 15–20 min, do not wait for a dry mouth.
Set out at dawn; in the heat rest 11:00–15:00 in the shade, cover the rest of the way in the evening.
In a frontline zone: groups of no more than 3–4 people, 20–30 m apart, along tree belts and buildings, not across the middle of a field or road (chapter 4).

blocks.text: Feet are your main asset

items.text: Broken-in footwear, socks without rubbing seams; dry spare socks on the backpack.
At the slightest rubbing or burning — STOP at once: cover it with a plaster or tape BEFORE a blister forms. "I'll hold out until the rest stop" = blister = minus 2 km/h.
Blister: do not tear off the skin. Large and painful — pierce at the edge with a disinfected needle, press out the fluid, antiseptic, plaster with a pad (sec. 7.14).
Every evening: wash or wipe your feet, check them, dry your footwear (stuff with paper or dry grass; do not dry right next to a fire — it hardens and cracks).

blocks.text: Weight and children

items.text: Overloading is the main mistake: over 20% of body weight = injuries and slowness. Throw out what you don't need before you set off, not at kilometre 10.
A child up to 4–5 years — in a sling, carrier or pushchair (the pushchair also carries things). Older children — their own small backpack and a "role" (navigator, keeper of the whistle).
A note in each child's pocket: name, your phone numbers, destination. Photograph the children in the morning (as they are dressed) — in case of a search (sec. 17.7).
At crowded stations and points: an agreed meeting place "if we get separated" and the rule "stay where you are, don't go anywhere with anyone, shout mum's name".
Register at official assistance points for displaced people: this gives access to housing, payments, humanitarian aid. Abroad — Appendix B.
Tell your contact go-between (section 1.5): "we have arrived, the address is…".
First 48 hours: sleep, food, a health check for everyone (sore feet, colds, blood pressure in older people), and only then — decisions about next steps.

intro.text: In a crisis people return to an environment where ticks, snakes, feral dogs and rats live. Most encounters are safe if you know three things: how to avoid them, what to do on contact, and when it is really dangerous. A warmer climate widens the range and season of ticks and mosquitoes — and of the diseases they carry.

sections.title: Ticks — threat No. 1 in our latitudes

blocks.text: Ticks carry borreliosis (Lyme disease) and tick-borne encephalitis. They are active from the first warm days until late autumn — in warm winters almost all year round. They sit on grass and bushes up to 1–1.5 m high and do not fall from trees.
Prevention

items.text: Trousers tucked into socks, shirt tucked into trousers, light-coloured clothing (ticks are visible), a hood or hat in bushes, repellent on clothing.
Check your body twice a day and after every trip into grass or woods: armpits, groin, behind the ears, hairline, behind the knees, navel.
After the woods, shake out clothing and do not bring it into the tent or bed; check animals too.

blocks.text: Removing an attached tick

blocks.caption: Fig. 27.1. Removing a tick: with tweezers (left) or a thread loop (right) — grip as close to the skin as possible, pull smoothly upwards

items.text: With tweezers (or a thread loop) grip the tick **as close to the skin as possible**, by the head, not by the body (if you crush it, its contents get into the wound).
Pull slowly, steadily, at right angles to the skin, without jerking or twisting (with a special hook-loop you may twist slightly — this is the only exception).
Do NOT smear it with oil, cream or petrol, do NOT burn it — a stressed tick injects more saliva with pathogens into the blood.
Antiseptic on the wound, wash your hands. If the head is left in — do not pick at it, it will come out by itself like a splinter; antiseptic daily.

Write down the date. Watch for 30 days: **a growing red patch with a pale centre ("target") around the bite, fever, aches, headache** — see a doctor without fail; borreliosis is treated with antibiotics at an early stage. If the tick was on the body for more than 36 hours or is already very swollen — see a doctor at once, without waiting for symptoms. According to the Ministry of Health, in 20–30% of cases there is no patch at all: do not dismiss fever and aches after a bite as a cold.

In Ukraine one group is dangerous — vipers (common adder, steppe viper, Nikolsky's viper): 50–70 cm, zigzag pattern or black, vertical pupil, triangular head. Grass snakes (yellow/white patches on the head, round pupil) are harmless. If unsure — do not touch any of them.

Prevention: in tall grass, on rocks and near haystacks — high footwear, watch where you step, check the path and stones with a stick before sitting down; do not put your hands into crevices; zip the tent at night and check footwear in the morning.

**Viper bite:** calm and minimal movement (venom spreads with movement); remove rings and watch before swelling starts; immobilise the limb as for a fracture and position it comfortably — at heart level or slightly above (do not let it hang down); drink plenty; an antihistamine and a painkiller (NOT aspirin); get to medics as quickly as possible — antivenom (if available) and anti-shock therapy are given only in hospital.

**Do NOT:** cut, suck out, burn, apply a tourniquet, drink alcohol. Fatal viper bites are rare; most deaths come from wrong "help" and panic. More dangerous for children, elderly people and people with allergies.
In a crisis feral dogs form packs and lose their fear of people. Packs near ruins, rubbish dumps and the bodies of the dead are especially dangerous: they are aggressive and more often have rabies.

Meeting a pack: do not run (fleeing triggers the chase), do not look them in the eye, do not turn your back; slowly move away sideways holding a stick or backpack in front of you; a loud firm voice; pretending to throw a stone often drives them off.
Attack: protect your neck and face, offer an arm wrapped in a jacket or the backpack as the "target" for the bite; if you fall — curl up into a ball, covering your neck and belly.

Bite from any animal: wash with soap under running water for 15 minutes, antiseptic, do not stitch tightly — and seek rabies vaccination (sec. 21.1). Any bite from a wild or unknown animal = risk of rabies. Rabies is 100% fatal, but the vaccine after a bite saves lives: start as soon as possible — and it is not too late even weeks later, as long as there are no symptoms.

A wild animal that is not afraid of people, approaches in daytime, foams at the mouth or walks as if "drunk" is a sign of rabies: get away, do not approach, do not "rescue" it. A fox in a village in daytime is exactly such a case.
Wild boar, and elk in spring and with young — give them a wide berth; boar do not climb trees, elk do not chase far.
In a crisis they multiply within weeks (rubbish, ruins, stocks). They carry leptospirosis, salmonellosis, haemorrhagic fever; they spoil and contaminate food with urine.
Prevention is the main weapon: rubbish covered and taken out (sec. 16.4), crumbs cleaned up, no standing open water, stocks in metal, glass or thick plastic, hung up or on shelves with "guards".
Traps are simple: a bucket of water with a baited "see-saw plank"; snap traps. Poisons — careful with children and animals; poisoned rodents die inside walls (stench for weeks).
Cleaning up droppings: in a mask and gloves, first spray with bleach (dust from dry droppings is a source of infection), do not sweep dry.

Throw away food with signs of rodents (gnawed, with droppings). If there is no other food — boil or fry it thoroughly: the pathogens of tularaemia and leptospirosis die in 5–20 min at 60 °C, instantly at 75 °C and above. Do not pick up mice with bare hands and do not crush them.
A cat in the household is a real means of rodent control and a psychological resource.

Wasps/bees: do not wave your arms, move away slowly; remove a bee sting as quickly as possible with anything (a fingernail, a card, tweezers): speed matters more than method. Cold, an antihistamine. **Danger:** a sting in the mouth or throat (ice in the mouth, to a medic immediately), 10+ stings, or an allergy: swelling of the face, shortness of breath, weakness — this is anaphylaxis: adrenaline (auto-injector) if available, an antihistamine, lie down with legs raised (if short of breath — half-sitting), do not get up suddenly, medics urgently.

Mosquitoes and midges: covered clothing at dawn and dusk, smoke, a face net; DEET repellent on clothing. With warming, mosquitoes in Ukraine carry **West Nile virus** (fever, headache, in older people — brain damage), and in Europe also dengue/chikungunya: fever 3–14 days after bites is not a "cold" but a reason to see a doctor. Treatment is symptomatic; the main thing is not to get bitten: standing water near homes (barrels, tyres, puddles) is a breeding ground — cover it or drain it.
Lice (in crowded conditions — within weeks): itching, nits in the hair; wash at 60°C+, iron the seams, haircut, fine-toothed comb; bedding — out into the frost or into boiling water.
Intestinal parasites: from raw water, unwashed greens, undercooked fish or meat — disinfection and heat treatment (chapters 8–9).

Most spiders and scorpions in Ukraine are not dangerous to a healthy person: for a bite — wash with soap, antiseptic, cold through a cloth, observe. **The exception is the karakurt** ("black widow"; south and east, steppe, gardens, firewood, footwear left outside; black female with a round abdomen up to 2 cm). The bite is barely noticeable, but within 15–30 min comes burning pain spreading through the body, pain in the abdomen and muscles, cramps, sweating, nausea, shortness of breath. This is life-threatening, especially for children and elderly people: calm, immobilise the limb, drink plenty, an antihistamine — and **go to medics immediately (103)**, without waiting for it to get worse; hospitals have pain relief and treatment. Suspected karakurt bite in a child — see a doctor at once, even without symptoms. **Do NOT:** cut, suck out, burn (including with a match), apply a tourniquet.

intro.text: A crush at a station, panic in a shelter, a queue for water that turns into a fight — in a crisis a crowd kills as often as the circumstances do. The rules are simple and do not require strength.

sections.title: Judging density: when to get out

items.text: Touching shoulders with neighbours now and then is still normal; constant contact from several sides and being unable to raise your hands to your chest is **critical density, get out immediately** while you still can.
Danger signs: "waves" of movement in the crowd, a narrowing ahead (doors, corridor, stairs, gates), movement in the opposite direction, shouting at the front.
In queues and gatherings in the open there are also drones and air-dropped munitions (chapter 4): spreading out and a roof over your head matter more than your place in the queue.

sections.title: You are trapped in a crush

items.text: **Arms bent in front of your chest** (like a boxer): they protect the chest from compression — that is what kills, not the fall.
Stay on your feet at any cost: feet slightly apart, knees soft; if you drop something — do not bend down.
Move with the crowd, not against it; in the pauses between "waves" move diagonally towards the edge of the crowd — into freer areas, not towards walls and fences (pressure is greatest there).
Breathe, keep air in your chest; if panicking — count your breaths out.

If you fall: instantly curl up on your side in the foetal position, arms covering your head, try to get up by grabbing people's legs; shout — people often help. If you see someone fall — stop and shout "STOP! PERSON DOWN!" — a chain of people stopping saves lives.
Children in a crowd — on your shoulders or held firmly in front of you with their back to you, not by the hand (hands get torn away).

sections.title: Panic in a shelter, the metro, transport

items.text: A calm, loud voice with simple commands ("Stop. Everyone stand still. We go out one by one, children first") stops panic more often than you might think — especially if you are the first to take on that role.
Do not run to the exit along with everyone: in the crowd at the door you will lose; the way out is a second or service exit, ground-floor windows, or waiting 1–2 minutes until it clears.
In darkness or smoke: a hand on the wall, move along it — that way you will not lose your direction or end up in the centre of the crush.
Separated from your family: do not search in the crowd — go to the agreed meeting point (sec. 22.1); whoever is lost stays put next to a noticeable landmark.
Come as a group: one stands, the others rest and take turns; women and children should not come alone.
Do not show large sums of money or full bags (sec. 17.1), keep documents ready.
Conflict in the queue: do not get physically involved, step back, calm voice; if it gets worse — leave the queue, life is worth more than a tin of stewed meat.
Community rule: an organised queue with a list and a volunteer "in charge" prevents fights — take on the organising, it makes everyone safer.

blocks.text: For a whistle, a torch, knocking. A dot is short, a dash three times longer; the pause between letters is as long as a dash, between words — about two dashes (7 dots). The international distress signal **SOS: ··· ––– ···** is sent without pauses; every rescue service in the world knows it.

In practice it is enough to know three things: SOS, your name or call sign, and the digits (house number, number of people). Latin letters are sent the same way (A ·–, B –···, C –·–·, D –··, E ·, ... — the Latin table matches the Cyrillic one for А, Б, В (W), Г (G), Д, Е, К, Л, М, Н, О, П, Р, С, Т, У, Ф, Х (H), Ц, І (I), Й (J)).

cells: 5 ml / 15 ml (salt 6–7 g / 20 g; sugar 5 g / 15 g)
200–250 ml; cereal grains ≈ 200 g; flour ≈ 130 g
Width of a finger / palm / span
≈ 2 cm / 8–10 cm / 20 cm; elbow to fingertips ≈ 45 cm; arm span ≈ your height
≈ 0.75 m / 1.5 m; 65 pairs of steps ≈ 100 m (sec. 13.1)
Facial features visible — up to 100 m; arm movements — 200–300 m; figure without details — 500 m; a convoy or individual vehicle — 1–1.5 km
3 seconds between flash and thunder = 1 km
Arm outstretched: each finger between the sun and the horizon ≈ 15 min, a palm (4 fingers) ≈ 1 hour
Angle in degrees at arm's length

sections.title: Storage times (without a fridge, in a cool dry place)

cells: Swollen or rusted through — throw away (sec. 9.3)
Airtight against moths; rice and buckwheat — longer
Dry; honey crystallises — this is normal
Goes rancid in light and warmth — dark place
Nuts go rancid — longer in the shell
Opened: formula — up to 4 weeks (as on the label), powdered milk — ~3 months; lid tight, dry
Chlorinated in clean containers — 6 months, rotate
Lithium — up to 15 years, work in frost
Metal containers, dark, away from living quarters
As on the label + usually several years of weaker effect
Liquids, insulin, antibiotic suspensions, nitroglycerin, adrenaline (auto-injector), eye drops — strictly by expiry date
1 min at a rolling boil (3 min in the mountains) — WHO/CDC minimum; the Ministry of Health advises 10 min
65°C for 30 min — kills most pathogens (milk, water when there is no fuel for boiling)
Zone where bacteria multiply in food
+5…+60°C; more than 2 hours in this zone — risk (in hot weather — 1 hour)
Mild 35–32°C (shivering) → moderate 32–28°C (shivering stops, confusion) → severe <28°C (unconsciousness, cardiac arrest possible)
Body 40°C+ and confusion — life-threatening, cool down immediately (sec. 7.10)

By wind chill index ("feels like"): in 30 min — at –28°C; in 10 min — at –40°C; in 5 min — at –48°C. A 30 km/h wind makes –10° "feel like" –20°, and –20° → –32°: frost with wind — cover face and hands without exception (sec. 7.10)
Pipes freezing in an unheated house
Normal up to 0.3 µSv/h; above 1–2 — limit time spent there; above 10 — go to a shelter (sec. 6.6)

sections.title: Hand signals for silent communication in a group

blocks.text: Agree on 6–8 hand signals for situations when you cannot shout (a drone, strangers nearby, noise). The first three match the international body signals for aircraft (sec. 14.3); the rest are internal to the group.

cells: Both arms raised straight up, motionless
No / don't come closer / danger ahead
STOP. Freeze where you are (mines, drone, strangers)
Palm down, waving towards the ground
Finger to the eyes, then pointing in a direction
Circular movements of the arm above the head
Everyone to me quickly / we're leaving

intro.text: These pages are for moments of stress, when reading long paragraphs is impossible. Each checklist is the order of actions for one situation, with a reference to the detailed chapter. Copy them, laminate them and put them in your go-bag.

sections.title: The first 60 seconds of any disaster

items.text: Stop. 3 slow breaths out. (sec. 1.2)
Safety: is there a threat right now (fire, water, shelling, gas, drone)? — get out of the area: from fire and smoke at right angles to the wind, from water — uphill.
People: is everyone unhurt? Massive bleeding → pressure on the wound IMMEDIATELY (sec. 7.2).
A second wave? (repeat strike, collapse, aftershock) — do not go back to the scene for at least 40 min (sometimes 1–2 h).
Contact: one SMS to your family "alive, [where], [going where]".
Go-bag, documents — if it takes seconds. Meeting point.
Get dressed, shoes on, go-bag
Turn off gas/water/electricity, close windows and curtains
Ballistic missiles or shelter far away → two-wall zone (hallway/bathroom)
Otherwise → shelter; in the shelter, not opposite the door
Do not go to the windows "to have a look"
Leave after the all-clear; after explosions nearby — expect repeat strikes for at least 40 min
I hear/see a drone → I assume it sees me
5–10 seconds: under a roof or behind a thick wall, freeze
Do not run in a straight line, do not look up, do not film it on your phone
In a car: stop — everyone away from the car 30–50 m into cover
The drone circles around — I change sides of the cover, keeping an obstacle between us
Afterwards — I count to 60, expect a second one; I do not run to the impact site for at least 40 min
A downed drone — do not approach, do not touch: move at least 100 m away (a large one — a "Shahed", a missile — 300 m) into cover, report to 101/102; do not touch a fibre-optic thread, go around it
I shout "Fire!", wake everyone; fight it only while the fire is smaller than a bucket (fat — cover it, not water; an appliance — unplug it)
Not out within 30 sec — we get out; close the door of the room with the fire
Crouching or crawling, wet cloth over the face, along the wall; test doors with the back of your hand
Never the lift; smoke on the stairs — go back, shut yourself in
Cut off: block gaps with wet cloth, open the window, signal, call 101 giving the floor; do not jump from above the 2nd floor
Clothes on fire: stop — drop — roll; burn — cool water (not ice) for 20 min
Press on the wound with all your weight, do not let go
Limb and blood "spurting" → tourniquet 5–8 cm above the wound, until bleeding stops completely, write down the time
Neck/groin/shoulder → pack the wound deeply with a bandage, press for 3–10 min, tight dressing
Keep warm, lay down, legs up (unless head/chest/abdomen injury)
Medics (103), check the condition every 5 min
Safety → call out, shake
Tilt the head back, check breathing for 10 sec
Breathing → recovery position, check every minute
Not breathing → CPR 30:2, 100–120/min, 5–6 cm, do not stop
One specific person calls 103
Do not touch, do not approach, do not photograph up close
Remember landmarks, step back in your own footprints
Mark it from a distance, warn people
Move 100+ m away (shells/aerial bombs — 300+ m) and only from there call 101 or 102 — do not use a phone or radio near the object
Walked into a minefield → FREEZE, call for help, wait for deminers
Returning home after occupation → deminers first (sec. 5.6)
Get indoors (basement/centre of the building), close windows and ventilation, tape up gaps
Outer clothing — into a bag outside the door, shower, wash your hair
Battery radio — instructions from the authorities
Potassium iodide — ONLY after an official announcement (doses — table 6.2)
Food/water — only from closed containers
Nuclear flash: do not look, drop down, 10–15 min to reach shelter, 24–72 h inside (sec. 6.6)
Let it settle → filter it (cloth/bottle filter)

Boil for at least 1 min (the Ministry of Health advises 10 min if you have fuel) or unscented ~5% bleach ("Білизна") — 2 drops/l (4 for cloudy water; ~1% or unknown concentration — 10 drops/l), 30–60 min, or SODIS 6 h in the sun
Chemicals/fuel in the water — boiling does not help, find another source
Store closed, label with the date

sections.title: Leaving home for good or for a long time (sec. 17.6, ch. 26)

items.text: Documents + copies + cash + medicines for 30 days
Water 2 l, food for 3 days, warm clothes, footwear
Phone + power bank, radio, torch, whistle
Shut off gas/water, turn off electricity, close windows
A note for your family in the agreed place
Inform your contact go-between; route written out in words, a "clean" phone for enemy checkpoints (ch. 18)

sections.title: A night in the cold without a roof (ch. 11–12)

items.text: 2 h before dark — stop and build
Place: not a hollow, not a hilltop, no "widowmaker" branches overhead, back to the wind
Bedding layer 20+ cm — insulation from the ground above all
Dry clothes next to the body, wet ones under your side
Fire + reflector; never a fire in an enclosed space
Eat, drink something warm, empty your bladder, hat + neck gaiter over the nose
Stay where you are, in the open
Three signals: 3 whistle blasts / 3 fires / 3 flashes, repeat
Mirror flashes across the horizon in series, even "into nowhere"
Ground sign V (need help) / X (need medical help), 3+ m in size, from contrasting material
Both arms up when you see a plane/helicopter
A call "I'm in trouble, send money" → code word; if they don't say it — hang up, call back on a known number
An evacuation order/"corridor" → confirmed by two official sources?
Satnav contradicts your eyes → compass, paper map, road signs
I do not post: strike locations, air defence activity, shelters, queues, "house empty"; geotags off
Cash for 2 weeks — yes; paper copies of documents — yes
Before an enemy checkpoint: phone "clean", copies in the cloud

cells: Free, from any network, with zero balance; Ukraine and the whole EU. Without a SIM — not everywhere (Germany, France, Belgium will not connect)
State Emergency Service (DSNS): fire, collapsed buildings, explosive objects, chemicals
Say: what happened, how many people, address, landmark
Smell of gas: do not switch on lights, get out, call from outside
Regional military administration, Point of Invincibility, housing maintenance office, water utility, a neighbour who is a medic

intro.text: Preparation does not need a lot of money — it needs 30 small steps, one a day. Tick off what you have done. After day 30, repeat the checks every 6 months (when the clocks change).

sections.title: Week 1: the plan and the essentials

cells: Family council: discuss scenarios, assign roles (sec. 1.5). Appoint a contact go-between in another city or country
Three meeting points (near home, in the district, outside the city) — write down the addresses. Agree on a family code word (ch. 18)
Identify the "two-wall zone" at home (sec. 3.2), clear it, put water, a torch and a sleeping mat there. Find the nearest shelter and walk to it
Copies of all documents: paper ones in a plastic sleeve + scans on a USB stick and in the cloud. A list of phone numbers on paper for everyone
A supply of regular medicines for 30+ days; a note with diagnoses and doses; discuss a "just in case" first aid kit with your doctor (sec. 7.16)
A battery radio; write down on paper the frequencies of Ukrainian Radio for your region, the official channels of the regional military administration and DSNS — the two-source rule (ch. 18)
Check: does everyone know by heart the go-between's phone number and the address of meeting point No. 2? Children — a rhyme with "name, parents, address, phone"
Stocktake at home: what from the list in sec. 2.2 you already have (usually 60–70%)
Buy what is missing from the "documents, water, light" group: water filter/tablets, head torch, batteries, whistle
First aid kit: certified tourniquet, bandages, haemostatic agent, rehydration salts, antiseptic (sec. 7.16)
Clothing and sleeping gear into the go-bag: emergency foil blankets ×2, socks, rain poncho, hat. A sit-mat
Pack the go-bag completely, weigh it (up to 20% of body weight), put it by the exit. Children — their own small backpacks
A 2-week home food supply according to the table in sec. 2.5: buy more cereals, tinned food, oil, salt, sugar; start rotation
Final weigh-in and a "out the door in 2 minutes" go-bag test with the whole family — as a timed game
Water: store 20–30 l of drinking water per person (2 weeks, sec. 2.5) in bottles or jerrycans, label with the date; plain bleach ("Білизна") without additives for disinfection (sec. 8.4)
Label the gas and water valves, show all adults and teenagers the circuit breakers. Fire extinguisher and smoke detector (sec. 2.6)
Windows: protective film or a grid of tape over the whole area in the room where you sleep; the bed more than 2 m from the window (sec. 2.6)
Energy: 2 charged power banks; gas burner + 4–6 canisters; candles in jars. If possible — a solar panel + portable power station (sec. 20.3)
Cash in small notes for 2–4 weeks, split between three places; part of it in foreign currency (sec. 17.4)
Car (if you have one): the "tank at least half full" rule, assemble the car kit (sec. 26.2). No car — learn the evacuation timetable and points, arrange with a neighbour who has a car
Evacuation routes: draw 3 options on a paper map, write them out in words; download offline maps to your phone (sec. 26.1, ch. 18)
Training: 30 min on the tourniquet and pressure on a wound — practise applying it to a partner's leg without tightening the windlass (sec. 7.2). Sign up for a first aid course
CPR — practise compressions on a pillow on the floor or on a manikin (do not practise on people — neither compressions nor rescue breaths); recovery position — on a partner (sec. 7.4, 7.7)
Drones: go over the rules from sec. 4.2–4.5 with your family; with children — the game "it buzzes — get under a roof"; find the "roofs" along your daily routes
Knots: figure-eight, bowline, reef knot, clove hitch — 20 times each, then with your eyes closed (ch. 15)
Disinfect 1 l of water with chlorine following the recipe and drink it; light a fire or burner with one match (sec. 8.4, 10.4)
Neighbours: get to know them, exchange phone numbers, find out who is a medic or has a car or generator (sec. 17.5). Find the nearest Point of Invincibility (sec. 20.5)
Digital hygiene: turn off geotags, make backups, remove unnecessary things from your phone, check that your social media do not reveal your home and supplies (ch. 18)
Special needs: a plan for elderly or sick people, animals, babies (ch. 22). A "search" folder with a photo of each person (sec. 17.7)
Full rehearsal: alert → two-wall zone → "evacuation" on foot with go-bags to meeting point No. 1. Debrief: what was forgotten. Calendar: next check in 6 months
Go-bag: a backpack with the minimum for 72 hours of self-sufficiency, packed in advance (ch. 2)
The survival minimum you always have on you (sec. 2.4)
Two-wall rule: at least two load-bearing walls between you and the street (sec. 3.2)
KAB, guided aerial bomb: a high-powered guided bomb; only an underground shelter protects against it (sec. 3.1)
FPV drone: a kamikaze drone controlled by an operator with a "first-person view"; hunts individual targets (ch. 4)
Drop: a drone that hovers and drops a grenade or mine (ch. 4)
Order of trauma care: massive bleeding → airway → respiration → circulation → hypothermia (sec. 7.1)
Tourniquet: a strap with a windlass for fully stopping arterial bleeding (sec. 7.2)
Wound packing: tightly filling a deep wound with a bandage under pressure (sec. 7.2)
CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation: compressions + rescue breaths (sec. 7.7)
Rehydration: restoring water and salts in dehydration (sec. 7.10)
Crush syndrome: deadly poisoning when a limb that was crushed for a long time is released (sec. 3.5)
Disinfecting water with sunlight in PET bottles (sec. 8.4)
Tinder / kindling: material that catches from a spark / small fuel to get the fire going (sec. 10.1)
Dakota fire hole: a concealed fire made of two connected pits (sec. 10.3)
Azimuth: direction of travel in degrees from north (sec. 13.1)
GPS spoofing: a faked GPS signal, so the satnav shows a false location (sec. 13.1, ch. 18)
Standing part / working end: the long part of the rope / the end used to tie the knot (sec. 15.1)
Grey man: the strategy of staying inconspicuous in a crisis (sec. 17.1)
Code word: a family password for checking calls "from relatives" (ch. 18)
Point of Invincibility: a place to get warm, charge devices and get a connection during a blackout (sec. 20.5)
Aftershock: a repeat tremor after an earthquake (sec. 19.2)
Clamp: a field store for the harvest under straw and earth (sec. 25.3)

intro.text: Millions of Ukrainians live in Europe, and a crisis can catch them there: a storm, a flood, a blackout, a terrorist attack, an escalation. Most rules in this book work everywhere, but the numbers, the warning system and the shelters are different. This page is about the differences.

cells: **112** — everywhere, free, from any network (also via another operator and with zero credit); but in Germany a call to 112 does NOT go through without an active SIM card inserted (the same in France, Belgium, Bulgaria, Romania, Slovenia) — keep a working SIM in your backup phone; in many countries operators also speak English (not guaranteed)
112 — fire brigade and ambulance; **110** — police; 116117 — on-call doctor (non-emergency)
Cell Broadcast (EU-Alert) in most countries: a loud signal and text without any app; in Poland — SMS from RCB
Cell Broadcast + the apps **NINA** (official, BBK) and **KATWARN**; sirens (being restored in many cities)
**Warntag** — a nationwide test of sirens and warnings every year in September: don't be alarmed
Regional ARD stations (e.g. Bayern 1, WDR 2) — official announcements in a crisis; write the frequencies in Appendix C

blocks.text: Install NINA/KATWARN (or the country's equivalent) right after arriving and allow notifications. Siren signals in Germany: a rising and falling tone for 1 min — danger, turn on the radio; a steady tone for 1 min — all clear.

sections.title: Shelters: almost none — prepare your own

items.text: Public bomb shelters in Germany and most of the EU have mostly been decommissioned; in a crisis people rely on their own basements, underground car parks, the metro (where there is one).
The two-wall rule (chapter 3) works here too: identify your zone in the flat and the building's basement (Keller) in advance — check that you have access and two exits.
For a storm or tornado — a basement or an inner room on the lowest floor (chapter 19); for a flood (the Rhine, Ahr, Elbe valleys) — upper floors and a route to high ground (sec. 19.1, 19.7).

In case of an accident at a nuclear power plant in a neighbouring country — the procedure in chapter 6; in Germany potassium iodide is handed out by local authorities after an announcement (do not buy or take it in advance).

sections.title: Home supplies as recommended by BBK (the German Federal Office of Civil Protection)

items.text: No-cook food for **10 days** for each person; water — **2 l per person per day** (20 l for 10 days; this is only for drinking and cold food preparation — including hygiene count 4 l, sec. 2.5)
Battery or wind-up radio, torches, candles, spare batteries
First aid kit, personal medicines for 2+ weeks, disinfectant
Cash (card terminals do not work during a blackout), copies of documents in an "emergency folder" (Notfallmappe)
Burner/camping stove, matches, hygiene supplies for 2 weeks

blocks.text: This is the official BBK recommendation for every family in Germany (minimum — 3 days, goal — 10), not "paranoia". The go-bag list in chapter 2 of this book covers it completely.

items.text: Keep together: international passport, residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel/Fiktionsbescheinigung), address registration (Meldebescheinigung), health insurance (card), children's birth certificates, pet passports with microchip and rabies vaccination; copies — in the cloud and with relatives.
Changing address or leaving for a long time — inform the foreigners' office (Ausländerbehörde) and the Jobcenter/Sozialamt, otherwise you lose payments and status.

The Ukrainian consulate for your district: write its address and phone number in Appendix C. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs consular hotline and the consulate's website — for lost documents and evacuation.
Cash in euros for 1–2 weeks; a Ukrainian bank card may not work during a cyberattack (chapter 18) — have a local bank card.
Medical care: in a crisis help is given even without insurance (112, the emergency department — Notaufnahme); poisoning — the regional Giftnotruf (write down the number for your federal state).

**Blackout:** the European grid is resilient, but cascading outages (Iberia 2025) showed that 8–12 hours without electricity, communications, banking and water in tall buildings is a reality. What to do — chapter 20; pumps in high-rise buildings stop, so a water supply is essential.
**Floods and storms** (Ahr valley 2021, downpours 2024): over the last 5–10 years such events have become more frequent; know your flood zone from your federal state's website (Hochwasserkarten).
**Heat of 40°+** in cities without air conditioning is the main cause of summer deaths in Europe: the rules in sec. 19.5.

**Sabotage and hybrid attacks:** damage to cables and railways, drone incidents over airports, cyberattacks on hospitals and administrations, disinformation — the rules of chapter 18 work here too; check news against two sources and do not spread panic.
**GPS disruption** in the Baltic, in Poland and in eastern Germany — the satnav may "jump"; keep a paper map in the car.
